regions.ardennes: Belgium and Luxembourg bracket the war in the West. At dawn on 10 May 1940 German glider troops landed on the roof of Fort Eben-Emael, the strongest fort on the Albert Canal, and silenced it within hours; the road into Belgium lay open and the Low Countries fell within weeks. Liberated in September 1944, the Ardennes then became the stage for Hitler's last great gamble in the West. On 16 December 1944 German armies struck thinly held American lines, aiming for the Meuse and Antwerp. Inexperienced regiments were cut off and captured in the Schnee Eifel, Kampfgruppe Peiper murdered prisoners at Baugnez, and St Vith held for five vital days. At Bastogne, where seven main roads meet, the 101st Airborne and armoured units held out under siege until Patton's Third Army broke through on 26 December. On 16 January 1945 the US First and Third Armies met at Houffalize and the Bulge was closed. The offensive used up Germany's last reserves in the West; the cemeteries at Henri-Chapelle, Hamm and Recogne show what it cost.
regions.britain: Britain was the one major European enemy of Germany that was never occupied, and that made it the base from which Western Europe was eventually liberated. In May and June 1940 the Navy, directed from tunnels under Dover Castle, brought more than 330,000 troops home from Dunkirk. That summer RAF Fighter Command, using the radar-and-telephone network built by Sir Hugh Dowding, denied the Luftwaffe the air superiority an invasion needed. The Blitz that followed hit London, Coventry, Liverpool and many other cities from September 1940 to May 1941. Meanwhile Churchill ran the war from underground rooms in Whitehall, codebreakers at Bletchley Park read German Enigma traffic, and a joint Navy and RAF headquarters in Liverpool fought the U-boats to keep the Atlantic supply line open. From 1942 Britain filled with American airmen and soldiers, and on 6 June 1944 the invasion fleet sailed for Normandy from the south coast around Portsmouth. The sites here show the command centres, airfields and scars of a country under siege that became a launch pad.
regions.central: Czechoslovakia was the first country Hitler dismembered without a shot: the Sudetenland was handed over at Munich in September 1938 and Prague was occupied in March 1939, becoming the 'Protectorate of Bohemia and Moravia'. Its arms factories fed the German war effort. In May 1942 two London-trained Czechoslovak soldiers, Jozef Gabčík and Jan Kubiš, ambushed Reinhard Heydrich, head of the Reich Security Main Office and acting Reich Protector, in a Prague suburb; he died on 4 June. The reprisals, including the destruction of Lidice and Ležáky, became a byword for Nazi terror and made Lidice a worldwide symbol. North of Prague the fortress town of Terezín became a ghetto and transit camp from which tens of thousands were sent to Auschwitz and other killing sites. Austria, annexed in March 1938, was part of the Reich throughout the war. At Mauthausen and its satellite camp Gusen near Linz, the SS ran one of the harshest camp complexes of all, working prisoners to death in granite quarries and, from 1944, in underground factories for jet fighters.
regions.dunkirk: In late May 1940 the German thrust through the Ardennes reached the Channel and cut the British Expeditionary Force and much of the French First Army off from the rest of France. The Allies fell back into a shrinking pocket around Dunkirk. Between 26 May and 4 June the Royal Navy, with French ships and hundreds of civilian craft, lifted 338,226 men from the harbour and the beaches in Operation Dynamo, while French divisions held the perimeter and about 40,000 of them were captured when it fell. The army that would fight again in North Africa and Normandy was saved, but almost all its equipment was lost, and the retreat was marked by atrocities such as the Wormhout massacre. After 1940 the same coast became the front line of the German war against Britain: heavy batteries on Cap Gris-Nez shelled Dover, and in the woods inland the Germans poured huge concrete bunkers at Éperlecques and Helfaut to launch V-2 rockets at London. Allied bombing wrecked both before they fired a shot, and the Canadians cleared the coast in September 1944.
regions.east: The Eastern Front was where most of the German army fought and died. Operation Barbarossa opened before dawn on 22 June 1941 at places such as Brest Fortress on the new Soviet border. By September German and Finnish forces had cut Leningrad off; the siege lasted 872 days and starvation killed hundreds of thousands of civilians. Moscow held in the winter of 1941. In the summer of 1942 the Germans drove for the Volga and the Caucasus, and from September to January the 6th Army fought street by street for Stalingrad until it was encircled and destroyed. In July 1943 the German offensive at Kursk, including the clash at Prokhorovka, failed, and the strategic initiative passed for good to the Red Army. Behind the lines, occupied Belarus suffered anti-partisan terror in which whole villages such as Khatyn were burned with their people. These sites explain why the war was won and lost in the east. All of them are in Russia or Belarus, where the UK government currently advises against all travel.
regions.germany-east: By early 1945 the war had come home to the cities where it was planned. Berlin held the machinery of the Nazi state: the Gestapo and SS headquarters, the army offices where the July 1944 plotters failed, and the lakeside villa where officials coordinated the murder of Europe's Jews. Around it lay the concentration camps of Sachsenhausen and Ravensbrück, with Buchenwald and Bergen-Belsen further west, whose liberation in April 1945 showed the world what the regime had done. Allied bombing reached Hamburg in July 1943 and Dresden in February 1945, and Peenemünde on the Baltic coast had produced the V-2 rocket. In April 1945 the Red Army broke through at the Seelow Heights and fought its way into Berlin; on 25 April American and Soviet troops met on the Elbe at Torgau. Hitler killed himself in his bunker on 30 April, the Reichstag fell on 2 May and the Wehrmacht's surrender was signed at Karlshorst on the night of 8–9 May. This region is where the war in Europe ended, and where its causes are best explained.
regions.germany-west: Western and southern Germany holds both ends of the story. Munich was where Hitler's party was born and where it kept its headquarters; Nuremberg staged the vast party rallies of 1933–38 and gave its name to the 1935 race laws; on the Obersalzberg above Berchtesgaden Hitler built a second seat of government where the attack on Poland was planned. Dachau, opened in March 1933, was the first regular concentration camp and the model for the system that followed. The war came back to Germany in autumn 1944. In the Hürtgen Forest, south-east of Aachen, American divisions fought a costly battle from September to December for little ground. In March 1945 the capture of the Ludendorff Bridge at Remagen put US troops across the Rhine before the Germans could organise a defence of the river, and within weeks Allied armies were deep in Bavaria. The story ends where it began: in Nuremberg, where the International Military Tribunal tried the surviving leaders of the regime in Courtroom 600 from November 1945.
regions.italy: The Allies invaded Sicily on 10 July 1943 and the Italian mainland in September. Mussolini fell, Italy changed sides, and Germany occupied the peninsula, including Rome. Field Marshal Kesselring then fought a slow defensive war along a series of fortified lines across the mountains. The strongest, the Gustav Line, was anchored on Monte Cassino, which blocked Highway 6, the inland road to Rome. Four battles were fought there between January and May 1944, while an Allied landing at Anzio on 22 January, meant to outflank the line, was itself hemmed in for four months. Only in May, with Operation Diadem, did the Gustav Line break: French colonial troops crossed the mountains, Polish II Corps took the abbey heights and VI Corps broke out of the Anzio beachhead. US Fifth Army entered Rome on 4 June 1944, two days before D-Day. In occupied Rome, the German security police jailed and tortured opponents in Via Tasso and carried out the Ardeatine Caves massacre. Italy tied down large German forces, but it was a costly, grinding campaign that lasted until May 1945.
regions.mediterranean: Malta lay across the Axis sea route from Italy to North Africa. From the first Italian air raid on 11 June 1940 to the lifting of the siege in November 1942, the island was bombed almost daily, and in March–April 1942 it became the most heavily bombed place on earth. Aircraft and submarines based on Malta sank the ships carrying fuel and supplies to Rommel, so Axis success in the desert depended on neutralising the island. Its people endured under ground in rock shelters, King George VI awarded Malta the George Cross in April 1942, and the tanker Ohio, with the Pedestal convoy, brought fuel in August 1942. In 1943 Malta became the Allied headquarters for the invasion of Sicily. Crete fell the other way. On 20 May 1941 Germany launched Operation Merkur, the first major airborne invasion in history. British, Commonwealth and Greek troops, supported by Cretan civilians, nearly defeated it, but the loss of Maleme airfield allowed reinforcements to fly in. The island fell by 1 June, and German airborne losses were so heavy that Hitler never again used paratroops on such a scale.
regions.netherlands: The Netherlands hoped to stay neutral, as it had in 1914–18. On 10 May 1940 Germany invaded. The Dutch army held the Grebbe Line for three days, but after the Luftwaffe bombed the centre of Rotterdam on 14 May and threatened Utrecht, the country capitulated the next day. Five years of occupation followed. Of roughly 140,000 Jews in the Netherlands, more than 100,000 were deported, most of them through Westerbork, a higher proportion than anywhere else in Western Europe; Anne Frank's hiding place in Amsterdam has become the best-known symbol of that persecution. In September 1944 Operation Market Garden tried to carry the Allies across the great rivers with airborne landings at Eindhoven, Nijmegen and Arnhem. Nijmegen's bridges were taken, but at Arnhem the British 1st Airborne Division was destroyed, and the war in the north-west was not won in 1944. The south was freed that autumn after hard fighting such as Overloon, and the Rhineland battles of early 1945 were launched from Groesbeek, but the western Netherlands endured the 'Hunger Winter' and was liberated only in May 1945. Arnhem, Nijmegen and Groesbeek together make one of the densest clusters of Second World War sites anywhere in Europe.
regions.normandy: On 6 June 1944 the Allies opened the long-awaited second front in the West. Airborne troops landed by night on both flanks: British 6th Airborne east of the Orne, and the US 82nd and 101st Airborne behind Utah Beach. At dawn, American, British and Canadian divisions came ashore on five beaches, Utah, Omaha, Gold, Juno and Sword, after a huge air and naval bombardment. Omaha came close to failure; elsewhere the troops got inland, but Caen, a D-Day objective, held out until July. For ten weeks the campaign became a grinding battle through hedgerow country and around Caen, where British and Canadian attacks drew in most of the German armour. The American breakout at the end of July (Operation Cobra) unhinged the German front, and in August two German armies were largely trapped in the Falaise Pocket. Normandy cost tens of thousands of soldiers' lives and many thousands of French civilians. It decided the war in the West: by the end of August Paris was free and the Germans were in full retreat towards their own border.
regions.norway: Germany invaded Norway on 9 April 1940 to secure the iron-ore route from Sweden through the ice-free port of Narvik and to gain naval and air bases on the Atlantic. German destroyers carried General Eduard Dietl's mountain troops into Ofotfjord, sinking the Norwegian coastal defence ships Eidsvold and Norge. The Royal Navy struck back in two battles at Narvik on 10 and 13 April, destroying the German destroyer force there, and Norwegian, French, Polish and British troops retook the town on 28 May. It was the first Allied land victory of the war, but the collapse in France forced the Allies to leave in early June, and Norway capitulated on 10 June. Five years of occupation followed under Reichskommissar Terboven and Vidkun Quisling's collaborationist government. Norwegians built a resistance movement linked to London, and in February 1943 Norwegian commandos trained by SOE sabotaged the heavy-water plant at Vemork, damaging German nuclear research. German forces in Norway, around 350,000 strong by 1945, were tied down until the surrender in May 1945.
regions.paris-east: Eastern France is where the war in the west was lost in 1940 and formally ended in 1945. The French put their faith in the Maginot Line in Alsace and Lorraine, but in May 1940 Guderian's panzers came through the Ardennes and crossed the Meuse at Sedan, splitting the Allied armies within days. On 22 June 1940 Hitler made France sign an armistice in the same railway carriage, in the same forest glade at Compiègne, where Germany had signed in 1918. The forts of the Maginot Line, still unbeaten, surrendered under its terms. Four years of occupation followed: resistance fighters and hostages were shot at Mont-Valérien, around 76,000 Jews were deported from France, and in the Vosges the SS ran Natzweiler-Struthof, the only concentration camp on French soil. Paris rose against the Germans in August 1944 and was liberated by Leclerc's French armour on 25 August. On 7 May 1945, in a schoolhouse in Reims that served as Eisenhower's headquarters, General Jodl signed Germany's unconditional surrender.
regions.poland: The war in Europe began in Poland. At dawn on 1 September 1939 German forces attacked Westerplatte and the Polish Post Office in the Free City of Danzig, and on 17 September the Soviet Union invaded from the east. Poland was defeated within five weeks but never formally surrendered: a government in exile fought on, and inside the country the Home Army grew into one of Europe's largest underground forces. Poland then became the centre of Nazi Germany's racial war. Most of the six million Jews murdered in the Holocaust died on occupied Polish soil, at Auschwitz-Birkenau, Treblinka, Bełżec, Sobibór, Majdanek and in ghettos and shooting pits, alongside millions of non-Jewish Polish civilians. Warsaw rose twice: the Jewish ghetto in April 1943 and the Home Army in August 1944, and both risings were crushed and the city systematically destroyed. Hitler ran the war in the East from the Wolf's Lair in East Prussia, where the July 1944 bomb plot failed. The Red Army's advance in 1944–45 liberated the camps but replaced German occupation with Soviet control. Visiting here is mostly about memory: the camp sites are cemeteries and should be treated as such.
regions.west-france: The fall of France in June 1940 handed Germany the Atlantic ports of Brittany and the Loire. From July 1940 U-boats sailed from Lorient, cutting days off every patrol, and Dönitz ran the wolf packs from a villa facing the harbour. The Organisation Todt then built enormous concrete pens at Brest, Lorient and Saint-Nazaire, with roofs so thick that Allied bombs could not break them. Bombing instead flattened the towns around them. In March 1942 British commandos rammed the great dry dock at Saint-Nazaire so that the battleship Tirpitz would have nowhere on the Atlantic coast to be repaired. After D-Day the Americans fought a costly siege for Brest, which they took in ruins in September 1944, while the Germans held Lorient and Saint-Nazaire as fortresses until May 1945. Inland, on 10 June 1944, an SS company destroyed the village of Oradour-sur-Glane and killed nearly all its people; its ruins were left untouched as a national memorial.

stops.name: Fort Eben-Emael
stops.text: Built in 1931–35 above the Caestert cutting of the Albert Canal, Eben-Emael was the largest fort of the Fortified Position of Liège, armed with 120 mm, 75 mm and 60 mm guns in turrets and casemates and linked by over 4 km of galleries. At dawn on 10 May 1940 Assault Group Granit of Sturmabteilung Koch, 85 men in 11 DFS 230 gliders, set out for its roof. Nine landed; Oberleutnant Rudolf Witzig's tow rope snapped, so Oberfeldwebel Helmut Wenzel took charge. Shaped charges and a flamethrower knocked out guns and cupolas while other groups seized the Veldwezelt and Vroenhoven bridges. The garrison surrendered at 12:30 on 11 May; Belgian losses were 23 killed and 59 wounded, Granit's 6 killed.
stops.look: The fort is still Belgian Army property. Inside are the underground barracks, a museum, a 180° film of the attack and long, cold galleries. Above ground you can walk the grassed roof between the blocks, see casemates and cupolas holed by German charges, and look down into the canal cutting.
stops.plan: Open mid-February to early January on set days, usually Tuesday–Sunday 10:00–17:00, last entry 15:00; check the opening calendar. Guided tours of a combat bunker are best booked online. Galleries stay at 11 °C and involve many stairs; bunkers are not wheelchair accessible.
stops.disputed: Garrison figures vary: about 1,200 on strength but perhaps 750 present on 10 May (Witzig's figure), while some books give 1,185 or even 2,000. Wikipedia's fort article gives the glider force as both 85 and 78 men.

aar.ev: German glider troops land on the fort's roof and blast its guns with shaped charges.
aar.st: At dawn on 10 May 1940, 85 men of Assault Group Granit flew to Eben-Emael in eleven gliders and nine landed on the roof. Shaped charges and a flamethrower knocked out the guns and cupolas, and the garrison surrendered at 12:30 the next day. Today you can explore the cold galleries, underground barracks and museum, then walk the roof past cupolas holed by the German charges.

q.t: Who led Assault Group Granit on the roof for most of the attack?
q.x: Witzig's glider snapped its tow rope and came down in Germany, so Oberfeldwebel Helmut Wenzel led on the roof until Witzig arrived in a replacement glider.

aar.rem: A few dozen glider troops with shaped charges silenced Belgium's strongest fort and opened the road into the Low Countries.

stops.notes: Coordinates are for the Belgian war memorial at the entrance on Rue du Fort (Block 1). French Wikipedia gives the fort as 50°47′49″N 5°40′47″E, i.e. the centre of the roof area about 500 m east. Ticket prices are not shown on the home page; check the visit page.

stops.name: Bastogne War Museum
stops.text: Opened on 21 March 2014 on the site of the former Bastogne Historical Center, the museum tells the story of the Battle of the Bulge from its origins to its aftermath. Bastogne mattered because all seven main roads through the central Ardennes met there. The 101st Airborne Division arrived on 19 December 1944 and, with Combat Command B of the 10th Armored Division and a scratch force of stragglers called Team SNAFU, held the town after Lüttwitz's XLVII Panzer Corps cut the roads on 20–21 December. The exhibition follows four fictional characters, an American paratrooper, a German Volksgrenadier officer, a Bastogne teacher and a 13-year-old boy, through the siege, with three immersive shows along the way.
stops.look: A long chronological walk-through with audio guide: original weapons, uniforms and vehicles, three immersive shows including a cellar scene under bombing, and near the end a restored 11th Armored Division tank stopped on 30 December 1944. The Mardasson Memorial stands next door.
stops.plan: Open daily 09:30–18:00 in October 2026. Tickets are sold online in time slots; booking ahead is advised in summer and around the December anniversaries. The ticket also covers the Bois Jacques Battlefield trail. Allow at least two hours. Check the website for prices.

aar.ev: The 101st Airborne Division arrives to hold Bastogne, where seven main roads meet.
aar.st: Bastogne mattered because all seven main roads through the central Ardennes met there. The 101st Airborne arrived on 19 December 1944 and, with armour and stragglers, held the town after German forces cut the roads on 20–21 December. Today a long walk-through with audio guide shows weapons, uniforms and vehicles, three immersive shows, and a restored 11th Armored Division tank near the end.

q.t: Why was Bastogne so important to both sides in December 1944?
o: It held the main US fuel depot
It was the headquarters of US First Army
All seven main roads in the area met there
q.x: Bastogne was the road hub of the central Ardennes: all seven main roads converged on it, so the Germans needed it to keep their advance moving.

aar.rem: Bastogne was fought over because of its roads: whoever held the town controlled movement across the central Ardennes.

stops.notes: TracesOfWar and uswarmemorials.org give near-identical coordinates for the museum and Mardasson hill; the point is the museum building. Prices were not readable on the site in October 2026.

stops.name: Mardasson Memorial, Bastogne
stops.coord_src: https://www.uswarmemorials.org/html/site_details.php?SiteID=185 ; corrected after GPS check: OSM: Battle of the Bulge Monument
stops.text: The memorial stands on Mardasson hill, chosen partly because it lies on the divide between the Meuse and Rhine basins and looks over the ground held during the siege. Earth from the site was presented to President Truman on 4 July 1946. Designed by the Belgian architect Georges Dedoyard, the memorial was inaugurated on 16 July 1950 in the presence of Prince Baudouin and General Anthony McAuliffe. It is a five-pointed star 12 m high with 31 m sides, carrying the names of the then 48 US states and, on its pillars, the history of the battle and the main American units. In 2020 the Belgian state handed its management to the American Battle Monuments Commission.
stops.look: Climb the spiral stairs to the walkway on top for a panorama of the siege perimeter. Read the ten stone panels describing the battle and the Latin dedication from the Belgian people, then go down to the crypt with three altars and mosaics by Fernand Léger.
stops.plan: Open-air memorial beside the Bastogne War Museum, free, with shared parking. Run since 2020 by the American Battle Monuments Commission, which now calls it the Battle of the Bulge Monument. Crypt access may be limited; check before you go.

aar.ev: Belgium dedicates a star-shaped memorial to the Americans who fought in the Battle of the Bulge.
aar.st: Designed by Georges Dedoyard, the Mardasson Memorial was inaugurated on 16 July 1950 with General McAuliffe present. The five-pointed star carries the names of the then 48 US states and, on its pillars, the history of the battle and the main American units. Today you can climb to the walkway for a view over the siege perimeter and visit the crypt with Fernand Léger's mosaics.
aar.rem: The star shape recalls the American Army emblem; the walkway on top shows the ground the defenders held around Bastogne.

stops.notes: No source opened gave coordinates for the star itself: the uswarmemorials.org point is for 'Mardasson Hill' and is effectively at the museum (about 100–200 m from the memorial). Editor may wish to refine with ABMC data (abmc.gov could not be fetched). ABMC has renamed it the Battle of the Bulge Monument; consider showing both names.

stops.name: Bastogne Barracks (McAuliffe's HQ)
stops.coord_src: https://www.tracesofwar.com/sights/8359/Bastogne-Barracks-Headquarter-Gen-McAuliffe.htm ; corrected after GPS check: OSM: Bastogne Barracks museum
stops.text: In December 1944 the Heintz Barracks on the La Roche road housed the headquarters of the 101st Airborne Division. With its commander, Maxwell Taylor, away, the division was led by Brigadier General Anthony McAuliffe. On 22 December General Heinrich von Lüttwitz of XLVII Panzer Corps sent a written demand for surrender; McAuliffe's reply was 'NUTS!'. Bad weather prevented air resupply until 23 December, and Patton's Third Army reached the town from Assenois on 26 December. The barracks remained a Belgian Army site and since 2010 has been an interpretation centre, now run by the War Heritage Institute, with a workshop restoring armoured vehicles from the national collection.
stops.look: Visits take you to the 'Nuts' cellar, where McAuliffe's headquarters is reconstructed, then through renovated halls of Second World War vehicles and equipment. You may see restorers at work in the vehicle workshop and, on some days, engines being run.
stops.plan: Tuesday–Sunday 09:00–17:00; closed Mondays and 1 Jan, 1 May, 1 Nov, 25 Dec. Adults €12, ages 6–18 and students €9, card only; free from 13:00 on the first Wednesday of the month. Guided group tours must be booked three weeks ahead. Check the website before you go.
stops.disputed: The barracks is spelled Heintz in most sources but Heinz in some veterans' material.

aar.ev: McAuliffe answers a German demand to surrender Bastogne with one word: 'NUTS!'
aar.st: In December 1944 the Heintz Barracks housed the headquarters of the 101st Airborne, led by Brigadier General Anthony McAuliffe. On 22 December General von Lüttwitz sent a written demand for surrender, and McAuliffe replied 'NUTS!'. Patton's Third Army reached the town on 26 December. Today visits lead to the reconstructed 'Nuts' cellar and halls of restored vehicles, with restorers often at work in the workshop.

q.t: What did McAuliffe reply to the German surrender demand on 22 December?
q.x: McAuliffe's written reply to General von Lüttwitz was the single word 'NUTS!'. Patton's Third Army broke through to the town four days later.

aar.rem: The 101st Airborne's headquarters was here, in an ordinary army barracks on the La Roche road.

stops.notes: Address given as Rue de La Roche 40 (365.be, Liberation Route) and 26 (TracesOfWar). The 365.be listing showed a one-off closure on 19 Oct 2026. Older sources say free entry; current pricing is from 365.be (October 2026).

stops.name: Bois Jacques foxholes, Foy
stops.text: During the siege, Easy Company, 2nd Battalion, 506th Parachute Infantry Regiment, 101st Airborne Division, held foxholes in the Bois Jacques as part of the Bastogne perimeter, facing German-held Foy. The men endured snow, shortages and German tree bursts that showered splinters and shrapnel into their holes. On 24 December about 45 Germans attacked the position and were beaten off, for one American casualty. On 13 January 1945 the company attacked out of the wood to retake Foy. Their story became widely known through Stephen E. Ambrose's book Band of Brothers and the television series. A memorial on the Bizory–Foy road honours the company and 14 of its men killed in the area.
stops.look: From the Easy Company memorial on the Bizory–Foy road, paths lead into the managed pine wood where the hollows of foxholes are still visible. Stay on the paths and leave anything you find. Look out across the open ground towards Foy, which the company attacked in January 1945.
stops.plan: Public woodland, free and open at all times; park near the memorial. The Bastogne War Museum's Bois Jacques Battlefield trail, with six geolocated 360° videos in an app, is included in a museum ticket. Wear boots outside summer.
stops.disputed: The memorial text says Easy Company dug in on 18 December, but the 101st Airborne only reached Bastogne on 19 December; the line was probably occupied a day or two later.

aar.ev: Easy Company climbs out of its frozen foxholes and attacks Foy.
aar.st: Easy Company of the 506th Parachute Infantry held foxholes in the Bois Jacques through the siege, under snow and German tree bursts. On 24 December they beat off an attack by about 45 Germans, and on 13 January 1945 they attacked out of the wood to retake Foy. Today paths from the Easy Company memorial lead into the pine wood, where the hollows of foxholes are still visible.

q.t: What made German shelling in the Bois Jacques so dangerous?
o: Shells burst in the treetops and showered splinters into the foxholes
It came from railway guns at Antwerp
q.x: Tree bursts exploded in the canopy and sprayed wood splinters and shrapnel down into the foxholes, so even dug-in men were exposed.

aar.rem: These shallow hollows were home to the men of Band of Brothers for most of the siege of Bastogne.

stops.notes: Coordinates are the Easy Company memorial on the Bizory–Foy road, beside the wood; the foxholes extend through the wood behind. TracesOfWar also lists a 'Memorial Battle of the Bulge' in the Bois Jacques at 50.044602, 5.749298. The woods are actively managed for timber.

stops.name: December 44 Historical Museum, La Gleize
stops.text: Kampfgruppe Peiper, the armoured spearhead drawn from the 1st SS Panzer Division, drove west from 16 December 1944 towards the Meuse. Without supplies or contact with other German units, it was stopped in the Amblève valley. American attacks at Stoumont forced its remnants back to La Gleize, where they were almost trapped; on 21 December they captured Hal McCown, commander of 2nd Battalion, 119th Infantry. Short of fuel and with heavy losses, Joachim Peiper abandoned his vehicles on 24 December and led his remaining men out on foot, leaving wounded and prisoners behind. By his own account 717 men got back out of 3,000. The village museum, renovated in 2013, is devoted to these events.
stops.look: On the square stands Tiger II number 213, abandoned in December 1944, its broken gun barrel repaired in 1972. Inside the museum are 17 dioramas, vehicles and guns, Peiper's map case and many objects found around La Gleize. The church opposite was badly damaged in 1944 and rebuilt.
stops.plan: Private museum on the village square opposite the church. Opening is seasonal and could not be checked online (the site blocks automated reading); check december44.com before you go. The Tiger II outside can be seen at any time, free.
stops.disputed: Peiper's figure of 717 survivors out of 3,000 is his own testimony; the battle group's strength is variously given, up to 4,800 men. The Tiger is said to have been saved from scrapping by a local woman's gift of a bottle of cognac to the Americans, a local story rather than a documented fact.

aar.ev: Trapped and out of fuel, Peiper's men abandon their tanks and slip away on foot.
aar.st: Kampfgruppe Peiper, the SS spearhead of the offensive, was stopped in the Amblève valley and forced back to La Gleize. Short of fuel and with heavy losses, Peiper abandoned his vehicles on 24 December and led his remaining men out on foot, leaving the wounded and American prisoners behind. Today Tiger II number 213 stands on the square, and the museum holds dioramas, vehicles and Peiper's map case.

q.t: How did Peiper's battle group leave La Gleize on 24 December?
q.x: Out of fuel and nearly surrounded, Peiper abandoned his vehicles and led his remaining men out on foot, leaving wounded and American prisoners behind.

aar.rem: The most powerful German spearhead of the offensive ended in this small village, its tanks left behind for lack of fuel.

stops.notes: Tiger II on the square: TracesOfWar 50.410113, 5.846017. december44.com could not be read (robots block); opening days unverified.

stops.name: Baugnez: Malmedy massacre memorial
stops.text: On 17 December 1944 the vanguard of Kampfgruppe Peiper met a convoy of Battery B, 285th Field Artillery Observation Battalion, at the Baugnez crossroads south-east of Malmedy. After a brief fight the Americans surrendered and were assembled in a field beside the road, where they were machine-gunned; many were then shot in the head. Eighty-four prisoners died. Some feigned death or ran, and 43 survivors reached American-held Malmedy, spreading word of the killings. At the Dachau trials in 1946, 73 men were convicted and 43 sentenced to death, Peiper among them. No death sentence was carried out, and Peiper was paroled in December 1956.
stops.look: A low stone wall at the junction carries a plaque explaining the events and stones naming the dead. The field where the prisoners were assembled and shot lies beside the road. Across the junction stands the building of the former Baugnez 44 museum.
stops.plan: Roadside memorial, free and accessible at all times; take care at the busy N62/N632 junction. The Baugnez 44 Historical Center opposite was reported closed in 2023 and its old web address now shows unrelated content, so do not plan on visiting it.
stops.disputed: Wikipedia's Baugnez article speaks of 'more than 70' victims and 72 stones in the wall, while the memorial and most accounts give 84 dead. Who gave the order to fire was never established at the trial; witnesses named Werner Poetschke, while Peiper bears command responsibility.

aar.ev: SS troops machine-gun captured American artillerymen in a field at the Baugnez crossroads.
aar.st: On 17 December 1944 the vanguard of Kampfgruppe Peiper overran a convoy of Battery B, 285th Field Artillery Observation Battalion, at this crossroads. The Americans surrendered, were assembled in a field and machine-gunned; 43 survivors reached Malmedy and spread the news. Today a low stone wall at the junction carries a plaque and stones naming the dead, beside the field where they were shot.
aar.rem: Word of the killings spread fast and hardened American attitudes towards the SS for the rest of the battle.

stops.notes: Stop renamed: the Baugnez 44 Historical Center (Route de Luxembourg 10) closed (BRF report, 26 Feb 2023); Malmedy planned to buy part of the collection for a museum in the Malmundarium, status unconfirmed. baugnez44.be now hosts an unrelated online-casino page: do not link to it. Wikipedia gives the massacre site as 50.40389, 6.0661944, about 40 m from the memorial.

stops.name: St Vith
stops.text: St Vith, a German-speaking town transferred to Belgium in 1925, controlled a road junction the German plan expected to take by 18:00 on 17 December 1944. Instead Brigadier General Bruce Clarke's Combat Command B of the 7th Armored Division, with the 424th Infantry of the 106th Division, CCB of the 9th Armored Division and the 112th Infantry, held the approaches until 21 December, wrecking the German timetable. Meanwhile the 106th's 422nd and 423rd Infantry, cut off in the Schnee Eifel, surrendered on 19 December, about 7,000 men. American and RAF bombers destroyed the town on 25–26 December, and American forces retook it on 23 January 1945.
stops.look: Almost nothing pre-war survived except the Büchel Tower. Look for the 106th Infantry Division monument on Klosterstrasse, the 2nd Infantry Division memorial and the plaques in the park on Pulverstrasse. The Prümerberg, just east of the town, was the last defensive line.
stops.plan: A town stop; the memorials are outdoors and free. Combine with the 106th Division POW memorial at Schönberg and the 168th Engineer Combat Battalion memorial on the Prümerberg. Ask the local tourist office for walking routes.

aar.ev: After five days' defence, American armour gives up St Vith and withdraws west.
aar.st: The German plan expected to take St Vith by the evening of 17 December 1944. Clarke's armour and the remnants of the 106th Division held the approaches until 21 December, wrecking the timetable, while two cut-off regiments surrendered in the Schnee Eifel. Today almost nothing pre-war survives except the Büchel Tower, but memorials to the 106th and 2nd Infantry Divisions stand in the town.

q.t: By when did the German plan expect to capture St Vith?
q.x: The Germans planned to take St Vith by 18:00 on 17 December. The Americans held it until 21 December, a serious blow to the German timetable.

aar.rem: Holding a road junction for four extra days could matter as much as winning a battle.

stops.notes: Coordinates are the 106th Infantry Division monument (Klosterstrasse) as a town reference point. The German-speaking Community; signage mainly in German.

stops.name: Houffalize and its Panther tank
stops.text: Houffalize, on the Ourthe north of Bastogne, was taken by the 116th Panzer Division on 19 December 1944 and became a crossroads for German supply columns. On the night of 5–6 January 1945 about ninety RAF Lancasters flattened the town to block it. The Germans withdrew on 15 January, and on 16 January the US First Army, attacking from the north, and the Third Army from the south met at Houffalize, closing the Bulge. The Panther now on display, originally numbered 111, had fought in Normandy, the Netherlands and the Hürtgen Forest. It overturned into the Ourthe from a bridge, killing its five crew, was pulled out in 1948 and restored in 2023.
stops.look: The restored Panther Ausf. G stands on Square Saint-Pair by the Bastogne road, with about a dozen information panels and a small exhibition in a reconstructed period barracks. Walk to the Ourthe bridge on the road to La Roche, where the tank fell.
stops.plan: The tank and panels can be seen at any time, free. The small exhibition has limited opening; contact the Houffalize tourist office (+32 61 28 81 16) or check coeurdelardenne.be before you go.
stops.disputed: Accounts differ on how the Panther ended up in the river: a driver's error or the partial collapse of the bridge. One source says the crew's bodies were recovered in 1947, another that the tank was raised by Namur engineers on 20 September 1948.
links: The Panther tank of Houffalize (Europe Remembers)

aar.ev: American armies from north and south meet at Houffalize, closing the Bulge.
aar.st: Taken by the 116th Panzer Division on 19 December 1944, Houffalize was flattened by RAF Lancasters on the night of 5–6 January 1945. On 16 January the US First and Third Armies met here, closing the Bulge. Today a restored Panther, which overturned into the Ourthe from a bridge, stands on Square Saint-Pair with information panels and a small exhibition.

q.t: What happened at Houffalize on 16 January 1945?
o: German paratroopers landed to hold the bridge
The US First and Third Armies met, closing the Bulge
q.x: On 16 January 1945 the First Army from the north and the Third Army from the south linked up at Houffalize. The RAF raid came ten days earlier.

aar.rem: Where the two American armies met, the Bulge was closed: Houffalize marks the end of the German salient.

stops.notes: Coordinates are the tank on Square Saint-Pair (Rue de Bastogne); Europe Remembers gives the address as Place Roi Albert. The tank is not at the spot where it fell (the Ourthe bridge on Rue de la Roche).

stops.name: Recogne German war cemetery
stops.text: The US Army opened a cemetery at Recogne, north of Bastogne, on 4 February 1945, burying about 2,700 Americans and over 3,000 Germans there. The American dead were later moved to Henri-Chapelle or repatriated, and the Belgian authorities concentrated German graves from field burials and local cemeteries here or at Lommel. Recogne now holds 6,807 German dead, most killed around Bastogne in the Battle of the Bulge, together with men who died in 1940 or during the occupation. The cemetery passed to the German War Graves Commission (Volksbund) in the 1950s and reopened to the public in 1960 after refurbishment.
stops.look: Beyond the entrance building, rows of low grey stone crosses stand on lawn among trees. Compare its subdued atmosphere with the white headstones and open lawns of the American cemeteries at Henri-Chapelle and Hamm.
stops.plan: Open-air cemetery, free to visit, just off the N30 about 4 km north of Bastogne. Opening arrangements could not be checked on the Volksbund website; check before you go.
stops.disputed: Sources differ on when the American dead were moved: Wikipedia says 1945–46, TracesOfWar summer 1948.

aar.ev: The US Army opens a cemetery at Recogne, burying American and German dead side by side.
aar.st: The US Army opened a cemetery at Recogne on 4 February 1945, burying about 2,700 Americans and over 3,000 Germans. The Americans were later moved to Henri-Chapelle or repatriated, and German graves from across the region were brought here. Today 6,807 German dead lie in rows of low grey stone crosses on lawn among trees, in the care of the Volksbund.
aar.rem: Recogne began as a shared American and German burial ground before becoming a German war cemetery.

stops.notes: The 'look' detail on stone crosses is from general knowledge of Volksbund cemeteries and was not confirmed on a source opened for this stop; the Volksbund page could not be fetched. Wikipedia gives 50.04833, 5.74083, matching TracesOfWar.

stops.name: Henri-Chapelle American Cemetery
stops.text: Troops of the US 1st Infantry Division liberated this area on 12 September 1944, and a temporary cemetery opened a few hundred metres to the north on 28 September. The permanent cemetery, dedicated in 1960, covers 57 acres on a ridge near Hombourg. It holds 7,992 American dead, 94 of them unknown, most killed in the Battle of the Bulge or the advance into Germany in 1944–45, together with airmen lost over the region. A colonnade lists 450 missing; bronze rosettes mark those since found and identified. In 1947 the first repatriation of American war dead to the United States began here.
stops.look: Headstones curve across a sloping lawn facing the memorial, with a road running through the site. The chapel and map room show carved granite maps of the American advance, the colonnade carries the names of the missing, and the Angel of Peace statue stands nearby.
stops.plan: Free. American Battle Monuments Commission cemeteries normally open daily 09:00–17:00, closed 25 December and 1 January; the ABMC website could not be checked, so confirm before you go. Staff at the visitor centre can help find a grave.
stops.disputed: Burial totals differ slightly between sources (7,989 on TracesOfWar, 7,992 on Wikipedia and Liberation Route).

aar.ev: A temporary US military cemetery opens on the ridge near Hombourg.
aar.st: A temporary cemetery opened here on 28 September 1944, soon after the 1st Infantry Division liberated the area. The permanent cemetery, dedicated in 1960, holds 7,992 American dead, most from the Battle of the Bulge and the advance into Germany, and lists 450 missing. Today headstones curve across a sloping lawn below a memorial with carved granite maps and the names of the missing.
aar.rem: A bronze rosette beside a name on the colonnade means that missing man has since been found and identified.

stops.notes: abmc.gov returned errors to every fetch, so hours follow the standard ABMC pattern and were not confirmed for 2026. Wikipedia gives 50.697, 5.900 (3 decimals); TracesOfWar used for precision. Some sources place it in Henri-Chapelle (Welkenraedt) though it lies in Hombourg (Plombières).

stops.name: Luxembourg American Cemetery, Hamm
stops.text: The 609th Quartermaster Company of the US Third Army opened a temporary cemetery here at Hamm on 29 December 1944, while the Battle of the Bulge was still being fought. Dedicated in 1960, the cemetery covers about 20 hectares and holds 5,076 American dead, most of whom died in Luxembourg between September 1944 and February 1945. Among them are 101 unknowns, 22 pairs of brothers, 118 Jewish soldiers under Star of David headstones and an army nurse. General George S. Patton, commander of the Third Army, who died in December 1945, is buried at the head of the graves between the two flagpoles.
stops.look: Pass the white stone chapel with its stained-glass window of five US command insignia and mosaic ceiling. Headstones fan out across the lawn; Patton's grave stands alone at the front between the flagpoles, facing his men.
stops.plan: Open daily 09:00–17:00, free, with a car park (Visit Luxembourg listing, October 2026). Run by the American Battle Monuments Commission; hours can change, so check before you go.
stops.disputed: Burial totals vary slightly: Wikipedia gives 5,074 and Visit Luxembourg 5,076.

aar.ev: Third Army quartermasters open a temporary cemetery at Hamm during the Battle of the Bulge.
aar.st: The 609th Quartermaster Company of the Third Army opened a temporary cemetery at Hamm on 29 December 1944. Dedicated in 1960, it holds 5,076 American dead, most killed in Luxembourg between September 1944 and February 1945, and General George S. Patton. Today you pass the white stone chapel and walk out to Patton's grave, alone at the head of the graves between the flagpoles.
aar.rem: General Patton lies at the head of his Third Army dead, between the flagpoles, not in a separate plot.

stops.notes: abmc.gov could not be fetched. The cemetery address is 50 Val du Scheid, L-2517 Luxembourg.

stops.name: National Museum of Military History, Diekirch
stops.text: Diekirch, on the Sauer in north-eastern Luxembourg, lay on the southern flank of the Bulge. On the night of 18 January 1945 units of the US 5th Infantry Division crossed the river here as the Americans went over to the offensive. The museum grew out of the Diekirch Historical Museum, opened in 1984 in part of the former brewery, and now fills about 3,200 m² over four floors. Its life-size dioramas, centred on the night crossing of the Sauer, are surrounded by weapons, uniforms, photographs and more than 50 vehicles and guns from both sides. A second section covers the Luxembourg Army from 1815 to its UN missions.
stops.look: Start with the large diorama of the night-time Sauer crossing, then work through four floors of dioramas, vehicles and personal belongings from both sides. Look for the working Enigma cipher machine. The museum is in the old brewery buildings about 200 m from the town centre.
stops.plan: Check opening days and prices on mnhm.lu before you go; the site could not be read in October 2026. Multilingual group tours can be booked through reception@mnhm.lu or +352 808 908.

aar.ev: Under cover of darkness, the US 5th Infantry Division crosses the Sauer at Diekirch.
aar.st: Diekirch lay on the southern flank of the Bulge. On the night of 18 January 1945 units of the US 5th Infantry Division crossed the Sauer here as the Americans went over to the offensive. Today the museum, in the old brewery, fills four floors with life-size dioramas centred on the night crossing, more than 50 vehicles and guns, and a working Enigma machine.

q.t: Which US division crossed the Sauer at Diekirch on 18 January 1945?
q.x: Units of the US 5th Infantry Division made a night crossing of the Sauer at Diekirch on 18 January 1945; the museum's central diorama recreates it.

aar.rem: The Bulge was fought in Luxembourg as well as Belgium, and Diekirch tells the story from both sides.

stops.notes: TracesOfWar gives 49.870992, 6.159558 (Bamertal 10). Chronicle.lu says the museum was started by volunteers in 1982; Wikipedia and Liberation Route say 1984. Hours unverified: mnhm.lu blocks automated reading.

stops.name: Battle of Britain Bunker, Uxbridge
stops.text: This bunker, about 60 feet underground at RAF Uxbridge, housed the Operations Room of No. 11 Group, Fighter Command, which defended London and the south-east and saw more fighting than any other group in 1940. Air Vice-Marshal Keith Park commanded from here, sending squadrons up against raids plotted on the large table map. On 15 September 1940, with Churchill watching from the gallery, every 11 Group squadron was committed at once. Churchill first spoke the words 'never was so much owed by so many to so few' as he left Uxbridge on 16 August, four days before he used them in the House of Commons. The bunker was part of the Dowding system, the first integrated air defence network.
stops.look: Down 76 steps you reach the Operations Room, laid out as it was on 15 September 1940: the plotting table with raid markers, the tote board showing squadron states, and the glazed controllers' gallery above. A modern visitor centre at ground level holds the museum.
stops.plan: Open daily 10:00–16:30. The bunker itself is seen only on a guided tour of about an hour; booking ahead is advised. Tour plus visitor centre about £14 adult, under-16s free. 76 steps, no lift. Check the website before you go.
stops.disputed: Churchill's 'so few' line is often placed on 15 September; the bunker's own history says he first said it leaving Uxbridge on 16 August 1940, before the Commons speech of 20 August.

aar.ev: Every 11 Group squadron is committed at once while Churchill watches from the gallery.
aar.st: From this bunker 60 feet below RAF Uxbridge, Keith Park's No. 11 Group defended London and the south-east in 1940. On 15 September every squadron was in the air at once, with Churchill looking on. Today you go down 76 steps to the Operations Room, with its plotting table, raid markers and the tote board of squadron states set as on that day.

q.t: Where did Churchill first say 'never was so much owed by so many to so few'?
o: In the House of Commons on 15 September
In a BBC broadcast from Downing Street
q.x: He said it to General Ismay as they left Uxbridge on 16 August 1940, then used it in the House of Commons on 20 August.

aar.rem: The Battle of Britain was run by telephone and table map: radar warning, filtered plots and fast decisions in rooms like this one.

stops.notes: Managed by Hillingdon Council. Underground area unsuitable for wheelchairs; visitor centre is accessible. Filming not permitted in the bunker.

stops.name: Bentley Priory Museum, Stanmore
stops.text: This country house was the headquarters of RAF Fighter Command throughout the Second World War. From here Air Chief Marshal Sir Hugh Dowding commanded the fighter force in the Battle of Britain and ran the defence system he had built: radar stations and Observer Corps reports fed into a filter room here, then out to group and sector operations rooms, which sent fighters to meet the raids. Dowding was removed from command in November 1940 but was made Baron Dowding of Bentley Priory in 1943. The RAF stayed until 2008. The museum opened in 2013 and tells the story of 'The One' (Dowding), 'The Few' (the aircrew) and 'The Many' who supported them.
stops.look: The Italianate mansion's ground-floor rooms hold the museum, including Dowding's restored office looking over the gardens. Galleries on the aircrew and ground staff, a Battle of Britain timeline and a heritage trail in the grounds complete the visit.
stops.plan: Open Wednesdays, Fridays, Saturdays and bank holiday Mondays; 10:00–16:00 from October to February. Closed mid-December to mid-January. Adult about £9.50; no booking needed. Phone lines unreliable, use the website.

aar.ev: Dowding directs RAF Fighter Command against the Luftwaffe from this country house.
aar.st: Bentley Priory was Fighter Command's headquarters for the whole war. Here Sir Hugh Dowding ran the system that turned radar and Observer Corps reports into orders for the fighter groups, and he was later made Baron Dowding of Bentley Priory. Today the mansion's rooms hold the museum, with Dowding's restored office and galleries on the aircrew and the people who supported them.

q.t: What title did Dowding take in 1943?
q.x: He was made Baron Dowding of Bentley Priory in 1943, tying his name to the headquarters from which he fought the battle.

aar.rem: Dowding's real achievement was the system: radar, plotting and communications that put scarce fighters in the right place.

stops.notes: The house is surrounded by private housing; follow signs to Mansion House Drive. Limited opening days, so plan around them.

stops.name: IWM Duxford
stops.text: Duxford became a fighter station in 1925, and in August 1938 its No. 19 Squadron was the first RAF unit to fly the Spitfire. In the Battle of Britain it was a sector station of No. 12 Group, guarding East Anglia and the Midlands and sending squadrons south to help 11 Group over London. From March 1943 the US Eighth Air Force's 78th Fighter Group flew from here, first with P-47 Thunderbolts and from December 1944 with P-51 Mustangs, escorting bombers and attacking ground targets until the war ended. The last RAF flight left in 1961, and the Imperial War Museum took over the site, which keeps many original wartime buildings.
stops.look: Original hangars, the control tower and the restored Operations Block, pilots' briefing room and crew rooms show a working 1940 fighter station. Spitfire N3200 is on display, and Norman Foster's American Air Museum holds a B-17 and other US aircraft.
stops.plan: Open daily; from 25 October the site closes at 16:00. Adult from about £26.80, booking online advised. Flying days and air shows are extra events. Check the website before you go.
stops.disputed: The 'Big Wing' of three to five 12 Group squadrons, assembled at Duxford in September 1940, remains debated: supporters credited it with large claims, while critics, Park among them, said it formed up too slowly and its claims were inflated.

aar.ev: No. 19 Squadron at Duxford becomes the first RAF unit to fly the Spitfire.
aar.st: Duxford's No. 19 Squadron received the RAF's first Spitfires in August 1938, and in 1940 the station fought the Battle of Britain as part of No. 12 Group. From 1943 the American 78th Fighter Group flew Thunderbolts and then Mustangs from here. Today original hangars, the control tower and the restored Operations Block stand beside the American Air Museum with its B-17.

q.t: Which American unit flew from Duxford from 1943?
q.x: The US 78th Fighter Group arrived in March 1943 with P-47 Thunderbolts and switched to P-51 Mustangs in December 1944.

aar.rem: Duxford is the best-preserved wartime fighter station in Britain: both RAF 1940 and USAAF 1943–45 on one airfield.

stops.notes: Large site; allow most of a day. Free shuttle bus links the hangars. Air show days are busy and priced separately.

stops.name: Battle of Britain Memorial, Capel-le-Ferne
stops.text: On the cliffs between Folkestone and Dover, under the air battles of 1940, stands the national memorial to the aircrew of the Battle of Britain. It was unveiled by Queen Elizabeth the Queen Mother on 9 July 1993. Its centre is Harry Gray's carved figure of a seated pilot looking out to sea; his flying jacket hides rank and nationality, so he stands for every Allied airman of 'The Few'. The Christopher Foxley-Norris Memorial Wall lists almost 3,000 aircrew who flew in the battle. The visitor centre, The Wing, shaped like a Spitfire's wing, was opened by Queen Elizabeth II on 26 March 2015.
stops.look: From the air the memorial is a three-bladed propeller cut into the clifftop. Look for the seated pilot, the long wall of names, Churchill's words on the Beaverbrook Wall, and replica Hurricane and Spitfire. The Wing has the 'Scramble Experience' and a clifftop café.
stops.plan: Grounds open on foot every day. Café, shop and Scramble Experience 10:00–17:00 to 31 October, 10:00–16:00 in winter, closed Mondays November–February. Scramble Experience about £6 adult. Car park £2–£6, card only.

aar.ev: The Queen Mother unveils the national memorial to the aircrew of the Battle of Britain.
aar.st: These cliffs lay beneath the air battles of 1940, and since 1993 they have held the national memorial to 'The Few'. Harry Gray's seated pilot looks out to sea, and a wall names almost 3,000 aircrew who flew in the battle. Today you walk the propeller-shaped memorial, read the names, and see replica fighters beside The Wing visitor centre.
aar.rem: The pilot's jacket hides rank and nationality on purpose: he stands for every airman, whatever his country.

stops.notes: On the B2011 clifftop road; combine with Dover Castle (about 15 minutes). The grounds can be visited free on foot; the ticket covers the Scramble Experience.

stops.name: Biggin Hill Memorial Museum
stops.text: Biggin Hill was the best known of the 11 Group sector stations guarding the southern approaches to London, and in 1940 the Luftwaffe tried hard to knock it out. Between August 1940 and January 1941 it was attacked twelve times; the worst raid, at the end of August, hit the WAAF quarters and killed 39 people on the ground. After the war a public appeal backed by Churchill paid for St George's RAF Chapel of Remembrance, built on the site of a hangar destroyed in 1940; Lord Dowding laid the foundation stone in July 1951. The museum beside the chapel opened in 2019 and tells the station's story through the people who served there.
stops.look: The brick chapel's twelve stained-glass windows by Hugh Easton each show a young airman with a squadron badge, and a tablet records airmen lost flying from Biggin Hill. Gate-guardian Spitfire and Hurricane replicas stand outside; the museum is next door.
stops.plan: Tuesday–Sunday, 10:00–16:00 from November to March (17:00 in summer), closed Mondays. Adult about £8.50, pay at the door. Allow about 90 minutes. Check the website before you go.

aar.ev: German bombers repeatedly strike Biggin Hill, the key fighter station south of London.
aar.st: Biggin Hill guarded the southern approaches to London and was bombed twelve times between August 1940 and January 1941. After the war a public appeal backed by Churchill built a chapel on the site of a hangar destroyed in 1940. Today Hugh Easton's stained-glass windows of young airmen fill the chapel, and the memorial museum stands beside it.

q.t: What stood on the site of Biggin Hill's memorial chapel in 1940?
o: A hangar destroyed in the bombing
q.x: St George's Chapel was built in 1951 on the site of a hangar destroyed in 1940; Lord Dowding laid its foundation stone.

aar.rem: Fighter airfields were front-line targets in 1940: ground staff, including WAAFs, came under bombing at Biggin Hill.

stops.notes: Coordinates are those of St George's Chapel (listed building record); the museum adjoins it on Main Road (A233), TN16 3EJ. Biggin Hill is still a working airport.

stops.name: RAF Manston Spitfire & Hurricane Memorial Museum
stops.text: Manston, on the tip of Kent, was the RAF fighter airfield closest to France and so one of the first targets in the Luftwaffe's August 1940 offensive against Fighter Command. At the height of the battle it was bombed almost daily and left littered with unexploded bombs, and many staff moved out to the nearby woods. Later it became a refuge for damaged bombers, fitted with the FIDO fog-clearance system, and in May 1943 No. 617 Squadron's Lancasters flew from here to drop inert test versions of Barnes Wallis's bouncing bomb off Reculver. The small free museum on the old airfield houses Spitfire XVI TB752 and Hurricane IIc LF751.
stops.look: Two aircraft fill the purpose-built hall: Spitfire TB752, which flew in combat in 1945, and Hurricane LF751. Around them are displays on Manston's war and wartime Ramsgate. The café overlooks the former airfield. The separate RAF Manston History Museum is close by.
stops.plan: Admission free; donations welcome. Opening hours vary by season (recently 10:00–17:00 in summer); check the website before you go. Flight simulator costs extra.

aar.ev: The Luftwaffe bombs Manston, the RAF fighter field nearest France, almost daily.
aar.st: As the closest fighter airfield to France, Manston took heavy bombing in August 1940 and was left strewn with unexploded bombs. In May 1943 Lancasters of 617 Squadron flew from here to test the bouncing bomb off Reculver. Today a small free museum on the old airfield displays Spitfire TB752 and Hurricane LF751, with a café looking over the runway.

q.t: What weapon was tested from Manston in May 1943?
q.x: 617 Squadron Lancasters loaded inert bouncing bombs at Manston and dropped them off Reculver in May 1943, days before the Dams Raid.

aar.rem: Forward airfields like Manston took the first blows of the Luftwaffe's campaign against Fighter Command.

stops.notes: Coordinates come from a directory site's map pin (picniq.co.uk), as no official or Wikipedia coordinate for the museum building was found; the RAF Manston Wikipedia airfield reference point is 51°20′53″N 1°21′00″E. Official opening-times page could not be loaded; editor should confirm hours.

stops.name: Dover Castle Secret Wartime Tunnels
stops.text: Tunnels cut into the chalk below Dover Castle during the Napoleonic Wars were turned in 1939 into an air-raid shelter, then a naval command centre and an underground hospital. From here Vice-Admiral Bertram Ramsay planned and directed Operation Dynamo, the evacuation of the British Expeditionary Force and French troops from Dunkirk between 26 May and 4 June 1940. Working with a scratch fleet of warships, ferries and small civilian boats, his staff brought about 338,000 men back to England, far more than the 45,000 first hoped for. The operation is said to take its name from the room that had housed an electrical generator. The tunnels later served through the war as a headquarters guarding the Channel.
stops.look: Guided routes take you through the tunnel complex: the Operation Dynamo galleries with projections telling the evacuation story, the operations rooms, and the reconstructed underground hospital. The medieval castle and Great Tower stand above, with views across the Channel to France on clear days.
stops.plan: Castle open daily 10:00–17:00 (last entry 16:00); winter hours may be shorter. Book online to save money. The Operation Dynamo section of the tunnels is currently closed for maintenance; the Underground Hospital is open. Check the website before you go.
stops.disputed: Totals vary by source: 338,226 is the usual figure for Dynamo, but counts that include earlier evacuations give higher numbers. Sources also differ on whether Ramsay was Vice-Admiral (his rank in 1940) or Admiral (later).

aar.ev: Ramsay orders Operation Dynamo from the chalk tunnels beneath Dover Castle.
aar.st: In tunnels first dug during the Napoleonic Wars, Vice-Admiral Bertram Ramsay directed the evacuation from Dunkirk between 26 May and 4 June 1940. His staff used warships, ferries and small civilian boats to bring about 338,000 men home. Today you follow the tunnels past operations rooms and a reconstructed underground hospital, with the medieval castle and Channel views above.

q.t: Where did Operation Dynamo get its name?
o: A room in the tunnels that had held a generator
q.x: The usual explanation is that the planning took place in the tunnel room that had housed an electrical generator, or dynamo.

aar.rem: Dunkirk was saved by planning as much as by little ships: the evacuation was run from offices in these tunnels.

stops.notes: Wikipedia coordinate for Dover Castle has only 4 decimals and marks the castle, not the tunnel entrance. As of October 2026 English Heritage says the Operation Dynamo section is closed for essential maintenance with no reopening date: tell readers before they travel. Renamed slightly from the stoplist.

stops.name: Churchill War Rooms, London
stops.text: The Cabinet War Rooms, in a basement beneath government offices off Whitehall, became operational on 27 August 1939, days before Germany invaded Poland. The War Cabinet met here 115 times, the last time on 28 March 1945, and Churchill made four wartime broadcasts from the site, the first on 11 September 1940. The Map Room, staffed day and night, tracked the war on every front. From 1943 a secure SIGSALY telephone link let Churchill speak to President Roosevelt from a room disguised as a private lavatory. The lights were switched off the day after Japan surrendered, and the rooms were preserved. They opened to the public in 1984.
stops.look: Low corridors lead past the Cabinet Room, the Map Room with its original maps, coloured pins and telephones, the Transatlantic Telephone Room and Churchill's bedroom. The Churchill Museum, opened in 2005, covers his whole life.
stops.plan: Open daily 09:30–18:00 (last entry 17:00), closed 24–26 December. Adult about £34; booking online is strongly advised as it often sells out. Check the website before you go.

aar.ev: Churchill makes the first of his four wartime broadcasts from the bunker under Whitehall.
aar.st: The War Rooms became operational on 27 August 1939, and the War Cabinet met here 115 times. From 1943 Churchill could talk securely to Roosevelt from a tiny room disguised as a lavatory. Today you walk the low corridors past the Cabinet Room, the Map Room with its original pins and maps, and Churchill's bedroom.

q.t: How was the Transatlantic Telephone Room disguised?
q.x: The room holding the secure line to Roosevelt was disguised as a private lavatory; the link itself was the SIGSALY system, in use from 1943.

aar.rem: The Map Room was left as it was in August 1945: the pins on the wall are where the war ended.

stops.notes: Busy and often sold out in summer; first entry slot is quietest. Entrance on Clive Steps, King Charles Street.

stops.name: Imperial War Museum London
stops.text: Britain's national museum of modern war has occupied the former Bethlem Royal Hospital on Lambeth Road since 1936. It is the best single place in Britain to see the Second World War as a whole: the Blitz, the war at sea and in the air, the home front and the campaigns from 1939 to 1945. In October 2021 it opened new Second World War and Holocaust galleries, which follow the war in Europe and the persecution and murder of Europe's Jews side by side. Outside stand two 15-inch naval guns, one from HMS Ramillies and the other mounted on HMS Resolution and HMS Roberts, which fired in support of D-Day.
stops.look: Head for the Second World War Galleries and the Holocaust Galleries on the upper floors; the central atrium holds aircraft, rockets and vehicles, including a V-2 and a Spitfire. The two huge 15-inch guns frame the entrance.
stops.plan: Open daily 10:00–18:00, closed 24–26 December. Free; no booking needed for general entry. Some special exhibitions are ticketed. Check the website before you go.

aar.ev: Britain's national war museum tells the whole Second World War under one roof.
aar.st: IWM London has been in the old Bethlem Royal Hospital since 1936. Its Second World War and Holocaust galleries, opened in 2021, follow the war in Europe and the murder of Europe's Jews side by side. Today two 15-inch naval guns guard the entrance, and inside the atrium holds aircraft and rockets, including a V-2.

q.t: What building does IWM London occupy?
q.x: Since 1936 the museum has been in the former Bethlem Royal Hospital on Lambeth Road, south of the Thames.

aar.rem: Start or finish a London trip here: the 2021 galleries give the big picture the individual sites cannot.

stops.notes: The Holocaust Galleries contain distressing material; IWM gives age guidance on its website.

stops.name: St Paul's Cathedral and the Blitz, London
stops.text: St Paul's became the symbol of London's survival in the Blitz. On 12 September 1940 a delayed-action bomb buried itself near the cathedral; a Royal Engineers team under Temporary Lieutenant Robert Davies dug it out and removed it, and Davies and Sapper George Wylie received the George Cross. A bomb destroyed the high altar on 10 October 1940, and another holed the north transept on 17 April 1941. On the night of 29 December 1940, the 'Second Great Fire of London', Churchill reportedly ordered that the cathedral be saved, and Herbert Mason's photograph of the dome rising through the smoke became one of the war's best-known images.
stops.look: Behind the high altar is the American Memorial Chapel, dedicated in 1958, with a Roll of Honour of over 28,000 Americans who died while based in or travelling to Britain. From the Stone Gallery you see the City rebuilt where the bombed streets stood.
stops.plan: Sightseeing Monday–Saturday, usually 08:30–16:30 (last entry 16:00). Adult about £27, booking online advised. Services are free. Times change for services and events; check the calendar before you go.
stops.disputed: Churchill's order to save St Paul's at all costs is widely repeated but rests on later accounts ('reportedly'); no written order is known.

aar.ev: The dome of St Paul's rises unscathed above the fires of the City of London.
aar.st: Through the Blitz St Paul's was hit several times: a delayed-action bomb was dug out in September 1940, the high altar was destroyed in October, and the north transept holed in April 1941. Herbert Mason's photograph of 29 December 1940 made the dome a symbol of survival. Today the American Memorial Chapel stands behind the high altar, and the galleries look out over the rebuilt City.

q.t: What did Robert Davies's bomb disposal team do at St Paul's in September 1940?
o: Put out a fire in the dome
Dug out and removed a delayed-action bomb
q.x: They removed a time-delayed bomb near the cathedral; Davies and Sapper George Wylie were each awarded the George Cross.

aar.rem: Much of the City around St Paul's was burnt out on 29 December 1940; the cathedral survived because fire-watchers fought for it.

stops.notes: Coordinate converted from Wikipedia's DMS (51°30′50″N 0°05′54″W). Sunday is for worship only (Dome Galleries open on some Sundays in season).

stops.name: Coventry Cathedral ruins
stops.text: On the night of 14–15 November 1940 the Luftwaffe attacked Coventry, a centre of aircraft and engineering factories, in one of the heaviest raids of the Blitz. The medieval cathedral of St Michael burned; only the tower, spire, outer walls and one tomb survived. Provost Richard Howard had 'Father Forgive' inscribed behind the ruined altar, stonemason Jock Forbes bound two charred roof beams into a cross, and a cross was made from three medieval nails. Rather than rebuild, the city kept the ruins and Basil Spence built a new cathedral beside them, consecrated on 25 May 1962. The cathedral became a worldwide centre for reconciliation, linked with Dresden among others.
stops.look: Walk through the roofless shell to the altar with the Charred Cross (a 1964 replica; the original is inside) and the 'Father Forgive' words. Look for Josefina de Vasconcellos's 'Reconciliation' statue, then climb the 87-metre spire tower if open, and enter the new cathedral through its glass screen.
stops.plan: Cathedral and ruins usually open Monday–Saturday 10:00–16:00, Sunday 12:00–15:30, subject to services. Entry is free with donations welcome; the tower climb is charged. Check the website before you go.
stops.disputed: A long-running claim says Churchill knew of the raid from Ultra decrypts and let Coventry burn to protect the secret; historians who have studied the records reject it, as the target was not identified in time.

aar.ev: German bombers set Coventry ablaze, and the medieval cathedral burns to a shell.
aar.st: In the raid of 14–15 November 1940 St Michael's burned, leaving only its tower, spire and outer walls. Provost Richard Howard had 'Father Forgive' inscribed behind the altar, and the ruins were kept beside Basil Spence's new cathedral of 1962. Today you walk through the roofless shell to the Charred Cross and the 'Reconciliation' statue before entering the new building.
aar.rem: Coventry chose reconciliation over revenge: 'Father Forgive' does not say 'Father forgive them'.

stops.notes: Coordinate converted from the Wikipedia OS grid reference SP 33627 79065 (old cathedral) using a standard OSGB36-WGS84 transform; Wikipedia's own decimal is 52.4083, -1.5072. Name shortened from stoplist.

stops.name: Bletchley Park
stops.text: The Government Code and Cypher School moved to this Victorian mansion on 15 August 1939. Here codebreakers including Alan Turing and Gordon Welchman built on Polish work against the German Enigma machine; their electromechanical bombes found daily settings, Hut 6 broke Army and Air Force Enigma and Hut 8 Naval Enigma. The intelligence, codenamed Ultra, was graded above Most Secret. Later the Colossus computers attacked the German high command's Lorenz cipher. By January 1945 nearly 9,000 people worked for Bletchley and its outstations, about three-quarters of them women. Nobody spoke of it publicly until the 1970s.
stops.look: Restored huts, including Huts 6 and 8, and Block B with a working rebuilt bombe and Enigma machines. Visit the mansion, the lake and the wooden huts. The National Museum of Computing in Block H, with a rebuilt Colossus, has a separate ticket.
stops.plan: Open daily 09:30–17:00 to 31 Oct, then 09:30–16:00 in winter; closed 24–26 December. Adult about £28.75, valid as an annual pass; 10% off when booked online in advance. Allow at least four hours.
stops.disputed: The claim that Bletchley shortened the war by two years comes from official historian Sir Harry Hinsley; others think the effect cannot be measured so precisely.

aar.ev: Britain's codebreakers move to a country house to attack German Enigma traffic.
aar.st: From August 1939 Bletchley Park attacked German ciphers, with Turing's bombes finding Enigma settings and the Colossus computers breaking the Lorenz cipher. By 1945 nearly 9,000 people worked for it, about three-quarters of them women. Today restored huts, the mansion and a rebuilt working bombe show how the work was done, with Colossus next door in the computing museum.

q.t: Roughly what share of Bletchley's staff in 1945 were women?
q.x: Of nearly 9,000 staff in January 1945, about three-quarters were women, working as operators, analysts, translators and codebreakers.

aar.rem: Ultra gave the Allies a window into German plans, but only if it could be used without revealing the source.

stops.notes: Opening and price details taken from the Destination Milton Keynes listing because the official visit page would not load; editor should confirm on bletchleypark.org.uk. Bletchley station is a five-minute walk.

stops.name: Western Approaches HQ, Liverpool
stops.text: Western Approaches Command, responsible for protecting convoys in the Atlantic, moved from Plymouth to a reinforced basement under Derby House in Liverpool on 7 February 1941. RAF Coastal Command's No. 15 Group moved in alongside, so ships and aircraft were directed from one room. Admiral Sir Percy Noble commanded from February 1941, followed by Admiral Sir Max Horton from November 1942, who led the escort groups through the decisive convoy battles of spring 1943. In the same building the Western Approaches Tactical Unit under Captain Gilbert Roberts, staffed largely by Wrens, wargamed U-boat tactics on the floor and devised countermeasures for escort captains.
stops.look: The main operations room with its two-storey wall map of the Atlantic and convoy plots, the commander's office overlooking it, the teleprinter and cipher rooms, and the reconstructed tactical unit with its floor gaming board.
stops.plan: Open daily 10:00–18:00, last entry 17:00. Adult about £16.50; tickets online or on the day, no time slots. Cashless. Check the website before you go.

aar.ev: The command fighting the U-boats moves into a bombproof bunker under Derby House.
aar.st: From February 1941 Western Approaches Command and the RAF's No. 15 Group ran the Battle of the Atlantic together from this basement. Admiral Max Horton took over in November 1942, and Gilbert Roberts's tactical unit, staffed largely by Wrens, wargamed U-boat tactics on the floor. Today you see the operations room with its huge Atlantic wall map, Horton's office and the tactical unit.

q.t: Who commanded Western Approaches from November 1942?
q.x: Max Horton, a former submariner, replaced Percy Noble in November 1942 and led the escort forces through the convoy battles of 1943.

aar.rem: Britain's survival depended on the Atlantic convoys; this room is where that battle was managed.

stops.notes: Entrance on Rumford Street, Liverpool L2. Operated by Big Heritage, which also looks after U-boat U-534 (planned new display). Official site URL is liverpoolwarmuseum.co.uk (westernapproaches.org.uk blocked fetching).

stops.name: The D-Day Story, Portsmouth
stops.text: Portsmouth and the Solent were the heart of the D-Day build-up: troops, ships and landing craft packed the south coast in spring 1944, and Eisenhower's forward headquarters was at Southwick House just north of the city. This museum on Southsea seafront opened in 1984 as the D-Day Museum and reopened in 2018 as The D-Day Story. Its centrepiece is the Overlord Embroidery, commissioned by Lord Dulverton: 34 panels, 83 metres long, made by twenty members of the Royal School of Needlework over seven years. Outside is LCT 7074, the last surviving landing craft tank of its kind from D-Day.
stops.look: Galleries follow D-Day from planning to the Normandy battle through personal stories, with a reconstructed Southwick House operations room. The Overlord Embroidery runs round its own gallery. Board LCT 7074 to see the open tank deck.
stops.plan: Open daily 10:00–17:00 (17:30 April–September); last entry 16:00, 15:30 for LCT 7074. Closed 24–26 December. Paid entry, ticket includes LCT 7074; buy online or on the day.

aar.ev: The invasion fleet sails from Portsmouth and the Solent for Normandy.
aar.st: In spring 1944 the Portsmouth area filled with troops, ships and landing craft, and Eisenhower's forward headquarters sat at Southwick House nearby. This seafront museum tells the D-Day story through the people involved and the 83-metre Overlord Embroidery. Today you can also go aboard LCT 7074, the last landing craft tank of its kind, beside the museum.

q.t: What is LCT 7074?
q.x: LCT 7074 is the last surviving D-Day landing craft tank of its kind; since 2020 it has been displayed beside the museum.

aar.rem: D-Day began in the harbours of southern England: the invasion was launched from places like this.

stops.notes: Ticket prices not shown on the main page; see theddaystory.com/plan-your-visit/tickets.

stops.name: Lidice Memorial
stops.text: After the attack on Reinhard Heydrich, the Gestapo falsely linked the mining village of Lidice, west of Prague, to the assassins on the strength of an intercepted love letter. On 10 June 1942 German security police shot the village's men and boys over 15 on the Horák farm, sent the women to Ravensbrück and took the children; most of the children were later gassed at Chełmno, while a few judged 'racially suitable' were handed to German families. The village was burned, blown up and levelled, and its name erased from maps. The crime was publicised by the Nazis themselves, and towns from Britain to Latin America answered by taking the name Lidice. The memorial landscape was laid out between 1946 and 1962.
stops.look: A grassy valley where the village stood, with the foundations of the church, school and Horák farm, the cross over the men's mass grave, Marie Uchytilová's bronze group of 82 children, a rose garden of some 21,000 bushes and a museum with the exhibition 'And Those Innocent Were Guilty...'.
stops.plan: Open daily 9:00–17:00. Adults 150 Kč, children 70 Kč. The memorial landscape is open-air; allow time to walk down to the village site. About 30 minutes by bus or car from Prague. Check the website before you go.
stops.disputed: Figures vary by source: 173 men were shot at Lidice on 10 June according to most counts, while other accounts give 199 men killed in total including those executed elsewhere; about 340 villagers died overall.

aar.ev: German police destroy Lidice in reprisal for Heydrich's assassination, falsely linking the village to his killers.
aar.st: On 10 June 1942 German security police shot Lidice's men, sent the women to Ravensbrück and took the children, most of whom were later gassed at Chełmno. The village was burned and levelled and its name erased from maps. Today a grassy valley holds the foundations of the church and school, the men's grave, a bronze group of 82 children, a rose garden and a museum.
aar.rem: The Nazis meant Lidice to vanish; instead its name was taken up by towns around the world.
