stops.notes: Coordinates are those of the village from the Wikipedia infobox (the Lidice massacre article gives 50°08′35″N, 2 seconds further south); the memorial area and museum lie on and beside the old village site. Ležáky, the second village destroyed, is in eastern Bohemia near Chrudim.

stops.name: National Memorial to the Heroes of the Heydrich Terror
stops.text: After the attack on Heydrich, the Orthodox Church of Sts Cyril and Methodius in Resslova Street hid seven Czechoslovak paratroopers in its crypt, including Gabčík, Kubiš and Josef Valčík. Karel Čurda, another parachutist, gave the Gestapo the names of their helpers, and after the arrest of the Moravec family the SS surrounded the church before dawn on 18 June 1942. Adolf Opálka, Josef Bublík and Kubiš fought from the prayer loft until all three were dead or dying. Gabčík, Valčík, Jaroslav Švarc and Jan Hrubý held the crypt for hours against gunfire, tear gas and attempts to flood it, then killed themselves. Bishop Gorazd and the church's priests were executed in September 1942. Čurda was hanged for treason in 1947.
stops.look: The crypt itself, with the narrow ventilation slit to Resslova Street still scarred by bullets and the hole the paratroopers dug towards the sewer, plus an exhibition on the operation and the Heydrich terror. A plaque and memorial outside mark the bullet-pocked window.
stops.plan: Open Tuesday to Sunday 9:00–17:00, last entry 16:30, closed Mondays. Admission free. Run by the Military History Institute (VHU). The church above is a working Orthodox cathedral. Check the website before you go.
links: Prague City Tourism: National Monument to the Heroes of the Heydrich Terror

aar.ev: SS troops besiege the paratroopers who killed Heydrich in the crypt of a Prague church.
aar.st: Betrayed by a fellow parachutist, the seven Czechoslovak soldiers hiding in this crypt were surrounded by the SS on 18 June 1942. Three fell in the prayer loft; the rest held the crypt for hours against gunfire, gas and flooding before taking their own lives. Today you can stand in the crypt, see the bullet-scarred ventilation slit and follow the story in the exhibition.
aar.rem: The seven men in the crypt chose to die fighting rather than surrender; their helpers and families paid with their lives too.

stops.notes: Address Resslova 9a, Prague 2. Coordinates from the directions link on Prague City Tourism's page. The crypt was renovated in 2022 for the 80th anniversary. Official URL is the Military History Institute (operator); the prague.eu page has current hours.

stops.name: Operation Anthropoid Memorial, Prague-Libeň
stops.text: On the morning of 27 May 1942 Reinhard Heydrich was driven in an open Mercedes from his country house towards Prague Castle. At a tight hairpin bend in Libeň, where Kirchmayerova třída (now Zenklova) met V Holešovičkách, Jozef Gabčík stepped out with a Sten gun, which jammed. Jan Kubiš threw a modified anti-tank grenade that burst against the rear wheel, wounding Heydrich; Josef Valčík kept watch further up the road. Both attackers escaped. Heydrich died of his wounds on 4 June. He was the most senior Nazi assassinated during the war, and the reprisals that followed killed thousands of Czechs.
stops.look: A tall corten-steel column on a traffic island of the modern interchange, with three bronze figures, two soldiers and one civilian, reaching out from its edges, unveiled on 27 May 2009 at 10:35. A bronze slab in front explains the attack. The original bend has been swallowed by the road layout.
stops.plan: Open-air memorial, accessible at all times and free. It stands amid busy roads: use the pedestrian crossings. Trams stop nearby on V Holešovičkách.
stops.disputed: Heydrich's exact cause of death is debated: the autopsy pointed to sepsis from wound fragments; others propose an embolism, and a fringe claim that the grenade carried botulinum toxin is rejected by most historians.

aar.ev: Czechoslovak paratroopers ambush Reinhard Heydrich's car at a hairpin bend in Libeň.
aar.st: At this hairpin bend on 27 May 1942 Jozef Gabčík's Sten gun jammed as Heydrich's open car slowed, but Jan Kubiš's grenade wounded him and both men escaped. Heydrich died on 4 June. Today a steel column with three bronze figures, unveiled in 2009, stands on a traffic island above the spot.

q.t: What went wrong for Gabčík when Heydrich's car reached the bend?
o: The car did not slow down
Heydrich was not in the car
q.x: Gabčík's Sten gun jammed. Kubiš then threw a modified grenade that burst against the rear wheel and wounded Heydrich, who died a week later.

aar.rem: The only successful assassination of a top Nazi leader was carried out by two soldiers sent from Britain.

stops.notes: Coordinates from the map link on the Prague 8 district page. The memorial stands on the spot of the attack but the road layout is completely changed.

stops.name: Terezín Memorial
stops.text: Terezín, an 18th-century fortress town 60 km north of Prague, served the Nazis in two ways. From June 1940 the Small Fortress across the river was the Prague Gestapo's main prison, holding about 32,000 people. From 24 November 1941 the town itself became the Theresienstadt ghetto, a transit camp for Jews from the Protectorate, Germany, Austria and beyond, including the elderly and prominent. About 33,000 died there of hunger and disease, and about 88,000 were deported on to Auschwitz, Treblinka and other killing sites. In June 1944 the SS staged a 'beautified' ghetto for a Red Cross delegation and later filmed it for propaganda. The Red Army reached Terezín on 8 May 1945.
stops.look: The Ghetto Museum in the former boys' home, the Magdeburg Barracks with rooms on the ghetto's art, music and theatre, the crematorium and cemetery outside the walls, and across the river the Small Fortress with its cells, courtyards and execution ground. The town is lived in today.
stops.plan: Small Fortress daily 9:00–17:00 (to 16:00 in winter); Ghetto Museum and Magdeburg Barracks daily 9:00–17:00; crematorium closed Saturdays. Combined tickets available. Some exhibitions are closed for reconstruction. Allow a full day. Check the website before you go.
stops.disputed: Totals vary: about 141,000–154,000 people passed through the ghetto depending on how late arrivals and repeat prisoners are counted, and onward deportations are given as 88,000–90,000.

aar.ev: The first transport arrives as the SS turns the fortress town into a ghetto and transit camp.
aar.st: From November 1941 the SS used Terezín as a ghetto and transit camp; about 88,000 people were sent on to Auschwitz and other killing sites, while the Small Fortress across the river served as a Gestapo prison. In 1944 the SS staged a fake 'model ghetto' for the Red Cross. Today you can visit the Ghetto Museum and Magdeburg Barracks in the town and the cells of the Small Fortress.
aar.rem: Terezín was presented to the world as a model Jewish settlement while it served as a waiting room for Auschwitz.

stops.notes: Coordinates are those of the ghetto town from the Wikipedia infobox; the memorial's sites are spread across the town (Ghetto Museum, Komenského 148; Magdeburg Barracks, Tyršova 204) and the Small Fortress (Principova alej 304) about 1 km east. The Ravensbrück exhibition is closed for reconstruction and the transports exhibition can only be seen with a pre-booked guide.

stops.name: Mauthausen Memorial
stops.text: The SS opened Mauthausen on 8 August 1938, five months after the Anschluss, on a hill above the Danube 20 km east of Linz, beside the Wiener Graben granite quarry owned by the SS company DEST. It became the centre of a system of about 100 subcamps, the largest at Gusen. About 190,000 people from across Europe were deported there; prisoners hauled granite blocks up the 186 'Stairs of Death', and many were killed by gas, shooting or deliberate starvation. In February 1945 about 500 escaped prisoners, mostly Soviet officers, were hunted down and murdered by the SS, police and local civilians in the 'Mühlviertel hare hunt'. A reconnaissance squad of the US 11th Armored Division under Staff Sergeant Albert Kosiek reached the camp on 5 May 1945.
stops.look: The granite walls and gate of the main camp, the roll-call ground, surviving barracks, the camp prison, gas chamber and crematorium, a large exhibition in the former infirmary, national memorials outside the walls, and the quarry with the Stairs of Death below.
stops.plan: Open daily 9:00–17:30, last entry 16:45. Admission free, no registration needed; guided tours and audio guides charged and bookable online. The Stairs of Death are open 1 April to 26 October. Check the website before you go.
stops.disputed: Because records were destroyed and prisoner numbers reused, death totals for Mauthausen and its subcamps range from 'more than 90,000' to about 120,000 depending on the source.

aar.ev: The SS opens a concentration camp beside the granite quarry above Mauthausen.
aar.st: Mauthausen opened in August 1938 beside an SS-owned granite quarry and grew into a system of about 100 subcamps. Prisoners carried stone up the 186 Stairs of Death, and in February 1945 escaped Soviet officers were hunted down in the surrounding countryside. Today you enter through the granite gate to the roll-call ground, barracks, crematorium and exhibition, and can walk down to the quarry.
aar.rem: Mauthausen was built around a quarry: killing through labour was its purpose, not a side effect.

stops.notes: Address Erinnerungsstraße 1, 4310 Mauthausen. The Melk subcamp memorial is closed until further notice. Coordinates supplied by the editor from Wikipedia; my own fetch of that page did not return a coordinate string, so worth a spot-check against the main gate.

stops.name: Gusen Memorial
stops.text: Gusen, 5 km west of Mauthausen, opened on 25 May 1940 as a subcamp but at times held more prisoners than the main camp. Polish intellectuals and Spanish Republicans were among the early inmates, worked in granite quarries under murderous conditions. From March 1944 Gusen II housed prisoners who dug the Bergkristall tunnels at St Georgen, where Messerschmitt built Me 262 jet fighter fuselages underground; 987 were completed before May 1945. Official records list 27,842 deaths, but estimates run to 35,000 or more, since many killed on arrival were never registered. US troops of the 11th Armored and 26th Infantry Divisions arrived on 5 May 1945. Most of the camp was later built over by housing.
stops.look: The memorial built by survivors around the camp's crematorium oven, a small visitor centre with an exhibition, and the surviving gatehouse (the 'Jourhaus', now a private house) among suburban homes. The site is being redesigned as a larger place of remembrance.
stops.plan: Open daily 9:00–17:00. Admission free, no registration needed; guided tours bookable through the Mauthausen Memorial. The memorial is being redeveloped, so expect changes. The Bergkristall tunnels open only on occasional guided tours. Check the website before you go.
stops.disputed: Death figures range from the 27,842 in official records to estimates of 35,000–37,000 or more, because unregistered prisoners killed on arrival are missing from the records.

aar.ev: The first prisoners and guards arrive at Gusen, Mauthausen's largest subcamp.
aar.st: Gusen opened in May 1940 and at times held more prisoners than Mauthausen itself. From 1944 prisoners of Gusen II dug the Bergkristall tunnels where Messerschmitt built Me 262 jet fuselages underground. Today a memorial built by survivors around the crematorium oven and a small visitor centre stand among the houses that cover most of the former camp.
aar.rem: Most of Gusen disappeared under post-war housing; the memorial exists because survivors insisted on it.

stops.notes: Memorial at Georgestraße 7, visitor centre Georgestraße 5, 4222 Langenstein. The gatehouse is privately owned and seen from the road. Austria is redeveloping the site after a design competition (2024/25). Coordinates supplied by the editor from German Wikipedia (not opened by me).

stops.name: Dunkirk 1940 Museum (Bastion 32)
stops.text: Bastion 32 is a casemate in the old fortifications by the harbour, a short walk from the East Mole and the evacuation beaches. During the Battle of Dunkirk it served as the headquarters of the French and Allied forces defending the town while Operation Dynamo ran from 26 May to 4 June 1940. From here the defence of the perimeter was coordinated as 338,226 men were taken off to England, 239,555 of them from the harbour and 98,671 from the beaches. The museum inside tells the story of the battle and the evacuation, with weapons, uniforms, models, photographs and maps of the operations.
stops.look: A long, low brick casemate set into the bastion wall on Rue des Chantiers de France. Inside, vaulted rooms hold uniforms, weapons, models of the ships and beaches, and maps of the shrinking pocket. Outside, a memorial to the French Navy of 1939–40 stands nearby.
stops.plan: Tourist office listing: open daily 10:00–18:00 from 7 Feb to 31 Dec 2026; adult €8, child/student €5. No booking needed for individuals. The 2026 remembrance guide gives early Feb to mid-Nov plus Christmas holidays, so check the website before you go.

aar.ev: Allied commanders direct the defence of the Dunkirk pocket from a casemate in the harbour walls.
aar.st: Bastion 32 was the headquarters of the French and Allied forces during the Battle of Dunkirk. While the perimeter held, Operation Dynamo took 338,226 men to England, most of them from the harbour rather than the beaches, while French troops held the perimeter. Today the long brick casemate holds uniforms, weapons, ship models and maps of the shrinking pocket.

q.t: Where did most of the men evacuated in Operation Dynamo board their ships?
o: From the harbour and its moles
q.x: About 239,555 men left from the harbour, chiefly the East Mole, against 98,671 lifted from the beaches.

aar.rem: The evacuation was run from this harbour bastion, and most of the army left from the harbour, not the sand.

stops.notes: Museum's own site could not be fetched (robots block). Hours/prices from the Dunkirk tourist office sheet (marked 'unsecured') and the 2026 remembrance guide PDF, which disagree on the closing season.

stops.name: Malo-les-Bains evacuation beach, Dunkirk
stops.text: The beaches running east from Malo-les-Bains towards Bray-Dunes and De Panne were where tens of thousands of British and French soldiers waited, often for days, under air attack. Small boats ferried men out to larger ships lying offshore, a slow process that led Captain William Tennant, the senior naval officer ashore, to send most troops to the harbour moles instead. In all 98,671 men were lifted from the beaches. At the western end of the promenade, the Digue des Alliés, the Allied memorial inaugurated in 1962 marks the annual commemoration of the battle and of Operation Dynamo.
stops.look: A wide, flat sandy beach backed by the promenade and rebuilt seaside villas. At its western end stands a block-like memorial, inscribed in French only, to the soldiers, sailors and airmen of the French and Allied armies, with British poppy wreaths on its anchor. From here you can walk to the root of the East Mole.
stops.plan: Free, open access at all times. The memorial is at the western end of the Digue des Alliés, close to the Dunkirk 1940 Museum. Best combined with the museum and the East Mole on foot.
stops.disputed: Popular memory credits the 'little ships' and the beaches with the rescue, but the official figures show about 239,555 men left from the harbour against 98,671 from the beaches, mostly in destroyers and larger vessels.

aar.ev: Soldiers queue on the open sand while small boats ferry them out to waiting ships.
aar.st: Tens of thousands of British and French soldiers waited on these beaches under air attack. Ferrying men out by small boat was so slow that Captain William Tennant switched most of the embarkation to the harbour moles; the beaches still yielded 98,671 men. Today a wide sandy beach stretches east from a French-only memorial at the end of the Digue des Alliés.

q.t: Why did Captain Tennant send most troops to the harbour moles?
o: The Germans had captured the beaches
Loading from the beaches by small boat was too slow
q.x: Lifting men from the shallow beaches in small boats was too slow, so Tennant used the moles, where ships could load far more men.

aar.rem: The beaches saved nearly 100,000 men, but the harbour saved more than twice as many.

stops.notes: Coordinates are for the Operation Dynamo / Allied memorial at the western end of the Digue des Alliés (komoot highlight); the beach itself is the 'event' and runs for kilometres, hence MEDIUM.

stops.name: East Mole (Jetée de l'Est), Dunkirk
stops.text: The East Mole was a long breakwater sheltering the harbour entrance, never designed for ships to berth against. With the port's quays wrecked by bombing, Captain William Tennant began using it as a jetty, and it became the key to Operation Dynamo: almost 200,000 troops boarded ships from its narrow walkway. Destroyers, ferries and paddle steamers came alongside under bombing and shellfire. On 29 May the paddle steamer HMS Crested Eagle sailed from here with about 600 men aboard and was set on fire by bombs less than a mile out.
stops.look: A narrow jetty about 1.5 km long running out to sea from the end of Rue Militaire, with a German blockhouse at its foot. The far end is closed. From the walkway you get a panoramic view along the Dynamo beaches towards Belgium.
stops.plan: Free, open access; the outer end is closed to the public. About a 10-minute walk from the Dunkirk 1940 Museum. Exposed to wind and spray, so take care in rough weather.

aar.ev: Ships berth against a breakwater never built for them and load troops by the thousand.
aar.st: With the harbour quays wrecked, Captain William Tennant turned the East Mole, a breakwater, into an improvised jetty. Almost 200,000 men boarded destroyers, ferries and paddle steamers from its narrow walkway under bombing. Today the 1.5 km jetty still runs out from Rue Militaire, with a German blockhouse at its foot and a view along the Dynamo beaches.

q.t: What was the East Mole built to be?
o: A breakwater, not a berth for ships
q.x: It was a breakwater sheltering the harbour mouth. Ships were never meant to tie up there, but almost 200,000 men boarded from it.

aar.rem: An improvised use of a breakwater did more than anything else to make Dynamo work.

stops.notes: The jetty has been rebuilt and repaired since 1940; I could not confirm how much of the 1940 structure survives, so the text avoids that claim.

stops.name: Fort des Dunes, Leffrinckoucke
stops.text: Built in 1878–80 in the dunes east of Dunkirk, the fort was the headquarters of the French 12th Motorised Infantry Division, part of the rearguard holding the perimeter while the British and French embarked. On the evening of 2 June 1940 dive-bombers struck it and General Janssen, the division's commander, was mortally wounded in a courtyard with several officers. Further bombing on 3 June killed more men inside the fort. The French held long enough for the evacuation to run to 4 June. In September 1944 the Germans used the fort to shoot captured members of the Resistance against the north moat.
stops.look: A sunken 19th-century fort with brick casemates, moats and courtyards, now a museum (the Musérial) on the 1940 battle and the evacuation. Plaques by the entrance remember the soldiers killed in 1940 and the executed resistance fighters. The national military cemetery lies next to the fort.
stops.plan: Open 3 Mar–1 Nov 2026, Tuesday to Sunday 10:00–18:00, closed Mondays. Adult about €7–8, child €3.50. Audio-guides and guided tours available. Bus C1 or C2 to 'Leffrinckoucke Fort des Dunes'. Check the website before you go.
stops.disputed: The commonly quoted toll of 150–200 dead in the June 1940 bombing is challenged by burial records suggesting nearer a hundred; sources also differ on whether seven or eight resistance fighters were shot here in September 1944.

aar.ev: Dive-bombers hit the French rearguard headquarters and mortally wound its commanding general.
aar.st: The fort was headquarters of the French 12th Motorised Infantry Division, part of the rearguard that let the evacuation run to 4 June. On 2 June 1940 dive-bombers mortally wounded General Janssen in a courtyard, and more men died in a raid the next day. Today the sunken fort is a museum, with plaques by the entrance and the national military cemetery next door.
aar.rem: The evacuation lasted until 4 June because French soldiers like those at this fort held the line.

stops.notes: Fort's own site not opened; hours/prices from the Dunkirk tourist office sheet (marked 'unsecured') and the 2026 remembrance guide. TracesOfWar gives 51.053383, 2.446813 for the fort itself; the tourist sheet point is used as it is the visitor address.

stops.name: Dunkirk Memorial and Town Cemetery (CWGC)
stops.text: The Dunkirk Memorial commemorates more than 4,500 men of the British Expeditionary Force who died in the 1939–40 campaign, or later in captivity after being taken prisoner then, and have no known grave. Designed by Philip Hepworth, it was unveiled by Queen Elizabeth The Queen Mother on 29 June 1957. It forms the entrance to the British war graves section of Dunkirk Town Cemetery, on the road towards Veurne (Furnes) in Belgium, where men of both world wars are buried.
stops.look: A colonnaded entrance with the names of the missing on its panels and an engraved glass panel by John Hutton showing the evacuation. Through it lie the Second World War plots (I and II) and First World War plots IV and V; the other First World War plots are reached via the civil cemetery entrance.
stops.plan: Free, open daily. Wheelchair accessible, with a disabled parking space in front of the memorial and a slope from the pavement. Address: route de Furnes, Dunkirk.
stops.disputed: CWGC lists 4,509 identified casualties on the memorial; the Dunkirk tourist office guide gives 4,528.

aar.ev: A memorial is unveiled to the British soldiers of 1940 who have no known grave.
aar.st: The memorial names more than 4,500 men of the British Expeditionary Force who died in 1939–40, or later in captivity, and have no known grave. Philip Hepworth designed it and the Queen Mother unveiled it in 1957. Today its colonnade, with John Hutton's engraved glass panel of the evacuation, leads into the war graves plots of the town cemetery.
aar.rem: The men named here are those the evacuation could not save and whose graves were never found.

stops.notes: CWGC coordinates have only 4–5 decimals.

stops.name: Zuydcoote and Bray-Dunes beach wrecks
stops.text: On 29 May 1940 the Thames paddle steamer HMS Crested Eagle, serving as an anti-aircraft ship, left the East Mole with about 600 men, including survivors of the bombed Grenade and Fenella. Bombs set her stern on fire less than a mile out and her captain, Lieutenant Commander Bernard Booth, ran her ashore opposite the Zuydcoote sanatorium; about 200 survivors were picked up. A few hundred metres away lies the Devonia, bombed on 30 May and beached to serve as a jetty. Further east at Bray-Dunes, soldiers drove lorries into the sea at low tide to build improvised piers.
stops.look: At low tide, the blackened ribs and paddle-wheel frames of the Crested Eagle rise from the sand, with a plaque placed in 2015; the Devonia lies a few hundred metres east. On the Bray-Dunes seafront a monument honours the French 12th Motorised Infantry Division.
stops.plan: Free. Wrecks visible only around low tide, best at spring tides: check tide tables (maree.info) first. Park on Rue de Wattrelos, Zuydcoote; the Crested Eagle is about 500 m from the beach access. Do not get cut off by the rising tide.
stops.disputed: Casualty figures for the Crested Eagle do not reconcile: about 600 aboard, about 200 rescued and a BBC-cited figure of about 300 killed.

aar.ev: A burning paddle steamer packed with soldiers is run ashore on Zuydcoote beach.
aar.st: HMS Crested Eagle left the East Mole with about 600 men aboard and was set ablaze by bombs less than a mile out. Her captain beached her opposite the Zuydcoote sanatorium; about 200 survivors were rescued. The Devonia was beached nearby the next day as a jetty. Today, at low tide, the Crested Eagle's blackened frames rise from the sand beside a 2015 plaque.
aar.rem: The wrecks show that the sea route home was as dangerous as the beaches.

stops.notes: Renamed: the best-known wrecks (Crested Eagle and Devonia) are on Zuydcoote beach between Zuydcoote and Bray-Dunes; coordinates are for the Crested Eagle. Devonia: 51.079289, 2.502140 (same guide). Treat as a war grave site.

stops.name: La Plaine au Bois massacre memorial, Esquelbecq (Wormhout)
stops.text: On 28 May 1940 British units held Wormhout to cover the retreat to Dunkirk: the 2nd Royal Warwickshire Regiment, the 4th Cheshire Regiment and 210 Battery of the 53rd (Worcestershire Yeomanry) Anti-Tank Regiment. After they were overrun by the SS Leibstandarte Adolf Hitler, about 95 prisoners were herded into a cowshed at La Plaine au Bois and killed with grenades and gunfire. A handful survived, among them Privates Bert Evans and Arthur Johnson and Gunner Brian Fahey. Post-war testimony blamed Wilhelm Mohnke, who denied it and was never tried; he died in 2001.
stops.look: A replica of the barn stands in the fields, reached by a path lined with 80 beech trees. Nearby are a stele inaugurated on 28 May 2010 to the Allied and civilian dead of Wormhout, Ledringhem and Esquelbecq, and an orientation table explaining the fighting. A separate memorial stands on the D17.
stops.plan: Free, open access. Address: Rue des Dunkirk Veterans, Esquelbecq. A €2 trail leaflet covering Esquelbecq, Ledringhem and Wormhout is sold by Terre de Flandre Tourisme; group guided tours in English on request.
stops.disputed: Victim numbers vary: about 80 killed outright, with sources giving 80 or 81 dead and differing on how many of the wounded later died.
links: Plaine au Bois site (Terre de Flandre Tourisme)

aar.ev: SS troops herd British prisoners into a cowshed and kill them with grenades and gunfire.
aar.st: Soldiers of the Royal Warwicks, the Cheshires and the Royal Artillery held Wormhout to cover the retreat to Dunkirk. Once captured, about 95 were packed into a cowshed at La Plaine au Bois by the SS Leibstandarte and murdered; only a handful survived. Today a replica barn stands at the end of a path lined with 80 beech trees.
aar.rem: No one was ever tried for the Wormhout massacre.

stops.notes: Coordinates are the tourist office's point for the Plaine au Bois site (barn replica). The roadside memorial on the D17 is at 50.884785, 2.445112 (TracesOfWar). The 2026 guide says a related museum is at the Maison du Westhoek; not verified further.

stops.name: La Coupole V-2 site, Helfaut
stops.text: From October 1943 the Organisation Todt, using forced labour, built a vast bunker in a chalk quarry near Saint-Omer to assemble, fuel and launch V-2 rockets against London and southern England. Its heart was a chamber under a concrete dome. Allied bombing under Operation Crossbow followed; in June and July 1944 RAF Tallboy bombs wrecked the outer works and blocked the launch tunnels. On 4 August an Operation Aphrodite drone aimed at the site overshot. The complex never entered service: work stopped, the Germans abandoned it and the Allies captured it in September 1944.
stops.look: The huge concrete dome sits on the edge of the quarry. Inside, tunnels and galleries lead to the history centre on the V-weapons, the occupation of northern France and the forced labour that built the site, plus a 3D planetarium on the space race.
stops.plan: Open daily 9:00–18:00 (10:00–19:00 from 5 July to 31 August). History Centre adult €13, child €9.50; combined ticket with planetarium €20.50. Tickets can be bought online. Check the website before you go.

aar.ev: RAF Tallboy bombs wreck the approaches to a giant V-2 launch bunker before it fires.
aar.st: Forced labourers built a launch base for V-2 rockets under a concrete dome in a quarry near Saint-Omer from October 1943. Tallboy bombs in June and July 1944 wrecked the outer works and blocked the tunnels, and the site was abandoned and captured in September. Today the dome houses a history centre on the V-weapons and occupation, with a planetarium alongside.

q.t: How many V-2s were launched from La Coupole?
q.x: Allied bombing blocked the tunnels in 1944; the site was abandoned unfinished and captured in September 1944.

aar.rem: La Coupole shows how much effort Germany spent on weapons that bombing kept out of action.

stops.notes: Prices page does not state the year; hours on the home page also undated.

stops.name: Blockhaus d'Éperlecques
stops.text: Under the cover name Kraftwerk Nord West, the Organisation Todt began this bunker in the forest near Watten in March 1943 as a launch facility for V-2 rockets, planned for over 100 missiles and up to 36 launches a day. It was built largely by prisoners of war and conscripted workers held in nearby camps. On 27 August 1943, 187 US B-17s bombed it while the freshly poured concrete was still setting. Part was later finished as a liquid oxygen plant. Tallboy raids in June and July 1944, including on 6 July, caused severe damage, and construction stopped that month.
stops.look: A colossal concrete block in the woods, its roof and walls scarred by bomb craters and the twisted reinforcing of the August 1943 raid. A woodland trail leads past V-weapons and a V-2 replica to the bunker, which you walk into and around.
stops.plan: March–October: March weekends only 14:00–17:00; April–June and September 11:00–17:30; July–August 10:00–18:30; October 13:00–17:00. Adult €11.50, child €6.50. No booking for individuals. Allow 1h45.

aar.ev: American B-17s bomb a giant V-2 bunker while its concrete is still setting.
aar.st: The Germans began this V-2 launch bunker near Watten in March 1943, using prisoners of war and conscripted labour. On 27 August 1943, 187 US B-17s bombed it before the concrete had set, and Tallboy raids in 1944 halted work. Today the scarred concrete block stands in the woods at the end of a trail past V-weapon displays.

q.t: What was the bunker's cover name?
q.x: It was disguised as 'Kraftwerk Nord West', a power station, though it was meant to launch V-2 rockets.

aar.rem: Bombing the bunker while the concrete was still wet did more damage than later raids on the finished structure.

stops.notes: Privately owned; listed monument historique since 1986. Official hours page gives no year; assumed current.

stops.name: Batterie Todt (Atlantic Wall Museum), Audinghen
stops.text: Work on the battery at Haringzelles, near Cap Gris-Nez, began on 22 July 1940. First called Siegfried, it was renamed after Fritz Todt, head of the Organisation Todt, who died in 1942. Four 380 mm naval guns in concrete casemates could reach the English coast, and the battery shelled shipping and the Dover area; the Cap Gris-Nez guns caused 3,059 alerts and 216 civilian deaths in England. On 29 September 1944, after heavy bombing, the North Nova Scotia Highlanders of the 3rd Canadian Infantry Division took it during Operation Undergo.
stops.look: Casemate 1, a massive concrete gun house, holds the private Atlantic Wall Museum with uniforms, weapons and posters. Outside stands a 280 mm K5 railway gun, one of two survivors, brought here from Fort Nieulay at Calais in 1992. The other casemates lie in the surrounding fields.
stops.plan: February–mid-November: Feb, Mar, Nov 14:00–17:30; Apr–Jun and Sep–Oct 10:00–18:00, closed Mondays; Jul–Aug 10:00–18:30; also open 26–31 Dec. Adult €9, child €6. Check the website before you go.
stops.disputed: Sources differ on when the battery first fired: English Wikipedia gives 20 January 1942, while French Wikipedia cites a 1940 German press report of a shell fired during construction.

aar.ev: Canadian infantry storm the giant cross-Channel gun battery after heavy bombing.
aar.st: Four 380 mm naval guns at Haringzelles could reach England, and the Cap Gris-Nez batteries shelled Dover and Channel shipping from 1942. On 29 September 1944 the North Nova Scotia Highlanders captured the battery in Operation Undergo. Today Casemate 1 houses the Atlantic Wall Museum, with a rare K5 railway gun standing outside.

q.t: Who captured Batterie Todt in September 1944?
q.x: The North Nova Scotia Highlanders of the 3rd Canadian Infantry Division took the battery on 29 September 1944 during Operation Undergo.

aar.rem: From here, German guns could hit England across the narrowest part of the Channel.

stops.notes: Museum is private. Hours/prices from guide-tourisme-france.com listing for 2026, which itself says to check batterietodt.com; the official site was not opened.

stops.name: Brest Fortress, Belarus (June 1941)
stops.text: At 04:15 Moscow time on 22 June 1941 German artillery, including 60 cm mortars, opened Operation Barbarossa against this 19th-century fortress on the Bug. The attackers were the Austrian 45th Infantry Division under Fritz Schlieper, about 17,000 men. Inside were around 9,000 Soviet troops from the 6th and 42nd Rifle Divisions and NKVD border guards, plus families. The Germans expected one day; it took about a week. Captain Ivan Zubachyov and Commissar Yefim Fomin led the citadel's resistance; Fomin was shot after capture. The East Fort surrendered on 29 June after Luftwaffe bombing. Major Pyotr Gavrilov, wounded, was taken on 23 July. About 6,800 Soviet soldiers were captured.
stops.look: Enter through the star-shaped main gate cut into the earth rampart, then walk to the huge stone head of the 'Courage' monument and the 100 m bayonet obelisk. Look for the battered Kholm and Terespol gates, the ruined barracks, the 'Thirst' sculpture and the defence museum in the old barracks ring.
stops.plan: FCDO advises against all travel to Belarus. The grounds are open; the Museum of the Defence opens 9:00–18:00, closed Mondays, with tickets on site. Some side exhibitions close on Tuesdays and the information centre is shut until 15 April 2027. Check the website before you go.
stops.disputed: Soviet accounts from the 1950s, popularised by Sergei Smirnov, said the fortress held out for a month and that nobody surrendered. Modern research finds organised resistance ended around 29 June, with only scattered holdouts after that.

aar.ev: German guns open Operation Barbarossa against the fortress on the Bug before dawn.
aar.st: At 04:15 on 22 June 1941 the Austrian 45th Infantry Division attacked Brest Fortress, expecting to take it in a day. Soviet troops, border guards and their families held parts of it for about a week, and the East Fort fell on 29 June. Today you enter through the star-shaped gate in the rampart and walk past ruined barracks to the giant 'Courage' head and the bayonet obelisk.

q.t: Which German formation attacked Brest Fortress on 22 June 1941?
q.x: The 45th Infantry Division under Fritz Schlieper, about 17,000 men with no tanks of their own, made the attack and needed about a week, not a day.

aar.rem: Brest was the first fight of Barbarossa, and its legend of endless resistance was built after the war.

stops.notes: TRAVEL ADVICE: the UK FCDO advises against all travel to Belarus (gov.uk advice updated 10 Sep 2026, still current 17 Oct 2026): risk of arbitrary arrest, dual nationals treated as Belarusian, very limited consular help, travel insurance may be invalid. Coordinates are TracesOfWar's point for the central memorial; Wikipedia gives 52.082961, 23.654251 for the fortress as a whole. 'Courage' and 'Thirst' are the usual English names of the two main sculptures; Wikipedia names 'Thirst' and the 'Main Monument'.

stops.name: Victory Museum, Poklonnaya Hill, Moscow
stops.text: Poklonnaya Hill, once a vantage point on the western road into Moscow, is where Napoleon waited in vain in 1812 for the keys to the Kremlin. In 1983 work began on a national museum of the 'Great Patriotic War', and the Central Museum of the Great Patriotic War, now called the Victory Museum, opened here on 9 May 1995 for the 50th anniversary of victory. It is Russia's main museum of the Soviet war of 1941–45, covering the battle for Moscow, Leningrad, Stalingrad, Kursk and the drive to Berlin. In front stands an obelisk 141.8 m high, 10 cm for each day of the war, and the surrounding Victory Park holds an outdoor display of weapons and vehicles.
stops.look: Approach across the Square of Victors to the tall obelisk with Nike, then enter the curved museum. Look for the Hall of Commanders with its 'Sword and Shield of Victory', the Hall of Remembrance, large dioramas of key battles and, outside, rows of tanks, guns and aircraft in the park.
stops.plan: FCDO advises against all travel to Russia. Museum open Tuesday–Sunday (some exhibitions until 21:00), closed Mondays; tickets from about 600 roubles, sold online and on site. Park free. Check the website before you go.
links: Museum of the Great Patriotic War, Moscow (Wikipedia)

aar.ev: Russia's national museum of the Soviet war opens for the fiftieth anniversary of victory.
aar.st: Poklonnaya Hill, where Napoleon waited for the keys to the Kremlin in 1812, became the site of Russia's main museum of the war of 1941–45. The museum opened on 9 May 1995, fronted by an obelisk 141.8 m high. Today you cross the Square of Victors to the obelisk, visit halls and battle dioramas inside, and walk among tanks and guns in the park.

q.t: What does the 141.8 m height of the Poklonnaya obelisk represent?
o: The height of the Kremlin's tallest tower
The number of Soviet divisions in 1945
10 cm for each day of the war
q.x: The Soviet-German war lasted 1,418 days, from 22 June 1941 to 9 May 1945, so the obelisk rises 10 cm for each day.

aar.rem: Russia's official memory of the war is presented here; compare it with what you see at the battlefields themselves.

stops.notes: TRAVEL ADVICE: the UK FCDO advises against all travel to Russia (gov.uk advice updated 18 Sep 2026, still current 17 Oct 2026): drone attacks and short-notice airspace closures, increased risk of British nationals being detained, dual nationals treated as Russian, extremely limited consular help, travel insurance may be invalid. The official site shows hours for the 'Path to Victory' exhibition only; general hours and prices were not fully listed. Museum interprets the war from the Soviet/Russian state perspective.

stops.name: Piskaryovskoye Cemetery, St Petersburg
stops.text: During the siege of Leningrad, from September 1941 to 27 January 1944, the city's dead were brought here by lorry and sledge and buried in trenches. The cemetery holds about 420,000 civilians, most of whom died of starvation and cold, and about 50,000 soldiers of the Leningrad Front, in 186 mass graves. Each grave is marked only with the year of burial. The memorial, designed by Alexander Vasilyev and Yevgeny Levinson, opened on 9 May 1960. Its centrepiece is the bronze figure of the Motherland by Vera Isayeva and Robert Taurit. On the granite wall behind her is a poem by Olga Berggolts, the poet whose radio broadcasts kept the besieged city company.
stops.look: Begin at the eternal flame between two small pavilions with the exhibition, then walk down the 480 m central avenue between the low grassy mounds of the mass graves, each with a granite slab giving only a year and a hammer and sickle or a star. The Motherland statue and Berggolts's wall close the view.
stops.plan: FCDO advises against all travel to Russia. Grounds open daily 9:00–18:00 in autumn and winter, to 21:00 in spring and summer; exhibition pavilion 9:00–18:00 daily. Admission and guided tours free. Check the website before you go.
stops.disputed: Burial figures vary: Wikipedia gives about 420,000 civilians and 50,000 soldiers, the Memorial Museums portal 470,000 residents, and a plaque on site cites 641,803 starvation deaths for the whole city. There is no complete register of those buried.

aar.ev: Lorries and sledges bring the dead of the starving city to mass trenches here.
aar.st: During the 872-day siege of Leningrad the dead were buried here in 186 mass graves, about 420,000 civilians and 50,000 soldiers. The memorial designed by Vasilyev and Levinson opened on 9 May 1960, with the bronze Motherland and a poem by Olga Berggolts. Today you walk from the eternal flame down a long avenue between grassy grave mounds, each marked only with a year.
aar.rem: Most of the people buried here were civilians killed by hunger and cold, not by bullets or bombs.

stops.notes: TRAVEL ADVICE: the UK FCDO advises against all travel to Russia (updated 18 Sep 2026): detention risk, drone attacks, extremely limited consular help, insurance may be invalid. Official address Prospekt Nepokorennykh 72. Wikipedia's own coordinates (59.9969, 30.4214) have only four decimals; TracesOfWar used. Wikipedia transliterates the poet's name Berggolts; also seen as Bergholz.

stops.name: Museum of the Defence and Siege of Leningrad
stops.text: This museum began while the siege was still on: an exhibition, 'Heroic Defence of Leningrad', opened in the Solyanoy Gorodok halls on 30 April 1944, and it became the Leningrad Defence Museum on 27 January 1946, the second anniversary of the siege being lifted. In 1949 it was closed during the 'Leningrad Affair', Stalin's purge of the city's wartime leadership; its managers were persecuted, it was liquidated in 1952, and weapons were melted down. It reopened in the same building on 8 September 1989. It covers the 872 days of encirclement, the Road of Life across Lake Ladoga and daily life on bread rations that fell to 125 g for dependants.
stops.look: The main exhibition is in one large hall on the upper floor: weapons, uniforms, posters and models, a big map of the Road of Life, a recreated siege-time room with a small iron stove, and a display of the 125 g bread ration. Labels are mostly in Russian; an audio guide is offered.
stops.plan: FCDO advises against all travel to Russia. Open 10:00–18:00, closed Tuesdays and the last Wednesday of the month (ticket office closes 17:30). Modest admission charge; audio guide extra. Check the website before you go.
stops.disputed: Sources disagree on the dates of its first life: the St Petersburg Encyclopaedia gives closure in August 1949 and liquidation in 1952, while some guides give closure in 1952 or 1953.
links: State Memorial Museum of the Defence and Siege of Leningrad (official)

aar.ev: Leningrad opens a museum of its own siege, two years after the blockade ended.
aar.st: An exhibition on the city's defence opened here in April 1944 and became a museum on 27 January 1946. Caught up in Stalin's 'Leningrad Affair', it was closed in 1949 and liquidated in 1952, and only reopened in 1989. Today you see one large hall of weapons, posters and a Road of Life map, a recreated siege room and the 125 g bread ration.

q.t: Why was the original siege museum closed after the war?
o: Its building was needed for a new metro station
It was caught up in the 'Leningrad Affair' purge
It was damaged by a wartime unexploded bomb
q.x: In 1949 Stalin's 'Leningrad Affair' purged the city's wartime leaders. The museum was closed, its managers persecuted and it was liquidated in 1952, reopening only in 1989.

aar.rem: Even remembering the siege was political: its museum was shut for almost forty years.

stops.notes: TRAVEL ADVICE: the UK FCDO advises against all travel to Russia (updated 18 Sep 2026). Address Solyanoy pereulok 9 (metro Chernyshevskaya). COORDINATES: no source with 5 decimals found (no coords on Wikipedia, official site or TracesOfWar); 59.9445, 30.3409 is the map pin on dark-tourism.com and rusmania gives 59.9432, 30.3397 - verify before publishing. Closed day: official site says Tuesdays plus last Wednesday 'sanitary day'; older guides say last Thursday. A 2014–18 plan for a new building near Smolny was dropped in 2019 in favour of expanding at Solyanoy. Name shortened from 'State Memorial Museum of the Defence and Siege of Leningrad' to fit 45 chars.

stops.name: Mamayev Kurgan and 'The Motherland Calls'
stops.text: Marked on military maps as Height 102.0, this hill overlooks central Stalingrad and the Volga crossings, and whoever held it could see and shell the river. From mid-September 1942 it changed hands repeatedly as the German 6th Army tried to reach the Volga and Chuikov's 62nd Army clung on. Fighting on the slopes went on until 26 January 1943, when Soviet forces advancing from the west broke through to the defenders. The memorial ensemble was built from 1959 and 'The Motherland Calls', 85 m to the tip of her sword, was unveiled on 15 October 1967. Yevgeny Vuchetich sculpted it; Nikolai Nikitin engineered it. About 34,505 defenders are buried on the hill, and Marshal Chuikov chose to be buried here.
stops.look: From the avenue at the foot, climb past the Square of Those Who Fought to the Death and the ruined-wall reliefs, to the circular Hall of Military Glory with its eternal flame and changing guard. Above, the vast sword-raising Motherland stands among the mass graves; Chuikov's grave is near her base.
stops.plan: FCDO advises against all travel to Russia. The memorial is open and free for all visitors; museum-reserve guided excursions run daily 9:00–15:30. Expect long flights of steps. Check the website before you go.

aar.ev: German and Soviet troops begin months of fighting for the hill above the Volga.
aar.st: Height 102.0 dominated central Stalingrad and the Volga crossings, and it changed hands repeatedly from mid-September 1942 until Soviet forces broke through to its defenders on 26 January 1943. About 34,505 defenders are buried here, with Marshal Chuikov. Today you climb from the avenue past reliefs and the Hall of Military Glory to the 85 m Motherland among the graves.
aar.rem: Whoever held Height 102.0 could see and shell the Volga crossings that kept Stalingrad alive.

stops.notes: TRAVEL ADVICE: the UK FCDO advises against all travel to Russia (updated 18 Sep 2026). Coordinates are for the statue; Wikipedia gives DMS 48°44′33″N 44°32′13″E, converted here. TracesOfWar puts the relief wall at 48.741571, 44.539024. The museum-reserve site lists restoration of the statue as a project but gives no dates; the exterior restoration of 2019–20 was criticised. The often-quoted '200 steps' could not be confirmed and is left out. Solemn: mass graves on the hill, so no quiz.

stops.name: Panorama Museum & Gerhardt's Mill, Volgograd
stops.text: The Panorama Museum on the Volga embankment is the main museum of the Battle of Stalingrad, with eight halls, four dioramas, a circular panorama painting and about 4,000 exhibits, among them the rifle of the sniper Vasily Zaitsev. Beside it stands the shell of Gerhardt's (or Grudinin's) mill. Bombed and set on fire on 14 September 1942, it was taken that night by men of General Rodimtsev's 13th Guards Rifle Division, newly ferried across the Volga. By 20 September the 3rd Battalion, 42nd Guards Rifle Regiment, held it as a strongpoint, and it stayed semi-encircled for 58 days. It was deliberately left unrestored after the war.
stops.look: Start with the scarred, roofless mill, its brick walls pitted by bullets and shells, then go into the museum for the dioramas, Zaitsev's rifle and the panorama on the top floor. Pavlov's House is across the square, which shows how close the lines were.
stops.plan: FCDO advises against all travel to Russia. Museum open Tuesday–Friday and Sunday 10:00–18:00, Saturday to 20:00, closed Mondays; ticket office closes 30 minutes earlier. Tickets sold online and on site. Mill seen from outside. Check the website before you go.
stops.disputed: The mill is named after its pre-revolutionary owner Gerhardt and after Grudinin, a Soviet-era name; sources use both. Russian Wikipedia gives the defenders as the 42nd Rifle Regiment, TracesOfWar as the 42nd Guards Rifle Regiment.

aar.ev: Rodimtsev's guardsmen cross the Volga and seize the burning mill as a strongpoint.
aar.st: The mill was bombed and set on fire on 14 September 1942, and that night men of the 13th Guards Rifle Division, just across the Volga, took it. Held as a strongpoint, it stayed semi-encircled for 58 days and was left unrestored after the war. Today you see the roofless, shell-pitted mill beside the Panorama Museum with its dioramas, panorama painting and Zaitsev's rifle.

q.t: Why does Gerhardt's Mill still stand as a ruin?
o: It was deliberately left unrestored as a memorial
Its owners never returned to claim it
Rebuilding was blocked by a court case
q.x: It was one of a handful of Stalingrad buildings kept in their wartime state on purpose, as a memorial to the street fighting near the Volga.

aar.rem: Stalingrad was won and lost a few hundred metres from the Volga, in buildings like this mill.

stops.notes: TRAVEL ADVICE: the UK FCDO advises against all travel to Russia (updated 18 Sep 2026). Coordinates are for the museum (ulitsa Marshala Chuykova 47); the mill is at 48.715588, 44.532828 (TracesOfWar). A section of the mill's brickwork collapsed in strong wind in May 2021. Prices not shown on the official page. Museum's own older site: panorama.volgadmin.ru.

stops.name: Pavlov's House, Volgograd
stops.text: This four-storey 1930s block on what was 9 January Square was seized in late September 1942 by a group under Sergeant Yakov Pavlov of the 42nd Guards Rifle Regiment, 13th Guards Rifle Division. Reinforced to about 31 men under Lieutenant Ivan Afanasyev, they mined the approaches, set up machine guns and fired an anti-tank rifle from the roof, holding the house until the Soviet counter-offensive on 25 November. Three of the garrison were killed. The house became the best-known symbol of Stalingrad's street fighting, and General Chuikov later joked that the Germans lost more men attacking it than they did taking Paris.
stops.look: The rebuilt house is still lived in. On the end wall facing Sovetskaya Street is the memorial wall of 1985, built of bricks gathered after the battle, with a soldier relief and the garrison's names. Gerhardt's Mill and the Panorama Museum stand across the square.
stops.plan: FCDO advises against all travel to Russia. A residential building seen from the street, so always accessible and free. Do not enter the flats or stairwells. Combine with the Panorama Museum next door.
stops.disputed: Who commanded is debated: the house is named after Sergeant Pavlov, but some historians credit Lieutenant Afanasyev. The start date (23 or 27 September) and the length of the defence (58 or 60 days) vary, and German records do not support claims of very heavy assaults on the house.

aar.ev: Pavlov's garrison still holds the apartment block as the Soviet counter-offensive begins.
aar.st: In late September 1942 Sergeant Yakov Pavlov's group seized this apartment block, and about 31 men under Lieutenant Afanasyev held it until 25 November. They mined the approaches and fired an anti-tank rifle from the roof. Today the rebuilt house is still lived in, and a memorial wall of battle bricks bearing the garrison's names faces Sovetskaya Street.

q.t: Besides Sergeant Pavlov, who is credited by some historians with commanding the house's defence?
q.x: Pavlov seized the house, but Lieutenant Ivan Afanasyev arrived with reinforcements and some historians see him as the real commander of the garrison.

aar.rem: Pavlov's House shows how a single building could become a fortress, and a legend, in Stalingrad's street fighting.

stops.notes: TRAVEL ADVICE: the UK FCDO advises against all travel to Russia (updated 18 Sep 2026). Current address Sovetskaya ulitsa 39 (pre-war Penzenskaya 61). 'private': true because it is a residential building viewed from outside. Memorial wall unveiled 4 May 1985 (architect V. Maslyaev, sculptor V. Fetisov).

stops.name: Rossoshka war cemeteries
stops.text: Rossoshka lies in the steppe about 37 km north-west of central Volgograd, in the middle of the pocket where the German 6th Army was encircled from November 1942 until its surrender in early February 1943. The villages of Bolshaya and Malaya Rossoshka were destroyed in the fighting. Two cemeteries face each other across the road. The Soviet cemetery opened on 23 August 1997 and holds about 18,520 Red Army dead, mostly unknown. The German cemetery, built by the Volksbund and dedicated in 1999, holds over 61,000 German soldiers, and granite cubes dedicated in 2006 carry the names of nearly 120,000 missing. A Chapel of Peace opened in 2016.
stops.look: On the German side, a circular enclosure about 150 m across with a central cross, and beyond it rows of tall granite cubes covered in names. Across the road, the Soviet cemetery with Vysotsky's lines on the entrance walls and the 'Mother in Sorrow' holding a bell without a clapper.
stops.plan: FCDO advises against all travel to Russia. Open-air cemeteries, free. No public transport: by car or taxi, past Volgograd airport then about 17 km on. Toilets on site. Check the Volksbund page before you go.
stops.disputed: Figures for the German cemetery differ: the Volksbund lists 61,791 buried (71,427 total recorded), Wikipedia about 65,000 after later reburials, and Volgograd State University's guide 'more than 50,000'.

aar.ev: In the frozen steppe pocket, the encircled German 6th Army slowly collapses.
aar.st: Rossoshka lies in the middle of the pocket where the German 6th Army was trapped from November 1942. Since 1997 and 1999 two cemeteries have faced each other here, one for about 18,520 Red Army dead and one for more than 61,000 Germans. Today you see a circular German enclosure, granite cubes of names, and across the road the Soviet 'Mother in Sorrow'.
aar.rem: Two cemeteries facing each other across one road, in the middle of the Stalingrad pocket.

stops.notes: TRAVEL ADVICE: the UK FCDO advises against all travel to Russia (updated 18 Sep 2026). Coordinates are for the German cemetery, converted from the Volksbund's DMS 48°49'31.61"N, 44°9'55.15"E; Wikipedia gives 48.82417, 44.16472. Volgograd State University puts the site '60 km from Volgograd' (by road); Volksbund and Wikipedia say about 37 km. Volsu says the German site was established in 1992 and dedicated 1999.

stops.name: Prokhorovka battlefield, Belgorod region
stops.text: On 12 July 1943, during the German Kursk offensive (Operation Citadel), Pavel Rotmistrov's 5th Guards Tank Army counter-attacked Paul Hausser's II SS Panzer Corps on the fields south-west of Prokhorovka, about 87 km south-east of Kursk. Some 500 Soviet tanks attacked in two waves against 294 German tanks and assault guns. The Germans stopped the attack, but the Red Army stopped the German advance; Hitler ended Citadel on 13 July, partly because the Allies had landed in Sicily. Soviet losses were heavy: Valery Zamulin counts 340 tanks and self-propelled guns, against about 60–80 German armoured vehicles damaged or destroyed. A memorial bell tower was built in 1995 and the 'Third Military Field of Russia' museum in 2010.
stops.look: The 52 m white bell tower stands on the open field with its bells ringing every 20 minutes. Look for the 'Tank Battle' sculpture of colliding tanks in front of the museum, the Church of Sts Peter and Paul, a tank museum, preserved Soviet armour, and the long rolling fields where the armour met.
stops.plan: FCDO advises against all travel to Russia, and the Belgorod region borders Ukraine. Museum open Tuesday–Sunday 10:00–17:00 (ticket office to 16:30), closed Mondays; memorial grounds open at all times. Check the website before you go.
stops.disputed: Soviet histories called Prokhorovka 'the greatest tank battle in history' and a decisive victory. Modern research (Zamulin, Frieser, Glantz) shows far fewer tanks than claimed and much heavier Soviet than German losses; the battle stopped the German advance but was a tactical Soviet defeat.

aar.ev: Rotmistrov's tank army charges the SS panzer corps across the fields near Prokhorovka.
aar.st: On 12 July 1943 the 5th Guards Tank Army attacked the II SS Panzer Corps here in two waves of about 500 tanks. The Germans stopped them with far lighter losses, but their own advance was halted and Hitler called off Operation Citadel the next day. Today a 52 m white bell tower rises over the open fields, with a museum, a church and preserved Soviet armour.

q.t: Which German formation did the 5th Guards Tank Army attack at Prokhorovka?
q.x: Rotmistrov's tanks struck Paul Hausser's II SS Panzer Corps, part of Hoth's 4th Panzer Army, which had 294 tanks and assault guns.

aar.rem: Prokhorovka halted the Germans but was costly for the Red Army; its fame owes much to Soviet legend.

stops.notes: TRAVEL ADVICE: the UK FCDO advises against all travel to Russia (updated 18 Sep 2026). The Belgorod region borders Ukraine and has been hit by cross-border drone and artillery fire since 2022; the official site mentions no restrictions but check locally. Bell tower height: TracesOfWar 52 m; other sources quote 59 m - not resolved. Museum-reserve address ul. Parkovaya 47; site redirects to a Cyrillic domain. Name: the Russian 'Третье ратное поле России' is also translated 'Third Battlefield of Russia'. Coordinates point to the bell tower; the tank fighting covered several kilometres around it.

stops.name: Kursk Arc memorial complex, Kursk
stops.text: The Battle of Kursk, from 5 July to 23 August 1943, began as Germany's last great offensive in the east, Operation Citadel, aimed at cutting off the Soviet salient around Kursk from north and south. Deep Soviet defences halted it within a week, and Soviet counter-offensives went on to take Orel and Kharkov. This memorial complex on Prospekt Pobedy opened in 1998 for the battle's 55th anniversary. It includes a mass grave with an eternal flame, a bronze statue of Marshal Georgy Zhukov unveiled on 5 July 1998, the Church of St George, a 24 m triumphal arch of 2000 crowned by St George slaying the dragon, and an alley of wartime weapons.
stops.look: A 600 m avenue lined by the triumphal arch with its soldier statues, the gilded-domed church of St George, the Zhukov statue, the mass grave and eternal flame, and an open-air line of equipment including a T-34, an ISU-152 and a Katyusha rocket launcher.
stops.plan: FCDO advises against all travel to Russia, and the Kursk region borders Ukraine. The memorial is open 24 hours and free. Check local conditions before you go.

aar.ev: Germany launches Operation Citadel against the Soviet salient around Kursk.
aar.st: Operation Citadel, launched on 5 July 1943, was meant to pinch off the Soviet salient around Kursk, but deep Soviet defences halted it within a week. Soviet counter-offensives then took Orel and Kharkov. Today a 600 m avenue leads past a triumphal arch, the church of St George, a statue of Zhukov, an eternal flame and a line of T-34s, guns and a Katyusha.

q.t: Whose bronze statue was unveiled at the Kursk memorial on 5 July 1998?
q.x: A bronze statue of Marshal Georgy Zhukov, who coordinated the Soviet fronts at Kursk, was unveiled on 5 July 1998, the 55th anniversary of the start of the battle.

aar.rem: After Kursk the Germans never again launched a major offensive on the Eastern Front.

stops.notes: TRAVEL ADVICE: the UK FCDO advises against all travel to Russia (updated 18 Sep 2026). The Kursk region borders Ukraine and saw a Ukrainian cross-border incursion from August 2024; check conditions locally. No dedicated official website found; Rusmania used as best page. Coordinates are for the triumphal arch at the entrance. Source discrepancy: one guide gives the complex opening in 1998 and the arch in 2000; others date the whole complex to 2000.

stops.name: Khatyn Memorial, Belarus
stops.text: On 22 March 1943, after a partisan ambush nearby, Schutzmannschaft Battalion 118, made up largely of Ukrainian and other Soviet collaborators, and the SS Dirlewanger unit surrounded the village of Khatyn, about 50 km north of Minsk. They herded the villagers into a barn, set it alight and shot those who broke out, then burned the village. About 149 people were killed, around 75 of them children. The blacksmith Yuzif Kaminsky was the only adult survivor. In 1969 the site became the Byelorussian SSR's national war memorial, designed by Yuri Gradov, Valentin Zankovich and Leonid Levin, and it stands for the hundreds of Belarusian villages destroyed in anti-partisan operations.
stops.look: Concrete outlines of the 26 houses, each with a chimney-shaped bell tower ringing in turn, the bronze 'Unbowed Man' of Kaminsky carrying his dead son, the stylised barn roof over the mass grave, the 'Cemetery of Villages' with 185 symbolic graves, and the wall naming camps and extermination sites in Belarus.
stops.plan: FCDO advises against all travel to Belarus. Memorial grounds open at all times; the Khatyn museum opens Tuesday–Sunday 10:00–19:00, closed Mondays. About an hour by car from Minsk; no regular public transport. Check the website before you go.
stops.disputed: Khatyn is often confused with Katyn, where the NKVD shot Polish officers in 1940; historian Norman Davies argues the Soviets chose Khatyn for a national memorial partly to exploit that confusion. Child victims are given as 70 or 75 depending on the count.

aar.ev: German-led auxiliaries lock Khatyn's villagers in a barn and set it on fire.
aar.st: On 22 March 1943 Schutzmannschaft Battalion 118 and the Dirlewanger unit burned Khatyn and its people after a partisan ambush. Only one adult, the blacksmith Yuzif Kaminsky, survived. In 1969 it became the national memorial to Belarus's destroyed villages. Today you walk among concrete outlines of the 26 houses with chimney bells, past the statue of Kaminsky holding his son, to the Cemetery of Villages.
aar.rem: Khatyn stands for hundreds of Belarusian villages burned with their people during anti-partisan operations.

stops.notes: ADDED STOP (not in stoplist): Belarus's national war memorial and the key site for the German occupation and anti-partisan war in the east. TRAVEL ADVICE: the UK FCDO advises against all travel to Belarus (updated 10 Sep 2026, still current 17 Oct 2026). Wikipedia gives 54.33500, 27.94500; TracesOfWar used (6 decimals). Architects' spelling varies (Zankovich/Sankovich). Admission prices not shown on the official site.

stops.name: Reichstag, Berlin
stops.text: Burnt out in the February 1933 fire and unused by the Nazi parliament, the Reichstag was still treated by the Red Army as the symbol of Berlin. Troops of the 3rd Shock Army stormed it from 30 April 1945 against a substantial German garrison, fighting room by room until the defenders gave up on 2 May. That day Yevgeny Khaldei photographed a soldier raising the Soviet flag on the roof, a picture that became the defining image of the war's end. Soviet soldiers covered the walls with graffiti. When Norman Foster rebuilt the building for the Bundestag in the 1990s, much of it was deliberately kept.
stops.look: Inside, preserved Soviet graffiti in Cyrillic and bullet scars survive on the walls, though most are seen only on guided tours. Visitors with a booking climb the glass dome and use the roof terrace. Outside, on the Tiergarten edge, slate plates remember the Reichstag deputies murdered by the Nazis.
stops.plan: Dome and roof terrace are free but need advance online registration with names and dates of birth; bring photo ID. The dome is closed for maintenance 19–30 October 2026 (terrace stays open). Check the website before you go.
stops.disputed: Khaldei's 2 May photograph was staged the day after the building was taken and retouched before publication; accounts also differ over which soldiers first raised a flag on 30 April.
links: Raising a Flag over the Reichstag (Wikipedia)

aar.ev: Soviet troops take the Reichstag after days of room-by-room fighting.
aar.st: The Red Army saw the burnt-out Reichstag as the symbol of Berlin and stormed it from 30 April 1945. The garrison fought room by room until 2 May, when Yevgeny Khaldei photographed the Soviet flag on the roof. Soldiers covered the walls with graffiti, much of it kept in the 1990s rebuild. Today you can climb the glass dome and see preserved Cyrillic graffiti and bullet scars on the walls.

q.t: What happened to the Soviet graffiti when the Reichstag was rebuilt in the 1990s?
o: Much of it was deliberately preserved
It was moved to a Moscow museum
q.x: Norman Foster's rebuild for the Bundestag kept much of the graffiti and bullet damage as traces of history; only offensive inscriptions were removed in agreement with Russian diplomats.

aar.rem: The Reichstag mattered to the Soviets as a symbol, not as a working seat of Nazi government.

stops.notes: Dome closed 19–30 Oct 2026. Graffiti tours inside the building are by separate booking with the Bundestag visitors' service.

stops.name: Topography of Terror, Berlin
stops.text: From 1933 the buildings on Prinz-Albrecht-Straße (now Niederkirchnerstraße) housed the Gestapo headquarters, with its notorious house prison at No. 8, and later the Reich Security Main Office (RSHA) formed in September 1939. Here Himmler's SS and police apparatus ran persecution across Germany and occupied Europe, directing the Einsatzgruppen that murdered Jews behind the Eastern Front. The buildings were wrecked by bombing and cleared after the war. The site lay forgotten beside the Berlin Wall until citizens' groups dug out the cellars in the 1980s. The present documentation centre opened in May 2010.
stops.look: A low grey pavilion holds the main exhibition on the SS and Gestapo. Outside, an open-air trench exhibition runs along excavated cellar walls of the Gestapo buildings, beneath the longest surviving stretch of the outer Berlin Wall on Niederkirchnerstraße.
stops.plan: Open daily 10:00–20:00; free admission. No booking needed for individuals. The official site could not be loaded in October 2026, so check the website before you go.

aar.ev: The Reich Security Main Office is formed to run the SS and police terror.
aar.st: From 1933 this street housed the Gestapo headquarters and its house prison, and from September 1939 the Reich Security Main Office. From here Himmler's apparatus ran persecution across occupied Europe and directed the Einsatzgruppen. Bombed and cleared after the war, the site was rediscovered in the 1980s. Today an exhibition pavilion stands beside excavated Gestapo cellars and a long surviving stretch of the Berlin Wall.
aar.rem: The offices that organised terror across Europe stood here, in the heart of government Berlin.

stops.notes: topographie.de failed to load during research; opening hours taken from a travel listing (tripomatic). Editor should confirm.

stops.name: House of the Wannsee Conference
stops.text: On 20 January 1942 Reinhard Heydrich, head of the Reich Security Main Office, met fifteen senior officials of ministries, the Nazi Party and the SS in this lakeside villa at Am Großen Wannsee 56–58. The meeting lasted about ninety minutes. The decision to murder Europe's Jews had already been taken; Heydrich's purpose was to secure the ministries' cooperation with deportations under SS control. Adolf Eichmann prepared the figures and the minutes, written in bureaucratic euphemism. Only one of thirty copies survived, found by US prosecutor Robert Kempner in Foreign Office files in 1947. The villa opened as a memorial and education centre on 20 January 1992.
stops.look: You walk through the rooms of the villa, including the dining room where the meeting is believed to have taken place. The exhibition explains the participants, the protocol and the course of the Holocaust. The garden runs down to the lake.
stops.plan: Exhibition and garden open daily 10:00–18:00; free. Closed 1–4 Jan, 8 Mar, Good Friday, 1 May, Ascension Day, 3 Oct and 24–31 Dec. Groups of 10+ must book. S-Bahn to Wannsee, then bus 114.

aar.ev: Heydrich gathers senior officials to coordinate the deportation and murder of Europe's Jews.
aar.st: On 20 January 1942 Reinhard Heydrich met fifteen senior officials in this villa for about ninety minutes. The decision to murder Europe's Jews had already been taken; he wanted the ministries' cooperation. Eichmann wrote the minutes, and the only surviving copy was found in 1947. Today you walk through the villa's rooms, including the dining room where the meeting probably took place, with the garden running down to the lake.
aar.rem: Wannsee did not decide the Holocaust; it organised the bureaucracy that carried it out.

stops.notes: Bus 114 from S-Bahn Wannsee; the transport detail is from general knowledge, not the official page.

stops.name: Memorial to the Murdered Jews of Europe
stops.text: Germany's central Holocaust memorial was designed by the American architect Peter Eisenman and dedicated on 10 May 2005, sixty years after the war ended. It covers a whole city block between the Brandenburg Gate and Potsdamer Platz, close to where Hitler's Chancellery stood. The field of 2,711 concrete stelae on undulating ground carries no names or symbols; Eisenman meant it to unsettle rather than explain. The explanation lies underneath, in the Information Centre, which tells the stories of individual families and holds the names of about three million Jewish victims obtained from Yad Vashem.
stops.look: Walk into the field: the ground dips and the stelae rise above head height, cutting off the city. The entrance to the underground Information Centre is at the south-east corner, with rooms on individual victims, families and the sites of murder across Europe.
stops.plan: Field of stelae open 24 hours, free. Information Centre Tue–Sun 10:00–18:00 (last entry 45 minutes before), free; closed Mondays and 24–26 Dec. Security checks can mean a queue.
links: Memorial to the Murdered Jews of Europe (Wikipedia)

aar.ev: Germany dedicates its national memorial to the six million Jews murdered in Europe.
aar.st: Peter Eisenman's memorial was dedicated on 10 May 2005, close to where Hitler's Chancellery stood. Its 2,711 concrete stelae carry no names; the explanation lies underneath, in an Information Centre holding the names of about three million Jewish victims from Yad Vashem. Today you walk into a field of stelae that rise above your head, then go down to rooms on individual victims and families.
aar.rem: Go below ground: the Information Centre turns the abstract field into individual lives.

stops.name: German Resistance Memorial (Bendlerblock)
stops.text: The Bendlerblock housed the headquarters of the Replacement Army, where officers planned Operation Valkyrie. On 20 July 1944 Colonel Claus von Stauffenberg planted a bomb at Hitler's headquarters in East Prussia and flew back here to launch the coup. Hitler survived, and by evening loyal troops had regained control. General Friedrich Fromm had the leaders arrested; Stauffenberg, General Friedrich Olbricht, Colonel Albrecht Mertz von Quirnheim and Lieutenant Werner von Haeften were shot in the courtyard that night, and Ludwig Beck was allowed to shoot himself. The memorial centre documents the whole breadth of German resistance.
stops.look: In the courtyard a bronze figure of a bound young man and a plaque mark the place of the executions. Upstairs, in the rooms used by the plotters, the permanent exhibition covers resistance from churches, workers, students, Jews and the military.
stops.plan: Free. Mon–Fri 9:00–18:00, weekends and holidays 10:00–18:00. Entrance at Stauffenbergstraße 13–14; no booking needed for individuals. Special exhibition on Ravensbrück resistance runs until 4 April 2027.

aar.ev: The plot to kill Hitler fails, and its leaders are shot in this courtyard at night.
aar.st: Officers here planned Operation Valkyrie. On 20 July 1944 Stauffenberg planted a bomb at Hitler's East Prussian headquarters and flew back to launch the coup, but Hitler survived. That night Stauffenberg, Olbricht, Mertz von Quirnheim and Haeften were shot in the courtyard. Today a bronze figure of a bound man marks the courtyard, and the plotters' rooms upstairs hold an exhibition on all forms of German resistance.
aar.rem: The exhibition covers all German resistance, not only the officers of 20 July.

stops.notes: The Bendlerblock is also still a Defence Ministry building; only the memorial section is open to the public.

stops.name: Soviet War Memorial, Tiergarten
stops.text: Built within months of the fighting and unveiled on 11 November 1945, this was the first Soviet memorial in Berlin. Architect Mikhail Gorvits designed the curved colonnade, and Lev Kerbel and Vladimir Tsigal sculpted the bronze soldier on top. More than 2,000 of the Red Army soldiers killed in the Battle of Berlin are buried behind it. Two T-34 tanks and two ML-20 152mm guns, said to be among the first to enter the city, flank the approach. The memorial stood in the British sector, so throughout the Cold War Soviet guards marched into West Berlin to mount guard here under British protection.
stops.look: A curved colonnade of reddish stone topped by a soldier with a rifle slung, on Straße des 17. Juni a few hundred metres west of the Brandenburg Gate. Look for the tanks and guns on their plinths and the inscriptions in Russian.
stops.plan: Open-air and free; accessible at any time, with no booking needed. Easily combined on foot with the Reichstag and the Brandenburg Gate, a few minutes away.

aar.ev: The Soviets unveil their first Berlin memorial over the graves of the city's attackers.
aar.st: Unveiled on 11 November 1945, this was the first Soviet memorial in Berlin, built within months of the fighting. More than 2,000 Red Army soldiers killed in the battle are buried behind it. It stood in the British sector, so Soviet guards mounted guard here throughout the Cold War. Today a curved colonnade topped by a bronze soldier stands near the Brandenburg Gate, flanked by T-34 tanks and heavy guns.
aar.rem: A Soviet war grave in what became West Berlin, guarded by Soviet troops all through the Cold War.

stops.notes: Official URL is a berlin.de listing; not opened during research. No coordinates more precise than 5 decimals available.

stops.name: Soviet War Memorial, Treptower Park
stops.text: Opened on 8 May 1949, the fourth anniversary of the German surrender, Treptow is the largest Soviet war memorial outside the former USSR. It commemorates 7,000 of the roughly 80,000 Red Army soldiers killed in the Battle of Berlin; some 5,000 are buried in the central lawns. Architect Yakov Belopolsky laid out the park, and sculptor Yevgeny Vuchetich made the 12-metre bronze of a Soviet soldier holding a German child and a sword, standing on a broken swastika. Sixteen stone sarcophagi, one for each Soviet republic, carry reliefs and quotations from Stalin in Russian and German.
stops.look: Enter through a granite gateway past the kneeling soldiers, walk down the long axis between the sixteen sarcophagi and the grave lawns, and climb the mound to the soldier statue. Inside its base is a mosaic hall.
stops.plan: Open-air park memorial, free and open at all times, with no booking needed. Take the S-Bahn to Treptower Park station, then walk about ten minutes through the park.

aar.ev: The Soviet Union opens its largest memorial in Germany over 5,000 of its soldiers' graves.
aar.st: Opened on 8 May 1949, Treptow is the largest Soviet war memorial outside the former USSR. Some 5,000 Red Army soldiers of the Battle of Berlin lie in its central lawns. Vuchetich's 12-metre bronze shows a soldier holding a German child and standing on a broken swastika. Today you walk past sixteen carved sarcophagi to the statue on its mound, with a mosaic hall in its base.
aar.rem: This is a cemetery as well as a monument: some 5,000 Soviet soldiers lie under the lawns.

stops.notes: The treaty protection of the Soviet memorials (1990 German–Soviet agreements) is general knowledge, not from an opened source; editor may wish to cut that remark. Official URL is a berlin.de listing not opened during research.

stops.name: Museum Berlin-Karlshorst
stops.text: Shortly before midnight on 8 May 1945, in the officers' mess of a former Wehrmacht engineer school in Karlshorst, Field Marshal Wilhelm Keitel, Admiral Hans-Georg von Friedeburg and General Hans-Jürgen Stumpff signed Germany's unconditional surrender for the army, navy and Luftwaffe. Marshal Georgy Zhukov signed for the Soviet high command and Air Chief Marshal Arthur Tedder for Eisenhower's SHAEF, with General de Lattre de Tassigny and General Carl Spaatz as witnesses. It ratified the surrender signed at Reims the day before. The building became Zhukov's headquarters, then a Soviet museum; it reopened in 1995 and dropped 'German-Russian' from its name in 2022.
stops.look: The signing hall is kept as it was in 1945, with the flags of the four powers behind the table. The upper floor covers the German–Soviet war from both sides. Outside stand Soviet guns, a T-34 and an SU-100 tank destroyer.
stops.plan: Tue–Sun 10:00–18:00, closed Mondays; admission free. No booking needed for individual visitors. Take the S-Bahn to Karlshorst, then walk about 15 minutes.
stops.disputed: Because the Karlshorst signing took effect just after midnight Moscow time, Russia marks Victory Day on 9 May while the West marks 8 May.

aar.ev: Keitel signs Germany's unconditional surrender before Zhukov and Tedder in an officers' mess.
aar.st: Shortly before midnight on 8 May 1945, Keitel, Friedeburg and Stumpff signed Germany's unconditional surrender in this officers' mess, before Marshal Zhukov and Air Chief Marshal Tedder. It ratified the surrender signed at Reims the day before. The building later became a Soviet museum. Today the signing hall is kept as it was in 1945, with the four powers' flags behind the table, and Soviet armour stands outside.

q.t: Why was a second surrender signed at Karlshorst on 8 May 1945?
o: To ratify the surrender signed at Reims the day before
Because the Reims document was lost
Because Dönitz refused to recognise Reims
q.x: Jodl had signed at Reims on 7 May. The Karlshorst ceremony, with Keitel signing before Zhukov and Tedder, ratified it with the Soviet high command present.

aar.rem: The war in Europe formally ended here, in a room you can still stand in.

stops.notes: Transport times from general knowledge.

stops.name: Site of the Führerbunker
stops.text: Hitler moved into the bunker beneath the Reich Chancellery garden in January 1945 and directed the last months of the war from there. The main bunker's floor lay 8.5 metres underground. On 29 April he married Eva Braun, and on 30 April 1945 both killed themselves in his study; their bodies were burned in the garden above. Soviet troops reached the bunker on 2 May. The Soviets and later the East German authorities demolished the Chancellery and most of the bunker, and flats and a car park were built over the site in the late 1980s. Nothing of it is visible.
stops.look: A car park and blocks of flats at the corner of Gertrud-Kolmar-Straße and In den Ministergärten. An information board put up by Berliner Unterwelten in 2006 explains the bunker's layout and fate. It is two minutes from the Holocaust memorial.
stops.plan: Public street, free and open at all times; there is nothing to book. Combine it on foot with the Holocaust memorial and the Topography of Terror.

aar.ev: Hitler and Eva Braun kill themselves in the bunker beneath the Chancellery garden.
aar.st: Hitler directed the last months of the war from this bunker, 8.5 metres underground.
