On 30 April 1945 he and Eva Braun killed themselves in his study, and their bodies were burned in the garden above. The Chancellery and most of the bunker were later demolished and built over. Today a car park and flats cover the site, with a 2006 information board explaining what lay below.

q.t: What marks the site of the Führerbunker today?
o: An information board beside a car park
q.x: The bunker was demolished and built over. The association Berliner Unterwelten put up an information board in 2006, partly to stop the site becoming a shrine.

aar.rem: Nothing survives above ground, deliberately; the board is there to inform, not to commemorate.

stops.notes: Coordinates from German Wikipedia DMS (52°30′44.9″N 13°22′51.9″E) converted to decimal. Berliner Unterwelten URL not opened during research.

stops.name: Seelow Heights Memorial
stops.text: The Seelow Heights rise above the flat Oderbruch about 70 km east of Berlin. Early on 16 April 1945 Marshal Zhukov's 1st Belorussian Front, close to a million men including the Polish 1st Army, attacked from its Oder bridgehead. Gotthard Heinrici had pulled General Theodor Busse's 9th Army back onto the heights, so the huge bombardment fell largely on empty ground, and searchlights meant to blind the defenders were defeated by dust and smoke. Zhukov fed his tank armies into the marshy valley and needed four days to break through. By 19 April the road to Berlin was open.
stops.look: On the crest stands the Soviet soldier statue by Lev Kerbel and Vladimir Tsigal, unveiled in November 1945, above graves of Soviet soldiers. The museum below, reworked in 2012, overlooks the Oderbruch. Soviet guns and vehicles stand outside. The view east explains the battle.
stops.plan: Tue–Sun 10:00–17:00; November–March 10:00–16:00; closed Mondays and over Christmas and New Year. Small admission charge for the museum; grounds free. Check the website before you go.
stops.disputed: Soviet losses are disputed: Hastings and Beevor put Soviet dead at 30,000–33,000, while Russian historian Aleksey Isaev, using archives, gives 5,000–6,000 killed and missing.

aar.ev: Zhukov's armies storm the heights guarding the last approach to Berlin.
aar.st: On 16 April 1945 Zhukov's 1st Belorussian Front attacked the Seelow Heights from the Oder. Heinrici had pulled the 9th Army back onto the heights, so the bombardment fell largely on empty ground, and dust defeated the searchlights. It took four days to break through. Today a Soviet soldier statue stands above soldiers' graves on the crest, with a museum overlooking the Oderbruch.
aar.rem: Stand on the crest and look east: the open valley below explains the Soviet losses.

stops.notes: Official site blocks automated reading; hours from bpb.de, which may lag. Admission price not verified. More than 7,000 Soviet soldiers are buried on the site according to German Wikipedia.

stops.name: Sachsenhausen Memorial and Museum
stops.text: Built in July 1936 just north of Berlin, Sachsenhausen was laid out as a model camp, a triangle overseen from a single gatehouse, and it trained SS camp staff. More than 200,000 people passed through, including Soviet prisoners of war murdered in large numbers in 1941. Station Z, with its crematoria and later a gas chamber, was built outside the wall in 1942, and prisoners forged British and American banknotes for Operation Bernhard. In April 1945 the SS drove most prisoners out on a death march; Soviet and Polish troops freed about 3,400 left behind on 22 April. The NKVD then used the camp as Special Camp No. 7 until 1950.
stops.look: Enter through Tower A, with its 'Arbeit macht frei' gate, onto the semicircular roll-call ground. See the reconstructed barracks, the cell block, the foundations of Station Z and the 1961 East German obelisk. Exhibitions cover the camp, the Soviet special camp and the memorial.
stops.plan: Grounds and exhibitions 8:30–18:00 (31 Mar–26 Oct), 8:30–16:30 (27 Oct–30 Mar). Free; audio guide €3.50. S1 to Oranienburg then 20 minutes' walk. Allow half a day.
stops.disputed: The death toll is uncertain because records were destroyed: historians estimate at least 30,000, while commandant Anton Kaindl acknowledged 42,000 deaths during his time.

aar.ev: Soviet and Polish troops free the prisoners the SS left behind.
aar.st: Built in 1936 as a model camp near Berlin, Sachsenhausen held more than 200,000 people and trained SS camp staff. Station Z, with crematoria and later a gas chamber, stood outside the wall. In April 1945 the SS forced most prisoners onto a death march; about 3,400 left behind were freed on 22 April. Today you enter through Tower A onto the roll-call ground and see barracks, cell block and Station Z.
aar.rem: The camp was a model and training school for the whole SS camp system.

stops.notes: Tour buses can no longer park at Schäferweg from 22 Sep 2026; private cars unaffected.

stops.name: Bergen-Belsen Memorial
stops.coord_src: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bergen-Belsen_concentration_camp ; corrected after GPS check: OSM: Gedenkstätte Bergen-Belsen documentation centre
stops.text: Bergen-Belsen began in 1940 as a Wehrmacht camp for prisoners of war; almost 20,000 Soviet prisoners died there. From 1943 the SS used part of it as an exchange camp for Jews, but in the last months it became a dumping ground for prisoners evacuated from other camps. Typhus spread through the overcrowded huts; Anne and Margot Frank died there in February or March 1945. On 15 April 1945 British troops, including 11th Armoured Division, found about 60,000 prisoners and more than 13,000 unburied bodies. Around 14,000 more died after liberation. The British burned the huts, and BBC reporter Richard Dimbleby's broadcast shocked Britain.
stops.look: Nothing of the camp stands. A documentation centre opened in 2007 leads onto open heath with grassed mass graves marked by stones giving numbers buried, an obelisk and inscription wall, the Jewish monument and memorial stones, including one for Anne and Margot Frank.
stops.plan: Daily 10:00–18:00 April–September and 10:00–17:00 October–March; grounds open daily. Free. No dogs or bicycles on the grounds; large bags go in lockers. Car is easiest.

aar.ev: British troops enter the camp and find thousands of dead and dying prisoners.
aar.st: Bergen-Belsen began as a prisoner-of-war camp, became an SS exchange camp in 1943 and in 1945 a dumping ground for evacuated prisoners. Anne and Margot Frank died of typhus there. On 15 April 1945 British troops found about 60,000 prisoners and more than 13,000 unburied bodies. Today a documentation centre leads onto open heath with grassed mass graves, monuments and a stone for the Frank sisters.
aar.rem: The camp's horror was largely the result of its final months, when it became a dumping ground.

stops.notes: Documentation centre closes during Lower Saxony's Christmas school holidays. The memorial's Soviet POW cemetery is a separate site nearby.

stops.name: Buchenwald Memorial, near Weimar
stops.text: The SS opened Buchenwald on the Ettersberg above Weimar in July 1937. About 280,000 prisoners passed through it and its subcamps, and 56,545 died. When US troops of the 6th Armored Division arrived on 11 April 1945, prisoners had already taken control from the remaining guards; the gate clock is kept at 3.15 pm, the hour of liberation. General Patton ordered Weimar's mayor to bring about 1,000 citizens to see the camp on 16 April. From 1945 to 1950 the Soviets used it as Special Camp No. 2, where about 7,000 died. The East German memorial of 1958 told a story of communist resistance.
stops.look: Pass through the gatehouse with its inscription 'Jedem das Seine', readable from inside. The barracks are gone, marked by foundations; the crematorium and storehouse exhibitions remain. Below the hill stands the 1958 GDR bell tower, with the mass graves of 1945.
stops.plan: Exhibitions Tue–Sun 10:00–18:00 April–October, 10:00–16:00 November–March; closed Mondays; grounds open daily until dusk. Free. Bus 6 from Weimar. Check the website before you go.
stops.disputed: The memorial gives 56,545 deaths, but the Soviet special camp death toll is variously given as 7,113 or 7,127, and the GDR's heroic account of communist self-liberation has been revised since 1990.

aar.ev: US tanks reach Buchenwald, where prisoners have already taken over the camp.
aar.st: The SS opened Buchenwald above Weimar in 1937; about 280,000 prisoners passed through. When the US 6th Armored Division arrived on 11 April 1945, prisoners had already taken control, and the gate clock still shows 3.15 pm. Patton made Weimar's citizens see the camp. Today you pass through the gate inscribed 'Jedem das Seine' to barrack foundations, the crematorium and exhibitions.
aar.rem: Goethe's Weimar and Buchenwald lie a few kilometres apart; that closeness is the lesson.

stops.notes: Official site returned only outdated 2024 pages; hours from bpb.de. Coordinates taken from the German Wikipedia page for Soviet Special Camp No. 2, which occupied the same camp grounds.

stops.name: Colditz Castle
stops.text: Perched above the Mulde, Colditz Castle became Oflag IV-C, a prisoner-of-war camp for Allied officers the Germans classed as escape or security risks. Concentrating persistent escapers in one place produced the opposite of what was intended: tunnels, forged papers, home-made uniforms and one of the best escape records of any camp. In the winter of 1944–45 prisoners built a two-man glider, the Colditz Cock, in a hidden attic workshop, but it never flew. In the last days Himmler ordered prominent prisoners moved away. US troops took the castle on 16 April 1945 after a two-day fight in the town.
stops.look: Tour the inner courtyard where prisoners exercised, the chapel with the excavated tunnel under its floor, and the museum of escape devices. Guided tours show the routes of famous escapes; a replica of the Colditz Cock has been displayed.
stops.plan: Museum Mon–Fri 10:00–17:00, Sat–Sun 10:00–18:00; €12 (reduced €10). English 'Legendary Escapes' tours run on set dates; book ahead. Check the website before you go.
stops.disputed: Popular accounts of the number of 'home runs' from Colditz vary, often around 30 or more, depending on whether escapes from hospitals or during transfers are counted.

aar.ev: US troops reach Colditz Castle and free the Allied officers held there.
aar.st: Colditz Castle became Oflag IV-C, a camp for Allied officers judged escape risks. Gathering persistent escapers together produced one of the best escape records of any camp. Prisoners even built a glider, the Colditz Cock, in a hidden attic, but it never flew. Today you tour the courtyard, the chapel with its excavated tunnel and a museum of escape devices.

q.t: What happened to the Colditz Cock glider built by the prisoners?
o: It carried two officers to Switzerland
It never flew because the camp was liberated first
The guards found and destroyed it
q.x: Prisoners built the two-man glider in a hidden attic workshop in winter 1944–45, but US troops reached Colditz on 16 April 1945 before it could be launched.

aar.rem: Putting all the escapers in one castle created an escape academy.

stops.notes: The official page showed an inconsistent Monday notice; confirm days before visiting. 'Replica displayed' should be confirmed by the editor.

stops.name: Torgau: the Elbe Day meeting
stops.text: On 25 April 1945 the US 69th Infantry Division and the Soviet 58th Guards Rifle Division met on the Elbe, cutting Germany in two. The first contact was made that morning near Strehla, some 30 km upstream, by Lieutenant Albert Kotzebue's patrol. At Torgau, Second Lieutenant William Robertson waved a home-made American flag from the tower of Hartenfels Castle; after confusion over signal flares he crossed the wreck of the blown bridge and met Soviet soldiers on it at about 4 pm. The famous handshake photographs were staged on the ruined bridge for the cameras the following day.
stops.look: On the riverbank stands the Monument to the Meeting, designed by Soviet architect Avraham Miletzki and dedicated in September 1945, beside a viewing platform that is all that remains of the old bridge. Hartenfels Castle, from whose tower Robertson signalled, rises behind.
stops.plan: The monument and riverbank are open-air and free. Torgau holds Elbe Day events each April. Check the town website for castle opening times.
stops.disputed: Torgau is remembered as the meeting place, but Kotzebue's patrol made the first documented contact earlier the same day near Strehla; the best-known photographs were staged on 26 April.
links: The meeting on the Elbe (Saxon Memorials Foundation)

aar.ev: American and Soviet soldiers meet on the wrecked Elbe bridge, cutting Germany in two.
aar.st: On 25 April 1945 patrols of the US 69th Infantry Division met the Soviet 58th Guards Rifle Division on the Elbe. At Torgau, Lieutenant William Robertson waved a home-made flag from Hartenfels Castle and crossed the wrecked bridge to meet Soviet soldiers. The famous handshake photographs were staged the next day. Today a 1945 Soviet monument stands on the bank beside the last fragment of the bridge.

q.t: Where was the first documented American–Soviet contact on 25 April 1945?
q.x: Lieutenant Albert Kotzebue's patrol of the 69th Infantry Division met Soviet troops near Strehla, about 30 km upstream, hours before Robertson's meeting at Torgau.

aar.rem: Torgau got the fame and the photographs; Strehla got there first.

stops.notes: Coordinates from a komoot highlight for the Denkmal der Begegnung; no Wikipedia coordinates found. Exhibition provision in Torgau on Elbe Day not verified.

stops.name: Dresden Frauenkirche and the 1945 bombing
stops.text: On the night of 13 February 1945 RAF Bomber Command attacked Dresden, followed by the US Eighth Air Force; over three days some 1,300 heavy bombers dropped more than 3,900 tons of bombs, and a firestorm destroyed the old city. The baroque Frauenkirche survived the night but, gutted by fire, its great stone dome collapsed at 10 am on 15 February. Under East German rule the heap of rubble was kept as a memorial against war. It was rebuilt from 1994 using original stones where possible and reconsecrated on 30 October 2005; the new orb and cross were made by Alan Smith, son of an RAF bomber crewman.
stops.look: Look at the exterior: darker, fire-blackened original stones are set among the pale new sandstone. Inside, the twisted original cross from the dome stands near the altar. A memorial room recalls the ruin, and the dome platform gives views over the rebuilt Altstadt.
stops.plan: Church open to visitors most days, roughly 10:00–11:30 and 13:00–17:30 between services; free. Dome ascent is charged. Times vary with services and concerts, so check the website before you go.
stops.disputed: Nazi propaganda claimed 200,000 dead and later deniers higher still; a 2010 Dresden historians' commission found 22,700 to 25,000. Whether the raid was militarily justified is still debated.

aar.ev: Gutted by the firestorm, the Frauenkirche's stone dome collapses two days after the raid.
aar.st: From the night of 13 February 1945 British and American bombers attacked Dresden, and a firestorm destroyed the old city. The Frauenkirche survived the night but its dome collapsed on 15 February. Its rubble was kept as a memorial against war until rebuilding began in 1994. Today blackened original stones are set among pale new sandstone, and the twisted old cross stands inside.
aar.rem: The new cross on the dome was made by the son of an RAF bomber crewman.

stops.notes: Official site gave only calendar times; exact visiting hours and dome price not verified. 'Original cross inside' from general knowledge; editor may check.

stops.name: Bundeswehr Military History Museum, Dresden
stops.text: Germany's national military museum occupies an arsenal built in 1873–1876 in Dresden's Albertstadt garrison quarter. When it reopened in October 2011, Daniel Libeskind had driven a steel and glass wedge through the old façade. Its tip points towards the former stadium in the Ostragehege, where RAF Pathfinders dropped the target markers for the bombing of 13 February 1945, and the wedge echoes the shape of the bombers' approach over the city. Rather than a parade of weapons, the museum asks about the causes and human cost of war, with strong sections on the Wehrmacht, the Holocaust and the bombing war.
stops.look: From outside, Libeskind's wedge splitting the neo-classical arsenal. Inside, a chronological route and themed displays in the wedge; climb to its viewing platform 29 metres up and look along the line to the marker point. Special exhibition 'WUNDERWAFFEN' runs to 9 March 2027.
stops.plan: Thu–Tue 10:00–18:00, Mondays until 21:00; closed Wednesdays and 24–26, 31 Dec and 1 Jan. Adults €5 (combined ticket €7); under-18s free. Allow at least three hours.
links: Military History Museum of the Bundeswehr (Wikipedia)

aar.ev: RAF Pathfinders mark the Ostragehege stadium as the aiming point for the Dresden raid.
aar.st: Germany's national military museum fills an 1870s arsenal in Dresden's garrison quarter. Daniel Libeskind's steel and glass wedge, added for the 2011 reopening, points towards the stadium where RAF Pathfinders dropped target markers on 13 February 1945. Today you can climb to the wedge's viewing platform, 29 metres up, and look along that line before exploring galleries on the human cost of war.

q.t: What does the tip of Libeskind's wedge point towards?
o: The stadium where RAF target markers were dropped in 1945
q.x: The tip points to the former Ostragehege stadium, where RAF Pathfinders set the target markers for the 13 February 1945 raid; the wedge echoes the bombers' approach.

aar.rem: A military museum that asks why wars happen and what they cost, not just how they were fought.

stops.name: St Nikolai Memorial, Hamburg
stops.text: In late July 1943 RAF Bomber Command, flying by night, and the US Eighth Air Force, by day, attacked Hamburg in Operation Gomorrah. On the first night the RAF used 'Window' metal strips for the first time to blind German radar. On the night of 27/28 July 787 RAF aircraft created a firestorm across the working-class districts of Hammerbrook, Hamm, Borgfelde and Rothenburgsort. Around 37,000 people died and about a million fled the city. The 147-metre spire of St Nikolai, then among the tallest buildings in the world, served the bombers as a landmark and was badly damaged; the ruined church was kept as a memorial against war.
stops.look: The blackened tower and fragments of the nave walls stand in a small park. A glass lift climbs inside the spire to a platform at 75 metres with views over the city and port. The crypt holds an exhibition on the raids and on Coventry, Warsaw and Rotterdam.
stops.plan: Exhibition and lift are charged; opening times vary by season. The official site could not be read in October 2026, so check the website before you go.
stops.disputed: Estimates of deaths range from 34,000 (police records) to 40,000 (a wartime German figure); 37,000 is the most widely accepted.

aar.ev: A firestorm sweeps through Hamburg's eastern districts during the RAF's Operation Gomorrah.
aar.st: In late July 1943 British and American bombers attacked Hamburg in Operation Gomorrah. On the night of 27/28 July 787 RAF aircraft created a firestorm across the eastern working-class districts, and about a million people fled. St Nikolai's spire, a landmark for the bombers, was badly damaged. Today a lift climbs the blackened tower to a platform at 75 metres, and the crypt holds an exhibition on the raids.
aar.rem: Hamburg's firestorm in 1943 showed both sides what area bombing could do to a city.

stops.notes: Official site returned empty pages; hours and prices not verified. Exhibition content (Coventry, Warsaw, Rotterdam) from general knowledge.

stops.name: Peenemünde Historical-Technical Museum
stops.text: From 1937 the Army Research Centre at Peenemünde, on the island of Usedom, developed Germany's long-range rockets under Walter Dornberger, with Wernher von Braun as technical director; the Luftwaffe tested the V-1 flying bomb next door. Here the A4, later called the V-2, was developed. On the night of 17/18 August 1943 RAF Bomber Command attacked in Operation Hydra, hitting the staff housing first and also the camp at Trassenheide, where forced labourers had no shelters. Production moved to the underground Mittelwerk in the Harz, built and worked by concentration camp prisoners. Soviet troops took the wrecked site in May 1945.
stops.look: The museum fills the huge brick power station of the research centre. Outside are replicas of the A4 rocket and V-1, a V-1 launch ramp and a model of Test Stand VII. Exhibitions cover forced labourers and camp prisoners as well as the engineers.
stops.plan: April–September 10:00–18:00; October–March 10:00–16:00, closed Mondays November–March. Admission charged. Allow at least three hours. Check the website before you go.
stops.disputed: The site is often presented as the birthplace of space flight; critics stress that more people died building the V-2 than were killed by it.

aar.ev: RAF bombers attack the rocket research centre, aiming first at the scientists' housing.
aar.st: From 1937 Peenemünde developed Germany's long-range rockets under Dornberger and von Braun, including the V-2. On the night of 17/18 August 1943 the RAF attacked in Operation Hydra, and production moved to the underground Mittelwerk, worked by camp prisoners. Today the museum fills the research centre's brick power station, with replica V-1 and V-2 rockets outside.

q.t: Where did V-2 production move after the RAF raid on Peenemünde?
o: To the underground Mittelwerk in the Harz
q.x: After Operation Hydra in August 1943, production moved to the underground Mittelwerk in the Harz mountains, built and worked by concentration camp prisoners.

aar.rem: The V-2 was built by prisoners in appalling conditions; the engineers are only half the story.

stops.notes: Admission price not verified (official visitor page failed to load). The 'more died building it' line is a widely cited assessment, not taken from an opened source; the A4 first reaching space on 3 Oct 1942 was not confirmed in opened sources and has been left out. Mittelbau-Dora (Nordhausen) is the natural companion stop.

stops.name: Cecilienhof: the Potsdam Conference
stops.text: From 17 July to 2 August 1945 Truman, Stalin and Churchill (replaced partway through by Clement Attlee after the British general election) met at Cecilienhof, a mock-Tudor country house in Potsdam's New Garden built for the last Crown Prince. It was the third and longest of the wartime summits, organised by the Soviets, who fitted the Great Hall with a round table. The conference settled the occupation of Germany, reparations, the move of Poland's border west to the Oder–Neisse line and the expulsion of Germans from the east, and issued the Potsdam Declaration demanding Japan's surrender.
stops.look: From outside you can see the half-timbered house in the New Garden and the red star of flowers the Soviets planted in the courtyard. When open, the Great Hall with its round table and the delegations' studies are shown.
stops.plan: The house is closed until further notice for restoration (October 2026); the park and exterior remain accessible and free. Check the SPSG website before you go.

aar.ev: Truman, Stalin and Churchill meet to decide the fate of defeated Germany.
aar.st: From 17 July to 2 August 1945 the Allied leaders met at Cecilienhof, in Potsdam's New Garden, around a round table the Soviets placed in the Great Hall. Churchill was replaced partway through by Attlee. The conference settled Germany's occupation and Poland's new western border. Today you can see the half-timbered house and its courtyard from the park while the interior is closed for restoration.

q.t: Who replaced Churchill partway through the Potsdam Conference?
q.x: Labour won the 1945 general election, so Clement Attlee took Churchill's place at the table for the conference's final days.

aar.rem: The post-war map of Central Europe was drawn up in this country house.

stops.notes: ADDED STOP. Interior closed until further notice (SPSG, Oct 2026). Attlee, Oder–Neisse and the Potsdam Declaration are general knowledge not confirmed in the opened Wikipedia page; the 'red star of flowers' is likewise from general knowledge. Editor should verify.

stops.name: Ravensbrück Memorial
stops.coord_src: https://de.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahn-_und_Gedenkstätte_Ravensbrück ; corrected after GPS check: OSM: Mahn- und Gedenkstätte Ravensbrück
stops.text: Ravensbrück, 90 km north of Berlin, opened in May 1939 when the SS moved 900 women there from Lichtenburg. It was the only large concentration camp built for women, and an estimated 130,000 to 132,000 passed through it, from across occupied Europe. Prisoners worked in SS textile workshops and for firms such as Siemens. From summer 1942 SS doctors carried out experiments on 86 women, mostly Polish, whom they called 'rabbits'. In January 1945 the SS converted a hut near the crematorium into a gas chamber. The Red Army liberated the camp on 30 April 1945, finding fewer than 3,500 prisoners alive.
stops.look: On the Schwedtsee shore Will Lammert's bronze 'Tragende', a woman carrying another, faces Fürstenberg across the lake. See the crematorium, the camp road, the female guards' houses and the main exhibition in the former commandant's building.
stops.plan: Exhibitions daily 10:00–18:00; grounds 9:00–20:00 (Apr–Sep), 9:00–18:00 (Oct–Mar). Free. Cell block closed for renovation until 2028. RE5 to Fürstenberg, then 25 minutes' walk.
stops.disputed: Death toll estimates vary widely; Britannica cites about 50,000 plus some 2,200 gassed, while the memorial's own figures are lower.

aar.ev: The Red Army liberates the women's camp, finding fewer than 3,500 prisoners alive.
aar.st: Ravensbrück opened in May 1939 as the only large concentration camp built for women; some 130,000 passed through. SS doctors experimented on Polish women they called 'rabbits', and in 1945 a gas chamber was set up. The Red Army arrived on 30 April 1945. Today Will Lammert's bronze of a woman carrying another stands on the lakeshore, near the crematorium and exhibitions.
aar.rem: The only large camp built for women; its prisoners came from every country Germany occupied.

stops.notes: ADDED STOP. 'Firms such as Siemens' is general knowledge not confirmed in opened sources. Memorial's own death-toll figure not obtained. Visitor centre closed Mondays. Neuengamme (Hamburg) and Mittelbau-Dora were considered as alternative additions.

stops.name: Museum Hürtgenwald 1944, Vossenack
stops.text: The Battle of the Hürtgen Forest began on 19 September 1944 as the US First Army pushed into the dense, hilly woods south-east of Aachen, partly to protect its flank and later to reach the Rur dams. The 9th Infantry Division was followed by the 28th, whose 112th Infantry Regiment took Vossenack and then Schmidt on 2–3 November. A German tank counter-attack threw them out of Schmidt on 4 November, and the narrow Kall Trail supply route through the ravine below Vossenack became a death trap. The 4th, 8th and 1st Infantry Divisions followed. The fighting cost the Americans tens of thousands of casualties for a few miles of forest. The museum, run by the local history society, grew from Konrad Schall's collection, first shown at Kleinhau in 1983, and moved to Vossenack in 2001.
stops.look: A village museum with themed rooms on the Siegfried Line, the Wehrmacht and the US Army in the forest, maps, uniforms, weapons and relics dug from the woods, plus the post-war years. Use it as the base for walking the Kall Trail into the valley below.
stops.plan: Open Sundays 10:00–17:00 from March to November, with extra openings at Easter and special events; weekday group visits by arrangement. The Simonskall medical bunker opens on some first Sundays. Small admission fee. Check the website before you go.
stops.disputed: American losses are given anywhere from about 33,000 to 55,000 depending on whether non-combat casualties (trench foot, exposure, combat fatigue) are counted. Historians such as Charles MacDonald judged the battle misconceived; others defend the need to clear the forest and reach the Rur dams.

aar.ev: The 28th Infantry Division attacks through Vossenack towards Schmidt along the narrow Kall Trail.
aar.st: In November 1944 the 112th Infantry Regiment of the US 28th Division took Vossenack and then Schmidt, supplied only along the narrow Kall Trail through the ravine. A German tank counter-attack drove them out of Schmidt on 4 November, and the trail became a death trap. Today the village museum shows maps, uniforms and relics dug from the forest, and makes a good starting point for walking the Kall Trail.

q.t: What was the 28th Division's only supply route to Schmidt in November 1944?
o: A railway line along the Rur valley
The narrow Kall Trail through a forest ravine
q.x: The Kall Trail was a narrow track along a deep ravine below Vossenack. Ill-suited to tanks and supply vehicles and infiltrated by Germans, it could not sustain the troops in Schmidt.

aar.rem: The Hürtgen Forest turned American advantages in armour, air power and artillery into almost nothing, and the infantry paid for it.

stops.notes: Opening is limited (essentially Sundays, March–November). The German war cemetery at Vossenack and the Kall Trail walk are nearby. Coordinates from TracesOfWar (address Pfarrer-Dickmann-Straße 21–23).

stops.name: Remagen bridge and Peace Museum
stops.text: On 7 March 1945 an advance party of the US 9th Armored Division under 2nd Lt Karl Timmermann reached the Ludendorff railway bridge at Remagen at about 13:00 and found it still standing. The German defenders set off their demolition charges, but the bridge lifted and settled back, damaged but passable. American infantry rushed across under fire, engineers cut the remaining wires, and within days several divisions were on the east bank: the first Allied crossing of the Rhine. Hitler's 'flying court martial' sentenced five German officers to death and four were shot. Weakened by the blast, shelling and air attack, the bridge collapsed into the Rhine on 17 March 1945, killing American engineers working on it. It was never rebuilt.
stops.look: The two black stone towers on the Remagen bank hold the Peace Museum, opened in 1980, with the story of the bridge, photographs and the theme of war and peace. On the far bank the Erpel towers stand in front of a railway tunnel. Only the stumps of the piers ever remained.
stops.plan: Open from early March to 1 November: weekends only in early March, then daily (Monday afternoons only) roughly 10:00–17:00, until 18:00 May–August. Adults €6. Guided group tours bookable. Closed November to early March.
stops.disputed: The number of US engineers killed in the collapse on 17 March is given as 28 in some accounts and 32 in others, and the injured as 63 or 93. Why the German charges failed (weak industrial explosive, a cut cable or a dud) is still argued.

aar.ev: US armoured infantry find the Rhine bridge standing and rush across as the demolition fails.
aar.st: On 7 March 1945 an advance party of the US 9th Armored Division under Lt Karl Timmermann found the Ludendorff Bridge intact. The German charges damaged but did not drop it, and American troops seized the first Allied foothold across the Rhine. The weakened bridge fell into the river ten days later. Today the two towers on the Remagen bank house the Peace Museum, facing the Erpel towers across the water.

q.t: What happened to the Ludendorff Bridge after the Americans captured it?
o: It was blown up by retreating US troops
It collapsed into the Rhine ten days later
q.x: Weakened by the failed demolition, shelling and air attack, the bridge collapsed on 17 March 1945 while US engineers were repairing it. It was never rebuilt.

aar.rem: Remagen gave the Allies a bridgehead over the Rhine two weeks before the planned set-piece crossings further north.

stops.notes: Coordinates are the bridge site from the Wikipedia infobox (museum in the west towers, An der Alten Rheinbrücke 11). External guides are not permitted inside the museum.

stops.name: Nazi Party Rally Grounds & Documentation Centre
stops.text: Six Nazi Party rallies were held at Nuremberg between 1933 and 1938, mass rituals of marching columns, floodlights and speeches designed to show a nation united behind Hitler. Albert Speer designed most of the grounds, including the Zeppelin Field grandstand; the Congress Hall was designed by Ludwig and Franz Ruff. At the 1935 rally the Reichstag, summoned to Nuremberg, passed the Nuremberg Laws that stripped German Jews of citizenship. The Congress Hall was never finished: work stopped in 1943 at about 39 m of a planned 68.5 m, and its interior was never roofed. In April 1945 the US Army blew the giant swastika off the Zeppelin grandstand. The Documentation Centre opened in the north wing of the Congress Hall in 2001.
stops.look: Inside the Congress Hall the new permanent exhibition explains the rallies, their staging and their victims. Then walk the grounds: the unfinished horseshoe of the Congress Hall, the Great Road, the lake and the crumbling Zeppelin grandstand where Hitler spoke.
stops.plan: Mon–Fri 9:00–18:00, Sat–Sun 10:00–18:00; adults €7.50. The new permanent exhibition has run on trial since 22 May 2026, with an official opening on 4 November 2026 (closed 3–4 Nov). Grounds partly closed during the DTM race and Rock im Park. Check the website before you go.

aar.ev: At the party rally the Reichstag passes the Nuremberg Laws, stripping German Jews of citizenship.
aar.st: Six Nazi Party rallies filled these grounds between 1933 and 1938, and at the 1935 rally the Nuremberg Laws took citizenship from German Jews. Construction of the Congress Hall stopped in 1943 with the building unfinished and unroofed. Today the Documentation Centre in its north wing tells the story, and you can walk on to the crumbling Zeppelin grandstand where Hitler spoke.

q.t: Why does the Congress Hall at Nuremberg have no roof?
o: It was never finished when work stopped in 1943
The city removed it after the war
q.x: Construction halted in 1943 at about 39 m of a planned 68.5 m height. The main hall was never roofed and is still an open courtyard of bare brick.

aar.rem: The rally grounds were built as theatre: architecture meant to make individuals feel small and the movement feel eternal.

stops.notes: Documentation Centre address Bayernstraße 110. The interim exhibition closed on 3 May 2026; the new permanent exhibition 'Nuremberg and the Nazi Party Rallies' replaces it. Combine with Courtroom 600 (same municipal museums ticket offer).

stops.name: Memorium Nuremberg Trials (Courtroom 600)
stops.text: Nuremberg was chosen for the trial of the major war criminals because its Palace of Justice had survived the bombing largely intact and had a prison attached, and because the city stood for the party rallies. Before the International Military Tribunal of the four Allied powers, 24 leaders were indicted; 22 were tried, Martin Bormann in absentia. The trial opened in Courtroom 600 on 20 November 1945 and the verdicts came on 1 October 1946: 12 death sentences, seven prison terms and three acquittals. Ten men were hanged on 16 October; Göring killed himself the night before. Twelve further US trials of doctors, judges, industrialists and SS officers followed in the same room until 1949.
stops.look: The courtroom itself, still with its panelling and doors, on the top floor of the Palace of Justice, plus an exhibition on the defendants, the trial and its legacy for international law. A media installation recreates the 1945–46 room layout.
stops.plan: Mon and Wed–Fri 9:00–18:00, Sat–Sun 10:00–18:00, closed Tuesdays. Adults €7.50. Courtroom 600 is occasionally closed for events, so check the website before you go.

aar.ev: The International Military Tribunal opens the trial of the surviving Nazi leaders in Courtroom 600.
aar.st: The four Allied powers tried 22 Nazi leaders here from November 1945, the first international trial for crimes against humanity. The verdicts of 1 October 1946 brought 12 death sentences, seven prison terms and three acquittals, and twelve more US trials followed in the same room. Today you stand in the courtroom itself on the top floor of the Palace of Justice, with an exhibition on the trials and their legacy.

q.t: Why did the Allies hold the main war crimes trial in Nuremberg?
o: It was the capital of the American zone
Its Palace of Justice was largely intact and had a prison
q.x: The Palace of Justice survived the bombing largely intact and had a prison attached for the defendants. The city's role as the rally city added symbolic weight.

aar.rem: Courtroom 600 is where 'crimes against humanity' were first tried before an international court.

stops.notes: Entrance at Bärenschanzstraße 72 (Palace of Justice, Fürther Straße 110). The courtroom stopped hosting trials in 2020 and is now part of the exhibition. Coordinates are those of the Palace of Justice (4 decimals in source).

stops.name: NS-Documentation Centre, Munich
stops.text: Munich was where the Nazi Party was founded and where Hitler first made his name; his failed Beer Hall Putsch of 9 November 1923 ended in gunfire at the Feldherrnhalle. After 1933 the regime styled Munich the 'Capital of the Movement'. The party's national headquarters, the Brown House, stood on Brienner Straße beside Königsplatz, flanked by the party's own buildings and 'temples of honour'. The NS-Documentation Centre, opened on 30 April 2015, stands on the site of the Brown House. Its white cube looks out over the surviving party buildings and explains why the movement grew in this city, who supported it, and what it did to its victims.
stops.look: Four floors of exhibition, read from the top down, with windows framing the surviving Nazi buildings on Königsplatz. Afterwards walk round the square to the Führerbau (now a music school) and the stumps of the Ehrentempel foundations.
stops.plan: Tuesday to Sunday 10:00–19:00, also open on public holidays that fall on a Monday. Admission free. No booking needed for individuals. Check the website for temporary exhibitions.
links: Munich Documentation Centre for the History of National Socialism (Wikipedia)

aar.ev: Hitler's Beer Hall Putsch collapses in gunfire in central Munich.
aar.st: Munich was the birthplace of the Nazi Party, the scene of Hitler's failed putsch in November 1923, and later the regime's 'Capital of the Movement'. The party's headquarters, the Brown House, stood on this site beside Königsplatz. Today a white-cube documentation centre, opened in 2015, looks out over the surviving party buildings around the square.

q.t: What stood on the site of the NS-Documentation Centre before the war?
o: The Nazi Party headquarters, the Brown House
The beer hall of the 1923 putsch
q.x: The centre was built on the site of the Brown House, the national headquarters of the Nazi Party on Brienner Straße next to Königsplatz.

aar.rem: The regime did not arrive from outside: it grew in ordinary city streets like these, with local support.

stops.notes: Address Max-Mannheimer-Platz 1. Pairs well with a Dachau visit (20 minutes by S-Bahn).

stops.name: Dachau Concentration Camp Memorial Site
stops.text: Dachau opened on 22 March 1933, weeks after Hitler came to power, as the first regular concentration camp. Its second commandant, Theodor Eicke, drew up the rules, layout and guard training that became the model for the whole camp system, and he went on to run it as inspector of concentration camps. Political opponents came first, then Jews, Roma, clergy, homosexuals and, during the war, prisoners from more than 30 countries; around 200,000 passed through it and its subcamps. Tens of thousands died of starvation, disease, abuse and execution, many in the typhus epidemic of the final months. Units of the US 45th and 42nd Infantry Divisions liberated the main camp on 29 April 1945.
stops.look: The roll-call square, the maintenance building with the main exhibition, two reconstructed barracks and the foundations of the rest, the bunker (camp prison), the 'Arbeit macht frei' gate, and the crematorium area with the gas chamber, plus religious memorials at the far end.
stops.plan: Open daily 9:00–17:00 (crematorium area until 16:30), closed 24 December. Admission free. English guided tours daily at 11:00 and 13:00; audio guides available; groups should book. Allow at least three hours.
stops.disputed: Death figures differ: the memorial cites about 41,500, while documented deaths in the archive number about 32,000 and many more are undocumented. The number of SS guards killed by liberating US soldiers and prisoners on 29 April 1945 is also disputed, with estimates from about 21 to 50.

aar.ev: The SS opens Dachau, the first regular concentration camp, outside Munich.
aar.st: Dachau opened in March 1933 and, under Theodor Eicke, became the model and training school for the whole SS camp system. Around 200,000 people from more than 30 countries passed through it before US troops liberated it on 29 April 1945. Today you walk from the gate across the roll-call square to the exhibition, the reconstructed barracks, the camp prison and the crematorium area.
aar.rem: Dachau was the template: its rules, layout and trained guards were exported to every camp that followed.

stops.notes: Visitor centre entrance at Pater-Roth-Straße 2a; coordinates from the German Wikipedia article on the memorial site. Parking is charged.

stops.name: Obersalzberg Documentation Centre
stops.text: Hitler rented a chalet on the Obersalzberg above Berchtesgaden in 1928, bought it in 1933 and rebuilt it as the Berghof. Martin Bormann turned the mountainside into a fenced 'Führer zone' with houses for Göring and Bormann, SS barracks and a network of bunkers. It became a second seat of government: Hitler spent much of August 1939 here preparing the attack on Poland, and his last stay ended on 14 July 1944. On 25 April 1945 RAF bombers wrecked most of the buildings, and the SS set fire to the Berghof before US and French troops arrived. Bavaria demolished the ruins in 1952. The Institute of Contemporary History opened the documentation centre in 1999; a new building and exhibition opened in 2023.
stops.look: The exhibition 'Idyll and Atrocity' links the mountain retreat to the crimes planned from it, then leads down into part of the original bunker system. The Berghof site itself is a short walk away in the woods, with only traces left.
stops.plan: Open daily 9:00–17:00, last entry 16:00. Adults €4.50, under 18 free. Closed 1 Nov, 24, 25 and 31 Dec, 1 Jan, and for maintenance 16–24 Nov 2026 and 1–8 Mar 2027. Free multimedia guide. Check the website before you go.

aar.ev: RAF bombers wreck Hitler's Berghof and the Nazi leaders' mountain compound.
aar.st: Hitler bought his chalet here in 1933 and rebuilt it as the Berghof, the heart of a fenced Führer zone with bunkers and barracks. He spent much of August 1939 here planning the invasion of Poland. Bombing on 25 April 1945 wrecked the compound and the ruins were cleared in 1952. Today the documentation centre's exhibition leads you down into part of the original bunker system.

q.t: What happened to the ruins of Hitler's Berghof after the war?
o: They became a US Army museum
They were restored as a hotel
q.x: The Bavarian government demolished the remaining buildings in 1952 so the site could not become a shrine. Only traces remain in the woods.

aar.rem: The holiday-postcard scenery was part of the propaganda: decisions for war and genocide were taken here.

stops.notes: Address Salzbergstraße 41. The Kehlsteinhaus buses leave from beside the centre. Coordinates from German Wikipedia.

stops.name: Kehlsteinhaus (Eagle's Nest)
stops.text: Martin Bormann had the Kehlsteinhaus built in 1937–38 just below the Kehlstein summit at about 1,838 m, with a road cut through five tunnels and a 124 m lift shaft inside the mountain. Designed by Roderich Fick, it cost some 30 million Reichsmarks and was presented to Hitler for his 50th birthday in 1939. Hitler, who disliked heights, visited only about 14 times; it was used for receptions and by Eva Braun. The French ambassador André François-Poncet called it the 'eagle's nest' after a visit in October 1938. In early May 1945 French troops of the 2e Division Blindée and US troops reached Berchtesgaden, and the building later served the Allies until 1960.
stops.look: Ride the bus up the narrow mountain road, walk the tunnel and take the brass-lined lift to the house, now a restaurant with a small history exhibition. On a clear day the views over the Berchtesgaden Alps and towards Salzburg explain the choice of site.
stops.plan: Open roughly early/mid May to early November (2026 season to 8 November), weather permitting. Access only by special bus from the Kehlstein bus station beside the Documentation Centre; the ticket includes the lift. Buy timed tickets online to avoid queues.
stops.disputed: Who got there first in May 1945 is argued: the 101st Airborne claimed it (repeated in 'Band of Brothers'), the US 3rd Infantry Division's 7th Infantry Regiment and the French 2e Division Blindée both entered Berchtesgaden on 4 May, and French soldiers were at the Kehlsteinhaus on 4–5 May.

aar.ev: French and American troops enter Berchtesgaden as the Nazi mountain retreat falls.
aar.st: Bormann built the Kehlsteinhaus in 1937–38 as a 50th-birthday gift for Hitler, with a road through five tunnels and a 124 m lift inside the rock. Hitler visited only about 14 times. French and American troops reached Berchtesgaden on 4 May 1945, and who reached the house first is still argued. Today a bus and the original brass lift take you up to a restaurant with a small exhibition and wide Alpine views.

q.t: Who coined the name 'Eagle's Nest' for the Kehlsteinhaus?
q.x: André François-Poncet, the French ambassador, used the phrase after his visit in October 1938, and it stuck.

aar.rem: The famous Eagle's Nest was a party showpiece Hitler rarely used; the real decisions were made at the Berghof below.

stops.notes: Only buses may use the Kehlstein road; walking up takes about two hours. Snow, wind or rockfall can stop the buses at short notice even in summer; ring +49 8652 2029 in doubtful weather.

stops.name: Abbey of Monte Cassino
stops.text: The Benedictine abbey on Monte Cassino looks down on Highway 6 and the Liri valley, the inland route to Rome and the hinge of the German Gustav Line. Four Allied offensives were fought below it between January and May 1944. On 15 February Allied bombers destroyed the abbey, killing about 230 Italian civilians sheltering inside. German paratroopers then occupied the ruins and made them a strongpoint. The New Zealand Corps, including 4th Indian Division, failed to take Monastery Hill in February and March. In Operation Diadem, Polish II Corps attacked the heights and on 18 May a Polish cavalry patrol raised its flag over the ruins. The abbey was rebuilt and Pope Paul VI consecrated the new basilica on 24 October 1964.
stops.look: A complete, rebuilt abbey on the summit, reached by a winding road. From the terraces you look down on the Polish cemetery, Cassino town, the Rapido valley and Highway 6, and can see why the hill dominated the battle. Look for photographs of the ruins and the abbey museum.
stops.plan: Summer (1 Apr–31 Oct) open daily 9:30–18:30; winter Mon–Sat 9:30–16:15, Sundays and holidays 9:30–17:15. A working monastery: dress modestly and keep quiet during services. Museum and guided visits by arrangement; check the website before you go.
stops.disputed: Whether German troops were in the abbey before the bombing is long disputed. Some Allied observers claimed they were, but the Germans had agreed with the Vatican not to occupy it, and the British official history and a 1969 US Army review concluded they made no military use of it before 15 February.

aar.ev: Allied bombers destroy the abbey; German paratroopers turn the ruins into a fortress.
aar.st: Four Allied offensives were fought below the abbey between January and May 1944. After bombers destroyed it on 15 February, German paratroopers held the ruins against the New Zealand Corps, until a Polish patrol raised its flag there on 18 May. Today a rebuilt abbey crowns the hill, and its terraces look down on the Polish cemetery, Cassino town and Highway 6.

q.t: What did German paratroopers do after the abbey was bombed?
o: Occupied the ruins and made them a strongpoint
Handed the site to the Vatican
q.x: The bombing did not clear the hill. German paratroopers moved into the ruins and used them as a strongpoint until Polish II Corps took the heights in May 1944.

aar.rem: Bombing the abbey gave the defenders better cover in the rubble than the intact building would have.

stops.notes: Price for the abbey museum not confirmed on the official site; the abbey phone is +39 0776 311529. About 9 km of hairpin road from Cassino town.

stops.name: Polish War Cemetery, Monte Cassino
stops.text: Polish II Corps under General Władysław Anders attacked the heights north-west of the abbey in May 1944, during Operation Diadem. After a week of fighting on Point 593 and the surrounding ridges, a patrol raised the Polish flag over the abbey ruins on 18 May. The cemetery lies on the slopes of Point 445, the Allied cemetery closest to the abbey. It was designed by Wacław Hryniewicz and Jerzy Skolimowski and consecrated on 1 September 1945. Crosses mark Christian graves and Stars of David mark Jewish ones. Anders, who died in London in 1970, chose to be buried among his men. A Memorial Museum on the 2nd Corps opened nearby in 2014.
stops.look: Terraced rows of travertine crosses rise to a large stone memorial, with the abbey directly above. Read the Simonides-style inscription ('Passer-by, go tell Poland...') and find General Anders' grave at the front. The small museum shows uniforms, photographs and film.
stops.plan: Free. Reached by the abbey road with parking nearby. Opening hours of the cemetery and the Memorial Museum could not be confirmed on an official site; check before you go and allow time if visiting with the abbey.
stops.disputed: Sources give different totals: Wikipedia states 1,072 Polish graves, while Italy's official tourism site counts 1,051 crosses.

aar.ev: A Polish patrol raises its flag over the abbey ruins after a week of fighting.
aar.st: Polish II Corps under General Anders attacked the ridges north-west of the abbey during Operation Diadem in May 1944. On 18 May a patrol raised the Polish flag over the ruins. The cemetery, consecrated in 1945, holds Anders himself among his men. Today terraced rows of crosses climb towards a stone memorial, with the rebuilt abbey directly above.
aar.rem: General Anders died in London in 1970 but chose to be buried here with his soldiers.

stops.notes: Grave count differs between sources (1,072 vs 1,051); avoid quoting an exact figure in the app or give both.

stops.name: Cassino War Cemetery and Memorial (CWGC)
stops.text: This Commonwealth cemetery lies on the valley floor below Monte Cassino, among the ground where British, Indian, New Zealand, Canadian and other Commonwealth troops fought between January and May 1944. It holds 4,271 Commonwealth servicemen, 289 of them unidentified. Inside the cemetery stands the Cassino Memorial, which carries the names of more than 4,000 Commonwealth servicemen who died in the Italian campaign and have no known grave. The New Zealand Corps attacks of February and March 1944 and the Eighth Army's crossing of the Rapido (Gari) in May were fought within sight of this spot.
stops.look: Rows of headstones in a walled garden, with the abbey on its hill above. The Cassino Memorial is a series of green marble panels around a pool. Look up from the cemetery to Monastery Hill to see the slopes the infantry had to climb.
stops.plan: Free. CWGC sites are normally open access; check the CWGC website for any works before you go. Short drive from Cassino town centre.

aar.ev: Commonwealth dead of the four Cassino battles are gathered beneath Monastery Hill.
aar.st: This cemetery lies on the valley floor where Commonwealth troops fought between January and May 1944. It holds 4,271 servicemen, and the Cassino Memorial inside names more than 4,000 more who have no known grave. Today rows of headstones fill a walled garden, with green marble memorial panels around a pool and the abbey on its hill above.
aar.rem: Look up from the headstones to Monastery Hill to understand the ground these men attacked.

stops.notes: The CWGC page could not be fetched (error); coordinates are from Wikipedia and only have 4 decimals. Verify on the CWGC page and exact gate position before publication.

stops.name: German War Cemetery, Cassino (Caira)
stops.text: About 3 km north of Cassino, on the southern foothills of Colle Marino, lies the largest German war cemetery in Italy. In 1959–1960 the Volksbund moved 20,076 German dead here from smaller cemeteries and field graves across the region, including the men who held the Gustav Line around Cassino and those who fought on the Garigliano and in the mountains. Around 3,100 graves have no name. The cemetery opened on 4 May 1965. In 2014 seven plaques were added in the memorial hall for 911 unidentified dead.
stops.look: Terraces and ellipses of graves climb the hillside, marked by stone crosses carrying several names each. The open-roofed, cube-shaped entrance building lights the sculpture 'Mourning and Consolation' by Suse Müller-Diefenbach. There is a small exhibition and wide views towards Monte Cassino.
stops.plan: Free. Summer: Mon–Fri 9:00–18:00, weekends and holidays 9:00–19:00; winter: daily 8:00–16:00. Parking at Piazza Marino Fardelli, Caira. Accessible. Check the Volksbund page before you go.

aar.ev: German dead from across the Cassino front are brought together on Colle Marino.
aar.st: In 1959–1960 the Volksbund moved more than 20,000 German dead here from smaller cemeteries and field graves, including the defenders of the Gustav Line. The cemetery opened on 4 May 1965, and thousands of its graves carry no name. Today terraces of stone crosses climb the hillside from an open-roofed entrance hall with a sculpture of mourning and consolation.
aar.rem: Many of the men buried here held the same ridges the Allied dead in the valley below were trying to take.

stops.notes: Volksbund gives both 'Via Colle Marino 1' and '2' as the address.

stops.name: Anzio Beachhead Museum (Museo dello Sbarco)
stops.text: On 22 January 1944 US VI Corps under Major General John P. Lucas landed at Anzio and Nettuno in Operation Shingle, to outflank the Gustav Line. US 3rd Infantry Division came ashore at X-Ray beach, British 1st Infantry Division at Peter beach and US Rangers took the port. Lucas consolidated rather than drive inland, and General von Mackensen's Fourteenth Army sealed the beachhead. Major General Lucian Truscott replaced Lucas on 22 February. The breakout, Operation Buffalo, began on 23 May, and Rome fell on 4 June. The museum was founded on 22 January 1994, the 50th anniversary, by a local research association.
stops.look: A single room in the 17th-century Villa Adele, organised in American, British, German and Italian sections: uniforms, weapons, maps, documents and veterans' photographs. Look for objects raised from the seabed off Anzio, including from HMS Janus, HMS Spartan and the hospital ship St David.
stops.plan: Open Tue and Thu–Sun 10:00–13:00 and 16:00–18:00; closed Mon and Wed. July–August 10:00–13:00 and 17:00–19:00. No booking needed. Short walk from Anzio station; check the website before you go.
stops.disputed: Mark Clark's decision on 25–26 May to turn north-west for Rome rather than cut Route 6 at Valmontone is still argued over; Truscott and others held that it let much of the German Tenth Army escape.
links: Museo dello Sbarco di Anzio (Ministero della Cultura)

aar.ev: US VI Corps lands at Anzio to outflank the Gustav Line, then is boxed in.
aar.st: On 22 January 1944 US VI Corps under Lucas landed at Anzio and Nettuno. Lucas consolidated instead of driving inland, and German Fourteenth Army sealed the beachhead for four months until the breakout of 23 May. Today a room in the 17th-century Villa Adele holds uniforms, weapons, maps and objects raised from ships sunk off Anzio.

q.t: Who replaced Major General Lucas in command of VI Corps at Anzio in February 1944?
q.x: Truscott, who had led US 3rd Infantry Division ashore, replaced Lucas on 22 February 1944 and commanded the May breakout.

aar.rem: Anzio was meant to unlock Cassino; instead it needed Cassino's fall to break out.

stops.notes: Admission price not stated on official pages seen. Museum is small; combine with the Beachhead and the Nettuno cemetery. Coordinates from TracesOfWar, not the museum.

stops.name: Sicily-Rome American Cemetery, Nettuno
stops.text: On the northern edge of Nettuno, inside the old Anzio beachhead, the American Battle Monuments Commission cemetery holds 7,858 American war dead on 77 acres. Most died in the campaigns from the landing in Sicily on 10 July 1943, through Salerno and the winter fighting, to the Anzio beachhead and the advance on Rome in June 1944. The white marble walls of the chapel carry 3,095 names of the missing. The memorial was designed by Murphy & Locraft and the grounds by Allyn R. Jennings; the cemetery was dedicated in 1956.
stops.look: Long curving rows of marble crosses and Stars of David on a lawn framed by Roman pines, leading to the chapel and the Tablets of the Missing. The memorial building has large maps of the Sicily and Italian campaigns. Staff in the visitor building can help find a grave.
stops.plan: Free; no booking. Open daily 9:00–17:00 (last entry 16:45), closed 25 December and 1 January. Piazzale Kennedy 1, Nettuno. Check the ABMC website before you go.

aar.ev: Americans killed from Sicily to Rome are buried inside the old Anzio beachhead.
aar.st: This cemetery lies inside the ground held by VI Corps during the Anzio beachhead battles. It holds 7,858 American dead from the Sicily landing to the capture of Rome, and the chapel names 3,095 missing. Today long rows of marble headstones under Roman pines lead to a chapel and a memorial building with large campaign maps.
aar.rem: The cemetery stands inside the beachhead that Allied troops held for four months.

stops.notes: Wikipedia also mentions 7,861 headstones; 7,858 burials used here.

stops.name: Fosse Ardeatine Mausoleum, Rome
stops.text: On 23 March 1944 Communist-led GAP partisans bombed a column of the 11th Company, 3rd Battalion, SS Police Regiment 'Bozen' in Via Rasella; 33 policemen eventually died. Hitler authorised a reprisal of ten Italians for each German killed. Herbert Kappler, head of the security police in Rome, drew up the list, using prisoners, Jews and others; Erich Priebke and Karl Hass led the killing squads. On 24 March 335 men and boys, five more than ordered, were shot in disused quarries on the Via Ardeatina, and the tunnels were blown to hide the bodies. The mausoleum, the result of a national competition, was inaugurated on 24 March 1949.
stops.look: You enter through a gate with bronze sculpture, then walk through the tunnels where the shooting took place. The mausoleum is a vast, low concrete slab over 335 identical tombs, plus one for all Italy's fallen of the liberation war. A small museum explains the events.
stops.plan: Mon–Fri 8:15–15:15, Sat–Sun 8:15–16:45. Entry has traditionally been free. Guided visits through ANFIM (info@anfim.org). Via Ardeatina 174, near the Appian Way catacombs. Check the website before you go.
stops.disputed: How much the Vatican knew in advance is debated: a Vatican note on the morning of 24 March expected a ten-for-one reprisal, and historians such as Robert Katz have argued Pius XII did too little, which his defenders reject.

aar.ev: German security police shoot 335 Roman prisoners and civilians in the Ardeatine quarries.
aar.st: After partisans bombed a German police column in Via Rasella on 23 March 1944, Hitler authorised a ten-for-one reprisal. Herbert Kappler's security police shot 335 men and boys in quarries on the Via Ardeatina the next day and blew the tunnels shut. Today you walk through the tunnels to a vast concrete mausoleum sheltering 335 identical tombs.
aar.rem: The reprisal was ordered at ten for one, and five more men were killed than even that order demanded.

stops.notes: Admission price not stated on the official site (traditionally free). Coordinates from Rome's official tourism site.

stops.name: Museum of the Liberation of Rome (Via Tasso)
stops.text: This late-1930s apartment block near St John Lateran was first rented to the German embassy. After the Germans took Rome in September 1943, the SS security police and SD under Herbert Kappler made it their headquarters, with a prison at number 145. More than 2,000 anti-fascists, resisters and Jews passed through its cells; many were tortured, and some were later shot at Forte Bravetta or the Fosse Ardeatine. When the Germans fled in June 1944 they left some prisoners behind. Princess Josepha Ruspoli donated the flats to the state in 1950, and the museum opened on 4 June 1955.
stops.look: Small former cells on several floors, some kept with prisoners' scratched graffiti on the walls. Displays cover the occupation, the round-up of Rome's Jews, the Resistance and the Ardeatine massacre, with documents, photographs and personal objects.
stops.plan: Open daily 9:00–19:00, including Sundays and holidays; closed some holidays and 14–16 August. Free (voluntary donation). Booking required only for groups over six. Free guided visit first Sunday of the month at 10:30. Metro Manzoni.
links: Museum of the Liberation of Rome (Wikipedia)

aar.ev: Kappler's SS security police turn an apartment block into a prison and interrogation centre.
aar.st: From September 1943 the SS security police under Herbert Kappler ran their headquarters and prison here. More than 2,000 people passed through its cells, many of them tortured, and some later died at the Fosse Ardeatine. Today the former cells hold displays on the occupation and Resistance, and some walls still carry prisoners' graffiti.
aar.rem: Victims of the Fosse Ardeatine were taken from these cells.

stops.notes: Treated as solemn (former prison and torture site).

stops.name: Lascaris War Rooms, Valletta
stops.text: Work on these tunnels beneath the Upper Barrakka Gardens and the Saluting Battery began in 1940, during the siege, and was finished in early 1943. They held the War Headquarters from which Malta's defence was run, including fighter control rooms that directed RAF squadrons against Axis raids. In July 1943 the complex served as the advance Allied headquarters for Operation Husky, the invasion of Sicily, with Eisenhower, Admiral Cunningham, General Montgomery and Air Chief Marshal Tedder working here. After the war it housed the Royal Navy's Mediterranean Fleet HQ and, from 1967, a NATO communications centre, until 1977. The heritage foundation Fondazzjoni Wirt Artna now runs it.
stops.look: A maze of rock-cut rooms deep under Valletta, with operations rooms restored with plotting tables, wall maps and figures, including the Sector Fighter Control room and the Operation Husky room. The ticket includes the separate Operation Husky Museum. Tickets can also be bought at the Saluting Battery above.
stops.plan: Mon–Sat 9:30–17:30 (last entry 17:00); closed Sundays and 24, 25, 31 Dec, 1 Jan, Good Friday and Easter. Adult €20, child €7, with audio guide; guided tours 10:30 and 12:30 (€5). Book online or at the entrance; check the website before you go.

aar.ev: Eisenhower and his commanders direct the invasion of Sicily from tunnels under Valletta.
aar.st: These tunnels under the Upper Barrakka Gardens were dug from 1940 and housed the War Headquarters that ran Malta's defence. In July 1943 Eisenhower, Cunningham, Montgomery and Tedder used them as the advance headquarters for the invasion of Sicily. Today restored operations rooms with plotting tables and wall maps lie deep in the rock, reached from Lascaris Ditch.

q.t: Which operation was directed from Lascaris as the Allies' advance headquarters in July 1943?
q.x: In July 1943 Eisenhower and his commanders used Lascaris as the advance headquarters for Operation Husky, the invasion of Sicily.

aar.rem: The rooms that defended Malta in 1942 helped launch the invasion of Europe in 1943.

stops.notes: Entry from Lascaris Ditch (walk through Ganado Gardens from the bus terminus) or from the Saluting Battery.

stops.name: National War Museum, Fort St Elmo, Valletta
stops.text: Fort St Elmo guards the mouth of Grand Harbour at the tip of Valletta. The National War Museum, in the Old Drill Hall of Lower St Elmo, tells the story of the siege of Malta from June 1940 to November 1942. On the first day the island's only fighters were a few obsolete Gloster Sea Gladiators of the Hal Far Fighter Flight, later nicknamed Faith, Hope and Charity. Between 20 March and 28 April 1942 the Luftwaffe flew 11,819 sorties and dropped 6,557 tons of bombs on Malta. On 15 April 1942 King George VI awarded the island the George Cross. The museum reopened in 2015 after the fort's restoration.
stops.look: The fuselage of Sea Gladiator N5520 'Faith', the George Cross itself, and the Willys jeep 'Husky' used by Eisenhower and by Roosevelt on his visit to Malta. The wider museum covers Malta's military history; the star-shaped fort walls overlook Grand Harbour.
stops.plan: Adults €10, concessions €7.50, children €5.50. Open daily; hours change by season and the Sunday In Guardia parade delays general entry to 12:00. Closed 24, 25, 31 Dec, 1 Jan and Good Friday. WWI section closed until further notice. Check the website before you go.
links: Fort St Elmo and National War Museum (Heritage Malta)

aar.ev: King George VI awards the George Cross to the whole island of Malta.
aar.st: When Italy declared war in June 1940, Malta's only fighters were a few obsolete Sea Gladiators at Hal Far. In March and April 1942 the Luftwaffe dropped more than 6,500 tons of bombs on the island, and on 15 April King George VI awarded Malta the George Cross. Today the museum shows the Gladiator 'Faith', the George Cross and Eisenhower's jeep 'Husky'.

q.t: What were Malta's only fighter aircraft on the first day of the siege?
o: A few obsolete Gloster Sea Gladiators
q.x: In June 1940 the Hal Far Fighter Flight had only a few obsolete Sea Gladiators, later nicknamed Faith, Hope and Charity. The fuselage of 'Faith' is in this museum.

aar.rem: The George Cross on show here is the one awarded to the people of Malta in 1942.

stops.notes: Exact hours are only shown as images on Heritage Malta's opening-hours page and could not be read; coordinates taken from the official page's 'Get Directions' link.

stops.name: Malta at War Museum, Birgu
stops.text: Birgu faces Valletta across Grand Harbour, beside the dockyard that was a prime target throughout the siege. The museum occupies the Couvre Porte, a 17th-century counterguard whose 18th-century casemates became barracks. During the war they served as a police headquarters and then a civil defence centre. In 1940 the police began digging an air-raid shelter into the rock below, which grew into a small underground village where the town's people slept, gave birth and sheltered from raids. The Luftwaffe's arrival in Sicily in January 1941, when Ju 87s bombed HMS Illustrious in the harbour, brought the war to Birgu's doorstep. The museum is run by Fondazzjoni Wirt Artna.
stops.look: Above ground, nine galleries of wartime memorabilia and the wartime documentary 'Malta G.C.'. Below, a rock-cut shelter with dormitories, a surgery, a birth room, family cubicles and long tunnels. Allow time for the hourly English guided tour.
stops.plan: Mon–Sat 9:30–17:30 (last entry 17:00); closed Sundays and 24, 25, 31 Dec, 1 Jan, Good Friday and Easter. Adult €14, child €7; guided tour and audio guide included, English tours hourly 10:00–14:00. Check the website before you go.

aar.ev: Birgu's people move into rock-cut shelters as German bombers attack the dockyard.
aar.st: Birgu sits beside the Grand Harbour dockyard, a constant target during the siege. From 1940 the police dug an air-raid shelter into the rock below the Couvre Porte, and it grew into an underground village with dormitories, a surgery and a birth room. Today you can walk through the shelter tunnels and see nine galleries of wartime objects and the film 'Malta G.C.'.

q.t: Who first began digging the air-raid shelter under the Couvre Porte in 1940?
q.x: The shelter was begun by the police in 1940, whose headquarters were in the Couvre Porte barracks, and grew into a small underground village.

aar.rem: Malta's siege was survived underground, in shelters cut into the island's soft limestone.

stops.notes: Wikipedia's decimal coordinates are rounded; values used are the exact conversion of its DMS figures (35°53′7.5″N 14°31′21.6″E).

stops.name: Maleme German War Cemetery and Hill 107, Crete
stops.text: Hill 107 overlooks Maleme airfield, the key objective of the German airborne invasion of Crete. On 20 May 1941 German glider and parachute troops attacked the airfield and the hill, held by the New Zealand 22nd Battalion under Lieutenant Colonel Leslie Andrew. Out of contact with two of his companies and refused reinforcements by Brigadier Hargest, Andrew withdrew from the hill that night. On 21 May the Germans took the airfield and Ju 52 transports began flying in the 5th Mountain Division. The Allied counter-attack on the night of 21/22 May started late and failed in daylight. This decided the battle. The German cemetery on the hilltop was consecrated on 6 October 1974.
stops.look: Terraced graves with flat stones and small groups of crosses on the hilltop. From the edge you look straight down onto the old Maleme airfield runway and along the coast towards Chania, the ground the 22nd Battalion held. Small visitor building with information.
stops.plan: Free. Greek war-tourism portal lists it as always accessible and wheelchair-accessible, but the Volksbund page gives no hours, so check before you go. About 17 km west of Chania, signposted from the coast road at Maleme.
stops.disputed: Andrew's withdrawal from Hill 107 is still argued over: some blame him, others the brigade and division commanders who did not reinforce him or counter-attack quickly. Historians also differ on how much the Ultra intelligence that warned of the attack could have helped Freyberg.
links: German Military Cemetery Hill 107 (Hellenic War Museum)

aar.ev: German airborne troops attack Maleme airfield; Hill 107's defenders withdraw that night.
aar.st: On 20 May 1941 German glider and parachute troops attacked Maleme airfield and Hill 107, held by the New Zealand 22nd Battalion. Its commander withdrew that night, the airfield fell, and transport aircraft flew in mountain troops, which decided the battle for Crete. Today German graves cover the hilltop, which looks straight down onto the old airfield runway.
aar.rem: Losing one hill above one airfield cost the Allies Crete.

stops.notes: Graves: Volksbund gives 4,468 dead; the Hellenic War Museum portal gives 4,465. Stop is a cemetery on the exact battlefield, so conf HIGH.

stops.name: Souda Bay War Cemetery, Crete
stops.text: In May 1941 Commonwealth forces on Crete held five defence areas along the north coast. After the German airborne landings began on 20 May, Maleme fell and the line west of Chania broke on 26 May. Souda Bay became indefensible, and the troops retreated over the mountains to Sfakia. Between 28 and 31 May the Royal Navy evacuated about 18,000 men from Crete, most of them from Sfakia. Of 32,000 Commonwealth soldiers on the island, about 12,000 were captured and 2,000 killed. After the war, Australian War Graves Units moved the dead here from German-made burial grounds at Chania, Heraklion, Rethymno and Galatas and from isolated graves. About 1,500 Second World War servicemen lie here, 776 unidentified.
stops.look: A quiet, walled cemetery in an olive grove on the shore of Souda Bay, designed by Louis de Soissons. Rows of headstones run down towards the water. Look for the grave of the archaeologist and SOE officer John Pendlebury and for the many headstones marked 'Known unto God'.
stops.plan: Free; open permanently. About 5 km east of Chania: follow Souda Boulevard to the Ellis junction, then CWGC signs via Mavridaki Street. Car park near the entrance.

aar.ev: Commonwealth troops abandon Souda Bay and retreat across the mountains to Sfakia.
aar.st: After the line west of Chania broke on 26 May 1941, Souda Bay could not be held, and the troops retreated to Sfakia for evacuation by sea. About 12,000 were left behind as prisoners. Today about 1,500 servicemen, half of them unidentified, lie in a walled olive grove on the shore of Souda Bay.
aar.rem: Half the men buried here could not be identified.

stops.notes: CWGC uses the spelling 'Suda Bay'. Unidentified count: CWGC 776, TracesOfWar 778. The Souda naval base nearby is military: no photography of installations.

stops.name: Galatas, Crete: the battle for the village
stops.text: Galatas, a hill village south-west of Chania, anchored the line held by Colonel Howard Kippenberger's 10th Brigade and later by 4th New Zealand Brigade. On 25 May 1941 German mountain and parachute troops attacked after heavy bombing. A covering force on Pink Hill held out until overrun, and Brigadier Inglis threw in 23rd Battalion and improvised troops, including bandsmen and the Kiwi Concert Party. The Germans entered Galatas. That evening Kippenberger sent two companies of 23rd Battalion and the remnants of 18th Battalion in behind two light tanks of 3rd Hussars under Lieutenant Roy Farran. They charged into the square and drove the Germans out, but were too weak to stay and withdrew that night.
stops.look: The village square where the bayonet charge ended, the Allied memorial on the edge of the village and views to Pink Hill and the former 'Prison Valley' to the south. A small local museum covers the battle. Annual commemorations are held here each May.
stops.plan: Free to walk the village. A small Battle of Galatas museum is nearby but its opening hours could not be confirmed; check locally before you go. Galatas is about 6 km south-west of Chania.
stops.disputed: Sources differ on the tanks' unit: NZHistory names 7th Royal Tank Regiment, while most accounts, including Farran's own, place him in the 3rd Hussars.

aar.ev: New Zealanders charge back into Galatas behind two light tanks and clear the square.
aar.st: On 25 May 1941 German troops broke through on Pink Hill and entered Galatas. That evening two companies of 23rd Battalion and the remnants of 18th Battalion followed two light tanks into the village and drove the Germans out, but withdrew the same night. Today you can stand in the village square where the charge ended and visit the Allied memorial nearby.

q.t: What happened after the New Zealand counter-attack recaptured Galatas on 25 May 1941?
o: They held it until the evacuation
Greek troops took over the village
They withdrew that night, too weak to stay
q.x: The charge drove the Germans out, but with few men, no air support and civilians in the village, the New Zealanders pulled back to a new line west of Chania that night.

aar.rem: Galatas was a brilliant local counter-attack that could not change the outcome of the battle.

stops.notes: Coordinates are the Allied War Memorial on the edge of the village (TracesOfWar); the Pink Hill museum is at 35.49919, 23.963531 (TracesOfWar). Tank troop: NZHistory says 7th Royal Tank Regiment; most accounts (and Farran's own) say 3rd Hussars. Text uses 3rd Hussars — editor to verify. The Galatas Wikipedia pages could not be fetched.

stops.name: Rotterdam 1940: 'The Destroyed City' monument
stops.text: On 14 May 1940 German forces besieging Rotterdam sent an ultimatum to the Dutch commander, Colonel Scharroo. While negotiations were still under way, around 90 Heinkel He 111 bombers approached in two groups. Red flares signalled a recall; the southern group mostly turned back, but the north-eastern group bombed the old city centre. The fires that followed destroyed about 25,000 homes, and around 85,000 people were made homeless. Faced with a similar threat to Utrecht, the Dutch high command capitulated that evening, signing on 15 May. Ossip Zadkine's bronze 'De Verwoeste Stad' (The Destroyed City), unveiled on 15 May 1953, shows a figure with its heart torn out.
stops.look: A tall bronze figure, arms flung to the sky and a hole where the heart should be, stands on Plein 1940 at the head of the Leuvehaven, beside the Maritime Museum. Almost nothing old survives around it: the modern skyline is itself the legacy of the 1940 fire.
stops.plan: Public square, open at all times and free. Central Rotterdam, a short walk from Beurs or Leuvehaven metro stations. The 'fire boundary' (brandgrens) of 1940 is marked by lights across the city centre.
stops.disputed: Allied wartime propaganda claimed some 30,000 dead; the true toll was far lower (about 900 by older counts, with a 2022 official list giving at least 1,150 overall). Whether Kesselring's staff knew the raid had been called off before it went in is still argued.

aar.ev: German bombers destroy Rotterdam's old centre while surrender talks are still under way.
aar.st: On 14 May 1940 German bombers attacked Rotterdam while the Dutch commander was still negotiating. One group saw the recall flares and turned back; the other bombed, and the fire destroyed about 25,000 homes. The threat to Utrecht forced the Dutch to capitulate. Today Zadkine's bronze figure with its torn-out heart stands on Plein 1940, surrounded by a city rebuilt from scratch.
aar.rem: The Rotterdam raid, and the threat to bomb Utrecht next, ended Dutch resistance within five days.

stops.notes: Coordinates from Wikipedia have only four decimals. The statue is at the Leuvehaven end of Plein 1940 by the Maritime Museum.

stops.name: Grebbeberg battlefield and military cemetery
stops.text: The Grebbeberg, a wooded hill above the Rhine east of Rhenen, anchored the southern end of the Grebbe Line, the main Dutch defence position in 1940. From 11 to 13 May the German 207th Infantry Division and the SS regiment 'Der Führer' attacked troops of the Dutch II Corps, including the 8th Infantry Regiment. The Dutch held for three days, but a counter-attack on 13 May failed and the line was abandoned that night, the army falling back to the Water Line. The military cemetery (Militair Ereveld) was laid out on the hill on 20 May 1940; the German dead once buried here were later moved to Ysselsteyn.
stops.look: Rows of white headstones on a slope under beech woods, a Cross of Remembrance at the entrance, regimental monuments to the 8th and 22nd Infantry, and J.J.P. Oud's national army monument. In the woods behind, Dutch casemates and trench lines of the Grebbe Line survive.
stops.plan: The cemetery is free and open in daylight; it lies on the Grebbeweg (N225) about 2 km east of Rhenen. Walking routes lead to bunkers on the hill. A national commemoration is held here in May.
stops.disputed: German losses are given variously: an official figure of 238 killed, with estimates of 250–300.

aar.ev: German infantry and SS troops break the Grebbe Line on the hill above Rhenen.
