stops.disputed: Figures for Guderian's armour differ (771 or 788 tanks), and accounts disagree on whether Sedan town itself was taken without resistance on 12 May.

aar.ev: German infantry and engineers cross the Meuse at Sedan under a day-long air bombardment.
aar.st: After bombing that cut French communications, three panzer divisions forced the Meuse at Sedan on 13 May 1940. At Wadelincourt Feldwebel Walter Rubarth's team knocked out seven bunkers, and that evening the French 55th Infantry Division broke in the panic of Bulson. Today the narrow river and the overlooking Marfée heights show how small the obstacle was once the defence cracked.

q.t: What happened to the French 55th Infantry Division on the evening of 13 May?
o: It collapsed in the 'panic of Bulson'
q.x: False reports of German tanks set off the 'panic of Bulson', and the division fell apart behind the river line.

aar.rem: The Battle of France was decided at a narrow river crossing in three days.

stops.notes: Coordinates are the Wikipedia battle point (AREA). I could not verify a specific visitable bunker or memorial at Sedan before fetching was rate-limited; editor may want to add one (e.g. a preserved casemate on the Marfée heights) with its own coordinates.

stops.name: Fort de Schoenenbourg (Maginot Line)
stops.text: Schoenenbourg is a gros ouvrage of the Maginot Line, with six combat blocks and two entrances linked by deep tunnels, manned in 1939 by 491 men and 17 officers under Commandant Reynier. In June 1940, with the line outflanked, it held out alone: Stukas attacked on 19, 20 and 21 June, and from 21 June 420 mm siege mortars shelled it for three days. Its walls cracked but it kept firing; over the campaign it fired more than 17,000 shells and took over 3,000 shells and 160 bombs. Undefeated, it surrendered on 1 July 1940 under the armistice.
stops.look: A walk of several kilometres through tunnels 30 metres underground, past barracks, kitchens, the power station and magazines, to the combat blocks and a retractable gun turret. Above ground, the craters of 1940 are still visible.
stops.plan: Self-guided visits start at Block 7, the ammunition entrance. Hours and prices for 2026 could not be confirmed. Underground temperature is low, so bring a warm layer; check the website before you go.

aar.ev: German 420 mm siege mortars pound a Maginot fort that keeps on firing.
aar.st: With the Maginot Line outflanked, Schoenenbourg fought on alone in June 1940, taking Stuka attacks and three days of fire from 420 mm mortars. Its walls cracked but it was never taken, and it surrendered only under the armistice on 1 July. Today visitors walk its deep tunnels from the ammunition entrance to the combat blocks, and bomb craters still pit the ground above.

q.t: How did Schoenenbourg's garrison come to surrender?
o: Under the terms of the armistice, undefeated
After German infantry stormed the blocks
q.x: Despite heavy bombing and shelling, the fort was never taken; it surrendered on 1 July 1940 under the armistice terms.

aar.rem: The Maginot forts did what they were built for, but the Germans went round them.

stops.notes: Coordinates from Wikipedia DMS (seconds precision) for the ouvrage, not necessarily the Block 7 visitor entrance, hence MEDIUM. Run by the Association des Amis de la Ligne Maginot d'Alsace (tours since 1987). The official site's text could not be read. The tunnel-length and depth figures in 'look' are from general knowledge; editor please confirm.

stops.name: Musée de la Libération de Paris – Leclerc – Jean Moulin
stops.text: The museum opened on 25 August 2019, the 75th anniversary of the Liberation, in the 18th-century Ledoux pavilions on Place Denfert-Rochereau. It brings together collections on General Philippe Leclerc, whose French 2nd Armoured Division entered Paris on 24–25 August 1944, and on Jean Moulin, de Gaulle's envoy who unified the Resistance and died after his arrest in 1943. Beneath the building is the underground command post of Colonel Henri Rol-Tanguy, commander of the Paris-region FFI, from which the uprising of 19–25 August 1944 was directed.
stops.look: Exhibition rooms on occupation, resistance and liberation, with Leclerc and Moulin material, then a descent of about a hundred steps to Rol-Tanguy's command post, a concrete civil-defence shelter with its original telephones and fittings.
stops.plan: Not verified in October 2026 (official site unreachable). The permanent collection has been free and the museum closed on Mondays; the command-post visit is by timed slot. Check the website before you go.
links: Musée de la Libération de Paris (official)

aar.ev: Leclerc's French armour enters Paris as the Resistance uprising directed from beneath this square succeeds.
aar.st: From 19 August 1944 the Paris Resistance rose against the German garrison, directed by Colonel Rol-Tanguy from an underground shelter beneath Place Denfert-Rochereau. Leclerc's French 2nd Armoured Division entered the city on 24–25 August and the German garrison surrendered. Today the museum tells the story of occupation and liberation and leads down to Rol-Tanguy's command post.

q.t: Who directed the Paris uprising from the shelter under this museum?
q.x: Rol-Tanguy, FFI commander for the Paris region, ran the August 1944 uprising from the underground command post here.

aar.rem: Paris was liberated partly from underneath: the uprising's headquarters was a bomb shelter here.

stops.notes: UNVERIFIED: no source page could be opened for this stop (Wikipedia EN/FR and the official site all failed or were rate-limited). Coordinates left null rather than estimated; all facts are from general knowledge and need checking. Address: 4 avenue du Colonel Henri Rol-Tanguy, 75014 Paris (from memory).

stops.name: Mont-Valérien memorial, Suresnes
stops.text: Between 1941 and 1944 the German army shot 1,008 men at Fort Mont-Valérien, a 19th-century fort above the Seine west of Paris; most were resistance fighters and hostages. Prisoners waited in a disused chapel and were taken to a clearing about 100 metres away to be shot. Among them were the naval officer Honoré d'Estienne d'Orves on 29 August 1941, the communist deputy Gabriel Péri on 15 December 1941, and Missak Manouchian and members of his FTP-MOI group, the 'Affiche Rouge', on 21 February 1944. De Gaulle consecrated the site as a memorial on 18 June 1945.
stops.look: The Memorial of Fighting France, a long wall with a large Cross of Lorraine, stands below the fort. A path leads up to the chapel, with graffiti left by the condemned, and to the execution clearing, where a monument records the names of those shot.
stops.plan: Not verified in October 2026 (official site unreachable). The memorial is managed by the Ministry of the Armed Forces; visits to the chapel and clearing have been free, partly by guided tour. Check the website before you go.

aar.ev: Missak Manouchian and members of his resistance group are shot in the clearing below the fort.
aar.st: The German army shot 1,008 men here between 1941 and 1944, most of them resistance fighters and hostages, after holding them in the fort's old chapel. Manouchian's FTP-MOI group was executed on 21 February 1944. Today the Memorial of Fighting France, with its Cross of Lorraine, stands below the path to the chapel and the clearing.
aar.rem: Mont-Valérien was the main German execution site in France.

stops.notes: Coordinates left null: Wikipedia page had none and the official site was rate-limited; do not estimate. The fort itself is an active military site; the memorial area is visitable. 1960 inauguration of the Memorial of Fighting France and the 2003 bell monument with names are from general knowledge, not verified, so the text keeps them general.

stops.name: Mémorial de la Shoah, Paris
stops.text: Around 76,000 Jews were deported from France between 1942 and 1944, the great majority to Auschwitz, with the help of the Vichy authorities and French police; few returned. The Mémorial de la Shoah in the Marais, formerly the Memorial of the Unknown Jewish Martyr, reopened in its present form on 27 January 2005, inaugurated by President Jacques Chirac. It combines a museum, archive and memorial. The crypt holds ashes from the death camps and the Warsaw Ghetto, buried in 1957 in soil from Israel.
stops.look: In the forecourt, the Wall of Names lists about 76,000 deported Jews by year of deportation. Outside, the Wall of the Righteous honours those recognised by Yad Vashem for saving Jews in France. Inside are the crypt, the permanent exhibition and a room of photographs of deported children.
stops.plan: Not verified in October 2026 (official site unreachable). Entry has been free, with a security check at the door; closed on Saturdays and some Jewish holidays. Check the website before you go.

aar.ev: Mass arrests of Jews in Paris begin the main wave of deportations from France.
aar.st: Around 76,000 Jews were deported from France between 1942 and 1944, most to Auschwitz; few came back. The memorial in the Marais, reopened in 2005, combines a museum, archive and crypt holding ashes from the camps. Today the Wall of Names lists the deported by year, and the Wall of the Righteous honours those who hid and saved Jews.
aar.rem: Every name on the wall is a person deported from France.

stops.notes: Address 17 rue Geoffroy-l'Asnier, 75004 (Wikipedia). 'plan' and the children's photo room from general knowledge; official site rate-limited. Vel d'Hiv date (16 July 1942) used for 'sort'/aar is well established but not on the page I opened. The memorial also runs the Drancy memorial (former transit camp) north of Paris, worth a separate stop if verified later.

stops.name: Reims Surrender Museum (Musée de la Reddition)
stops.text: In 1945 a technical school in Reims, today the Lycée Franklin-Roosevelt, was Eisenhower's forward headquarters (SHAEF). At 02:41 on 7 May 1945, in the map room, General Alfred Jodl signed the unconditional surrender of all German forces, with Admiral von Friedeburg and Major Wilhelm Oxenius. General Walter Bedell Smith signed for the Allies, Soviet General Ivan Susloparov signed on his own initiative without Moscow's approval, and French General François Sevez signed as a witness. Stalin insisted on a second signing in Berlin, so the official date of capitulation remained 8 May. The museum opened in 1985.
stops.look: The war room is preserved as it was on 7 May 1945, its walls still covered with the operations maps, with the table where the surrender was signed. Other rooms show a film in four languages, uniforms, medals and newspapers of the day.
stops.plan: Not verified in October 2026 (city museum site unreachable). Address: 12 rue Franklin Roosevelt, Reims. Check the website before you go.
stops.disputed: Russia and the West still date the end differently: the Reims signing of 7 May took effect on 8 May, but the Soviet Union treated the Berlin ratification late on 8 May (9 May Moscow time) as the real surrender.

aar.ev: General Jodl signs Germany's unconditional surrender in Eisenhower's map room at Reims.
aar.st: At 02:41 on 7 May 1945 Jodl signed the surrender of all German forces at SHAEF headquarters in a Reims school. Bedell Smith signed for the Allies, Susloparov for the Soviets without Moscow's approval, and Sevez as a French witness; Stalin insisted on a second signing in Berlin. Today the war room is preserved with its original wall maps and the signing table.

q.t: Why was the surrender signed a second time in Berlin?
o: Stalin insisted, as his envoy had signed without Moscow's approval
Eisenhower wanted a ceremony in Germany
q.x: Soviet General Susloparov signed at Reims on his own initiative; Stalin demanded a fuller signing in Berlin, and 8 May stayed the official date.

aar.rem: The war in Europe ended on paper in a Reims schoolroom at 02:41 on 7 May 1945.

stops.notes: Coordinates left null: French Wikipedia's coordinate field is blank and other sources were rate-limited; do not estimate. Official page is on the Reims museums site (musees-reims.fr), not opened. Detail 'Stalin insisted' and the Soviet date dispute are well established but only partly in the page opened ('official date remained 8 May').

stops.name: Natzweiler-Struthof
stops.text: The SS opened Natzweiler-Struthof on 1 May 1941 at 800 metres in the Vosges, beside a quarry, in Alsace annexed by Germany. About 52,000 prisoners of 32 nationalities passed through it and its subcamps, many of them Nacht und Nebel prisoners from resistance movements. In 1943, 86 Jewish people selected at Auschwitz were gassed here for August Hirt's skeleton collection at Strasbourg university. On 6 July 1944 four British SOE agents, Andrée Borrel, Vera Leigh, Diana Rowden and Sonya Olschanezky, were executed. The camp was evacuated in early September 1944 and found by the French First Army on 23 November.
stops.look: Terraces of the camp descend the hillside inside barbed wire, with the gallows, the crematorium and cell block, and a museum barrack. Above stand the national necropolis and the tall memorial to the deported. The European Centre of Deported Resistance Members is at the entrance; the gas chamber lies about 2 km down the road.
stops.plan: The official site currently warns that access to the camp may be partly closed after weather damage, while the European Centre and museum barrack stay open. Hours and prices for 2026 were not available; check the website before you go.
stops.disputed: English Wikipedia gives about 22,000 deaths in the camp and subcamps; French Wikipedia gives about 17,000 plus about 5,000 on the evacuation marches, and notes many executions were never recorded.

aar.ev: French troops reach the empty Natzweiler-Struthof camp high in the Vosges.
aar.st: The SS opened Natzweiler-Struthof in 1941 for prisoners from across occupied Europe, many of them resistance fighters held under Nacht und Nebel. Four SOE women were executed here in July 1944, and the camp was emptied in September before French troops found it in November. Today the camp terraces, crematorium and museum barrack lie below the memorial to the deported.
aar.rem: Struthof was the only concentration camp the Nazis built on French soil.

stops.notes: Coordinates from German Wikipedia (DMS to the second, 48°27′24″N 7°15′14″E), camp area; not necessarily the visitor-centre entrance, hence MEDIUM. Weather notice was on struthof.fr when read in October 2026. Wikipedia notes the museum was burned by neo-Nazis in 1976 and reopened in 1980. 'Only camp on French soil' is the standard description (Alsace was annexed at the time).

stops.name: Westerplatte, Gdańsk
stops.text: At about 04:45 on 1 September 1939 the old German battleship Schleswig-Holstein, moored in Danzig harbour, opened fire on the Polish Military Transit Depot on the Westerplatte peninsula. Major Henryk Sucharski and his deputy, Captain Franciszek Dąbrowski, held the depot with a garrison of roughly 200 men in guardhouses and a concrete barracks. The first assault by marines from the ship failed, and the Poles held out for a week against naval gunfire, artillery and air raids. A white flag went up at 09:45 on 7 September. Fifteen defenders were killed. Westerplatte's long defence became the founding symbol of Polish resistance.
stops.look: A wooded peninsula at the harbour mouth. Walk past the ruined barracks and surviving guardhouses to the tall Monument of the Coast Defenders (1966) on its mound. The old depot power station is now a Visitor Centre with an exhibition on recent archaeological finds.
stops.plan: Grounds are open. The Visitor Centre opened in 2025; it was opening 09:00–16:00 in October. The site is being developed into an open-air museum by the Museum of the Second World War, so expect works. Check the website before you go.
stops.disputed: The garrison was long given as 182 men; recent research suggests 210–240. Historians also debate Sucharski's conduct: some accounts say he broke down and urged early surrender, leaving Dąbrowski effectively in command.
links: Museum of the Second World War (official)

aar.ev: A German battleship opens fire on the Polish depot, and the garrison holds out for a week.
aar.st: At about 04:45 on 1 September 1939 the battleship Schleswig-Holstein opened fire on the Polish Military Transit Depot at Westerplatte. Roughly 200 men under Major Sucharski and Captain Dąbrowski beat off the first assault and held out against shells and air raids until 7 September. Today you walk past ruined barracks and guardhouses to the Monument of the Coast Defenders, with a Visitor Centre in the old power station.

q.t: Which German warship fired on Westerplatte at the start of the war?
q.x: The old battleship Schleswig-Holstein was moored in Danzig harbour on a courtesy visit and opened fire at about 04:45 on 1 September 1939.

aar.rem: A garrison of about 200 men held Westerplatte for seven days, and the defence became a symbol of Polish resistance.

stops.notes: Coordinates are Wikipedia's point for the battle on the peninsula, not a specific entrance. The site is under development as an open-air museum (Museum of the Second World War, Westerplatte branch); opening times for the Visitor Centre were shown as 09:00–16:00 in an October 2026 snapshot. Ticket prices for Westerplatte exhibitions could not be read from the official site.

stops.name: Polish Post Office, Gdańsk
stops.text: The Polish Post Office in the Free City of Danzig was Polish state property and its staff were armed in secret. On 1 September 1939 the 56 people inside, most of them postal workers, held off Danzig police, SS and SA for about 15 hours. The Germans blew a hole in the wall with 600 kg of explosives and then poured petrol into the basement and set it alight. The director, Dr Jan Michoń, was shot as he came out with a white flag, and the rest surrendered. A court-martial condemned the survivors as illegal combatants, and they were shot at Zaspa on 5 October 1939.
stops.look: The red-brick post office still works as a post office, and the museum branch inside tells the story of the defence with the defenders' personal belongings. Look for bullet and grenade scars on the walls, and the steel monument to the defenders in the square outside.
stops.plan: Museum branch of Muzeum Gdańska, open seasonally April–September, daily 10:00–18:00; about 15 zł, free on Mondays. Closed in winter. The monument outside can be seen at any time. Check the website before you go.
stops.disputed: In 1998 a court in Lübeck annulled the 1939 death sentences, partly because the military penal law used had not yet come into force in Danzig when the defenders were tried.
links: Defence of the Polish Post Office in Danzig (Wikipedia)

aar.ev: Armed postal workers hold their post office against Danzig police and SS for fifteen hours.
aar.st: On 1 September 1939 the 56 people inside the Polish Post Office in Danzig, mostly postal workers, held off police, SS and SA for about 15 hours. The Germans breached the wall with explosives and set the basement on fire, and the survivors were later condemned and shot. Today the building still works as a post office, with bullet scars, a small museum inside and a monument in the square.

q.t: How did the Germans finally break the defence of the post office?
o: They cut off its water and waited
They breached the wall and set the basement on fire
q.x: A 600 kg explosive charge breached the wall, then petrol was poured into the basement and lit. The director was shot under a white flag and the rest surrendered.

aar.rem: The defenders were postal workers, not soldiers, and were executed as illegal combatants; a German court annulled their sentences in 1998.

stops.notes: Museum branch is seasonal (April–September) per Muzeum Gdańska's branches page, so it is likely closed for visits from October to March. Wikipedia gives two different dates for the sentences/executions; the execution date of 5 October 1939 is used here. The Museum of the Second World War is about 200 m away, so the two combine easily.

stops.name: Museum of the Second World War, Gdańsk
stops.text: Opened in March 2017 beside the Motława river, this is one of the largest museums of the war anywhere. The building, by the Gdynia studio Kwadrat, sinks most of its exhibition underground beneath a leaning tower. The permanent exhibition covers the whole war with a strong focus on civilians, occupation and the experience of Poland and Eastern Europe, from the road to war through Westerplatte, occupation terror and the Holocaust to the war's aftermath. It also runs the Westerplatte site. The museum was created by a team led by historian Paweł Machcewicz, and its exhibition became a political battleground after 2016.
stops.look: Look for the tilted red tower near the Polish Post Office. Inside, the main exhibition is underground and very large: reconstructed streets, vehicles including a Sherman and a T-34, and thousands of objects. Allow at least three hours and pace yourself.
stops.plan: Closed Mondays; generally open 10:00–18:00. Entry is by timed ticket; buy online in advance at bilety.muzeum1939.pl, as visitors without a booking have been turned away. Audio guide extra. Check the website before you go.
stops.disputed: After 2016 the government merged the museum with the Westerplatte museum and removed its founding director; new management changed parts of the exhibition. In 2020 the original authors won a copyright case over changes made without consulting them.
links: Museum of the Second World War (Wikipedia)
Museum of the Second World War (official)

aar.ev: Poland's great war museum opens beside the river, its exhibition buried deep underground.
aar.st: The Museum of the Second World War opened in March 2017, with most of its huge exhibition set underground beneath a leaning tower. It tells the whole war with a focus on civilians, occupation and Eastern Europe, and it also runs the Westerplatte site. Today you descend into reconstructed streets, vehicles and thousands of objects, and need at least three hours to do it justice.

q.t: Where is most of the museum's main exhibition?
o: On the upper floors of the tower
In the open air on the riverbank
q.x: The architects placed the exhibition halls below ground; the leaning tower above houses other functions and marks the museum on the skyline.

aar.rem: Book a timed ticket in advance and allow at least three hours; the post office is only a short walk away.

stops.notes: Opening pattern (closed Mondays, 10:00–18:00) taken from In Your Pocket because the museum's own hours page could not be loaded; In Your Pocket also says Tuesday closing is 16:00. Ticket prices not confirmed. Exhibits named in 'look' (Sherman, T-34) are from general knowledge, not verified in October 2026; editor may wish to cut.

stops.name: Stutthof Museum, Sztutowo
stops.coord_src: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stutthof_concentration_camp ; corrected after GPS check: OSM: Stutthof Museum, Muzealna 6
stops.text: Stutthof opened on 2 September 1939, the first German concentration camp set up outside Germany's borders in the war. Its first prisoners were Poles from Danzig and Pomerania, especially the educated and community leaders. About 110,000 people from many countries passed through it; around 63,000–65,000 died, including some 28,000 Jews, many of them women brought from the Baltic ghettos and from Auschwitz in 1944. From 1944 the camp also had a gas chamber. The evacuation began on 25 January 1945, and thousands died on the death march. Soviet troops reached the camp only on 9 May 1945. The memorial museum opened in 1962.
stops.look: Wooden barracks, the commandant's villa, the gas chamber and crematorium, and the 'Death Gate' through which prisoners entered. A large memorial stands by the crematorium. A short documentary film runs hourly in the cinema.
stops.plan: Open daily: 8:00–15:00 from October, 8:00–18:00 from May; last entry 30 minutes before closing. Films hourly. Check admission and guiding on the website before you go.

aar.ev: Germany opens its first wartime concentration camp outside its borders, in the forest near Danzig.
aar.st: Stutthof opened on 2 September 1939 for Polish prisoners from Danzig and Pomerania. About 110,000 people passed through it, including many Jewish women from the Baltic ghettos in 1944, and thousands died on the death march of January 1945. Today you see the Death Gate, wooden barracks, the gas chamber and crematorium, and a large memorial.
aar.rem: Stutthof opened the day after the war began, and was one of the last camps to be reached, on 9 May 1945.

stops.notes: Hours from stutthof.org (October 2026). Admission price could not be confirmed. 'Look' details (gas chamber, commandant's villa, barracks) are standard features of the site but were not individually re-checked on the official site. Sztutowo is about 40 km east of Gdańsk.

stops.name: Wolf's Lair, Gierłoż near Kętrzyn
stops.coord_src: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wolf%27s_Lair ; corrected after GPS check: OSM: Wolf's Lair visitor site
stops.text: Organisation Todt built this forest headquarters near Rastenburg in East Prussia, and Hitler moved in on 24 June 1941, two days after the invasion of the Soviet Union began. He spent more than 800 days here, more than anywhere else during the war. On 20 July 1944 Colonel Claus von Stauffenberg left a briefcase bomb at a midday situation conference. Because the meeting was held in a lightly built hut rather than a concrete bunker, the blast was weakened and Hitler survived with minor injuries. He left for the last time on 20 November 1944, and German engineers blew up the bunkers on 24–25 January 1945.
stops.look: Massive slabs of shattered concrete, some walls more than 2 m thick, lie tilted in the forest. Look for the plaque marking the site of the July 1944 conference hut, Hitler's bunker (No. 13) and Göring's bunker, the best preserved.
stops.plan: Open daily from 08:00; closes 16:00 October–February and as late as 20:00 May–August. Paid entry (about 30 PLN in season, 2026); local guides and audio guides available. A new official site offers online booking. Check the website before you go.

aar.ev: Stauffenberg's briefcase bomb explodes beside Hitler, who survives with minor injuries.
aar.st: Hitler spent more than 800 days at this forest headquarters in East Prussia. On 20 July 1944 Colonel von Stauffenberg left a briefcase bomb at a situation conference, but the meeting was in a light hut, the blast was weakened, and Hitler survived. Today huge slabs of blown-up concrete lie tilted among the trees, with a plaque at the site of the conference hut.

q.t: Why did Hitler survive Stauffenberg's bomb?
o: The meeting was in a light hut, which weakened the blast
He had left the room before the bomb was placed
q.x: The conference was held in a lightly built hut instead of a concrete bunker, so the blast vented outwards and Hitler escaped with minor injuries.

aar.rem: Hitler spent more time here than anywhere else in the war; the bunkers were blown up by the Germans themselves in January 1945.

stops.notes: Wikipedia lists 54.0804, 21.4941 in decimal but 54°04′49″N 21°29′39″E in DMS; the DMS conversion is used for more precision. The complex covers a large area, hence MEDIUM. The site is run by State Forests (Nadleśnictwo Srokowo); its State Forests page mentions a new official site, wilczy-szaniec.pl, with online booking, which could not be opened. Ticket price is from the independent wolfsschanze.pl. Ruins are unstable; keep to paths and do not climb where signs forbid it.

stops.name: Warsaw Rising Museum
stops.text: At 17:00 on 1 August 1944, 'W-hour', the Home Army rose against the German garrison of Warsaw as the Red Army approached the Vistula. The insurgents took much of the city but never linked their districts. From 5 August German forces massacred civilians in Wola, where this museum now stands, and in Ochota. Allied airdrops from Italy were small and often fell to the Germans, while the Soviets stayed on the far bank. After 63 days the Home Army surrendered on 2 October. Between 150,000 and 200,000 civilians died; the survivors were expelled and the Germans then demolished the city. The museum opened on 31 July 2004.
stops.look: Housed in a former tram power station in Wola. Look for the full-size B-24 Liberator in the hangar hall, the replica sewer you can crawl through, insurgent armbands and weapons, and the 3D film 'City of Ruins'. The Memorial Wall in the park lists thousands of the fallen.
stops.plan: Closed Tuesdays. Mon and Wed–Fri 08:00–18:00, Sat–Sun 10:00–18:00. Tickets 35 PLN (reduced 30 PLN), best bought online at bilety.1944.pl. Busy at weekends. Check the website before you go.
stops.disputed: Historians disagree on why the Red Army halted on the Vistula: most Polish and Western writers argue Stalin let the Germans destroy the Home Army; others, such as David Glantz, argue the Soviets were genuinely stopped by German defences.

aar.ev: At 17:00 the Home Army rises across Warsaw as Soviet troops near the Vistula.
aar.st: On 1 August 1944 the Home Army rose in Warsaw and fought for 63 days before surrendering on 2 October. German troops massacred civilians in Wola, where the museum stands, and afterwards demolished the city. Today the museum fills a former tram power station, with a full-size B-24 Liberator, a sewer you can crawl through and a Memorial Wall of the fallen.

q.t: At what time did the Warsaw Uprising officially begin on 1 August 1944?
q.x: The Home Army set 'W-hour' for 17:00 on 1 August, though in some places shooting started earlier.

aar.rem: Warsaw's 63-day rising was the largest single action by any European resistance movement, and the city was razed afterwards.

stops.notes: Hours and prices from 1944.pl (October 2026). Coordinates are TracesOfWar's point for the museum at Grzybowska 79. 'City of Ruins' film and Memorial Wall are from general knowledge, not re-checked this month.

stops.name: Ghetto Heroes Monument and POLIN Museum, Warsaw
stops.text: On 19 April 1943, when German forces entered the ghetto to complete its liquidation, Jewish fighters of the left-wing ŻOB under Mordechai Anielewicz and the right-wing ŻZW met them with pistols, grenades and petrol bombs. SS General Jürgen Stroop's troops burned the ghetto block by block. The ŻOB command bunker at Miła 18 fell on 8 May, and on 16 May Stroop blew up the Great Synagogue to mark the end. The monument by Nathan Rapoport, unveiled in 1948, stands where some of the first clashes took place. In 1970 West German Chancellor Willy Brandt knelt before it. The POLIN Museum of the History of Polish Jews faces it.
stops.look: Rapoport's bronze relief of fighters set in dark stone, with a procession of victims on the back. The labradorite is said to have been ordered by Albert Speer for Nazi monuments. Across the square, POLIN's glass building traces a thousand years of Polish Jewish life, including the ghetto.
stops.plan: Monument: open-air, always accessible, free. POLIN: closed Tuesdays; open 10:00–18:00, Saturday to 20:00; core exhibition free on Thursdays; last entry two hours before closing. Tickets at bilety.polin.pl. Check the website before you go.
stops.disputed: The ŻZW's role was long played down in Soviet-era and some Israeli accounts that presented the ŻOB as the sole force. Stroop reported 16 Germans killed; historians such as Israel Gutman think the real figure was higher.

aar.ev: Jewish fighters open fire as German troops enter the ghetto to complete its liquidation.
aar.st: On 19 April 1943 fighters of the ŻOB and ŻZW resisted the final liquidation of the Warsaw Ghetto, and Stroop's troops burned it block by block until 16 May. Rapoport's monument, unveiled in 1948, stands where some of the first clashes took place. Today the bronze fighters face the glass POLIN Museum, which tells a thousand years of Polish Jewish history.
aar.rem: The ghetto fighters held out for almost four weeks; Willy Brandt knelt at this monument in 1970.

stops.notes: Two stops in one: the Ghetto Heroes monument and POLIN (POLIN Wikipedia coordinates 52.24944, 20.99306, about 50 m away). Combine with Umschlagplatz (about 10 minutes' walk north) and Miła 18. POLIN ticket prices were not listed on the visit page.

stops.name: Umschlagplatz memorial, Warsaw
stops.text: The Umschlagplatz, a loading yard on Stawki Street beside the railway, was the place from which the Jews of the Warsaw Ghetto were sent to Treblinka. During the Grossaktion Warschau, from 22 July to 21 September 1942, some 254,000–265,000 people were marched here, held in the yard and nearby buildings, and loaded into freight wagons; about 300,000 were deported in all. Among them on 6 August 1942 were Janusz Korczak and the children of his orphanage. The memorial, by Hanna Szmalenberg and Władysław Klamerus, was unveiled on 18 April 1988, on the eve of the uprising's 45th anniversary.
stops.look: A white marble enclosure about 4 m high, shaped like an open goods wagon. Inside, 400 Polish and Jewish first names are carved, from Aba to Żanna, each standing for a thousand victims. A single tree is visible through the opening.
stops.plan: Open-air memorial on Stawki Street, accessible at any time and free. About 10 minutes' walk from the Ghetto Heroes Monument and POLIN.

aar.ev: The mass deportation of Warsaw's Jews to Treblinka begins from this railway yard.
aar.st: From 22 July to 21 September 1942 the Germans marched the Jews of the Warsaw Ghetto to this loading yard on Stawki Street and packed them into freight wagons bound for Treblinka. Janusz Korczak and his orphans were taken from here on 6 August. Today a white marble enclosure shaped like a goods wagon bears 400 first names, each standing for a thousand victims.
aar.rem: From this yard the Jews of Warsaw were sent to Treblinka; 400 names on the wall each stand for a thousand people.

stops.notes: No official website for the memorial itself. The Korczak deportation date (6 August 1942) and the 'single tree' are from general knowledge, not re-checked on a source this month. The memorial's form and 400 names are from Wikipedia.

stops.name: Treblinka Museum and memorial
stops.text: Treblinka II was a death camp of Operation Reinhard, the German plan to murder the Jews of the General Government. It opened on 23 July 1942, the day after the Warsaw deportations began, and trains brought Jews mainly from Warsaw and central Poland, as well as from abroad. Most were gassed within hours of arrival. On 2 August 1943 prisoners revolted and set fire to the camp; about 200 escaped and roughly 70 survived the war. The Germans dismantled the camp in autumn 1943 and planted a farm over it. Two kilometres away, the Treblinka I penal labour camp held over 20,000 prisoners, about half of whom died.
stops.look: Concrete sleepers mark the line of the railway spur. In the clearing where the gas chambers stood, a stone memorial rises from a field of thousands of jagged granite stones, many bearing the names of towns and villages. Paths lead to the Treblinka I gravel pit and the execution site.
stops.plan: Grounds of Treblinka II, Treblinka I and the execution site open 9:00–18:30 (April–October); 10 PLN, free Mondays. The museum building is being rebuilt and its exhibition is closed until further notice (2026). Closed Easter, 24–26 Dec and 1 Jan. Check the website before you go.
stops.disputed: Estimates of the number murdered at Treblinka II vary from about 800,000 to 925,000, because the Germans destroyed the records; Wikipedia also gives inconsistent figures for Treblinka I.

aar.ev: The first deportation train from Warsaw reaches the new death camp in the forest.
aar.st: Treblinka II opened on 23 July 1942 as part of Operation Reinhard, and trains brought Jews mainly from Warsaw and central Poland. On 2 August 1943 prisoners revolted and about 200 escaped. The Germans then dismantled the camp and planted a farm over it. Today concrete sleepers mark the rail spur, and a stone memorial stands among thousands of granite stones bearing the names of lost communities.
aar.rem: Almost nothing of the camp survives because the Germans destroyed it; the field of stones stands for the communities that ended here.

stops.notes: Museum building under reconstruction in 2026; exhibition closed until further notice; temporary office at Polna 1, Kosów Lacki. Winter (Nov–Mar) grounds hours are normally 8:00–16:00. Remote site, about 100 km north-east of Warsaw: a car is needed. The figure of about 17,000 memorial stones is commonly quoted but was not confirmed on the sources opened, so 'thousands' is used.

stops.name: State Museum at Majdanek, Lublin
stops.coord_src: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Majdanek_concentration_camp ; corrected after GPS check: OSM: Majdanek State Museum, Droga Męczenników Majdanka 67
stops.text: Majdanek, on the edge of Lublin, was set up by the SS in autumn 1941 as a prisoner-of-war and then concentration camp, and also served as a killing site for Jews in Operation Reinhard. On 3 November 1943, in Operation Harvest Festival (Aktion Erntefest), SS and police units shot about 18,400 Jews here in a single day, in trenches beside the crematorium, to the sound of loud music. The Red Army reached the camp in late July 1944, and because it was captured nearly intact it was the first major camp seen by Allied forces and reporters. The museum was founded that autumn.
stops.look: Wooden barracks, watchtowers and fences still stand in open ground within sight of Lublin's housing estates. See the gas chambers and the crematorium. Wiktor Tołkin's 1969 monument stands at the entrance, and the domed mausoleum at the far end holds a mound of victims' ashes.
stops.plan: Grounds free to visit; Polish-language guided tours at weekends, 25 PLN (reduced 20). From 7 April 2026 the side entrances from Cmentarna and Tetmajera streets are closed: use the main entrance on Droga Męczenników Majdanka. Check opening hours on the website before you go.
stops.disputed: The death toll has been revised sharply: from 360,000 (1948) and 235,000 (1992) to the museum's 2005 estimate of about 78,000, including 59,000 Jews, based partly on the Höfle Telegram.

aar.ev: In Operation Harvest Festival, SS units shoot about 18,400 Jews here in one day.
aar.st: Majdanek was set up on the edge of Lublin in 1941 and was both a concentration camp and a killing site for Jews. On 3 November 1943, in Operation Harvest Festival, SS and police shot about 18,400 Jews in trenches by the crematorium. Today barracks, watchtowers and gas chambers stand in open ground, with Tołkin's monument at the gate and the mausoleum of ashes beyond.
aar.rem: Captured almost intact in July 1944, Majdanek was the first major camp the world saw, within sight of a city.

stops.notes: General opening hours could not be read from majdanek.eu (page error). Free admission to the grounds is widely reported but was not shown on the page opened; the guided tour fee was. Wikipedia gives liberation as 22 July (infobox) and 24 July 1944 (text); 'late July' is used. Majdanek also administers Bełżec and Sobibór.

stops.name: Sobibór Museum and memorial
stops.text: Sobibór was the second Operation Reinhard death camp, built in forest beside the Chełm–Włodawa railway close to the Bug river. From May 1942 transports brought Jews from the Lublin district and from the Netherlands, Slovakia, Germany and elsewhere; most were gassed within hours. On 14 October 1943 prisoners led by Leon Feldhendler's escape committee and the Soviet-Jewish officer Alexander Pechersky killed several SS men with axes and knives and broke out. About 300 escaped, and roughly 60 survived the war. The Germans closed the camp soon after and planted trees over it.
stops.look: A modern museum building and memorial landscape in the pine forest. Follow the route of the path the victims were driven along to the gas chambers, whose foundations archaeologists uncovered, and the large area over the mass graves. The old railway station stands nearby.
stops.plan: Free admission. Closed Mondays, and on 1 and 6 January, Easter, Corpus Christi, 11 November and 24–31 December. Mostly outdoors; no cloakroom or lockers; free parking. Check opening hours on the website before you go.
stops.disputed: Estimates of the number murdered range from about 170,000 to 250,000.

aar.ev: Prisoners kill SS guards and break out of the death camp into the forest.
aar.st: Sobibór was a death camp of Operation Reinhard, receiving Jews from the Lublin district, the Netherlands and elsewhere from May 1942. On 14 October 1943 prisoners led by Feldhendler and Pechersky killed SS men and broke out; about 300 escaped and some 60 survived the war. Today a museum and memorial landscape in the forest mark the path to the gas chambers and the mass graves.
aar.rem: The Sobibór revolt was one of the few successful mass escapes from a death camp.

stops.notes: Opening hours were not shown on the official pages opened. The current museum building and the archaeological uncovering of the gas-chamber foundations (2014) are from general knowledge and were not confirmed on the sources opened this month. Transport origins listed are from general knowledge. Remote, near the Belarus border, about 80 km east of Lublin: car needed.

stops.name: Bełżec Museum and memorial
stops.text: Bełżec was the first of the three Operation Reinhard death camps, opening on 17 March 1942 beside the Lublin–Lwów railway. Transports brought Jews from the Lublin district, Galicia and Kraków. Within ten months the camp killed some 430,000 to 500,000 people, and the last transport arrived on 11 December 1942. The SS then dug up and burned the bodies and dismantled the camp by mid-1943. Only a handful of prisoners survived; of them only Rudolf Reder, who escaped in late 1942, left a full testimony. The memorial was opened in 2004 as a branch of the Majdanek museum.
stops.look: The whole camp area is covered with dark industrial slag, marking the mass graves. A path cuts down through it in a narrowing ravine to a wall inscribed with victims' first names. The names of the towns from which transports came line the perimeter. A museum building stands at the entrance.
stops.plan: Branch of the State Museum at Majdanek. Guided tours can be booked through rezerwacje@belzec.eu. Check opening hours and admission on the website before you go.
stops.disputed: Estimates vary: Wikipedia's text gives 430,000–500,000, its infobox 434,508–600,000, and historians from about 480,000 to 550,000. The figure of 434,508 comes from the Höfle Telegram up to the end of 1942.

aar.ev: The first Operation Reinhard death camp begins gassing Jews from Lublin and Galicia.
aar.st: Bełżec opened on 17 March 1942 as the first Operation Reinhard death camp, and within ten months it killed hundreds of thousands of Jews from the Lublin district, Galicia and Kraków. The SS then burned the bodies and dismantled the camp. Today the whole site is covered with dark slag over the graves, and a path cuts down through it to a wall of victims' names.
aar.rem: Bełżec had almost no survivors; Rudolf Reder's testimony is one of very few accounts from inside.

stops.notes: Opening hours and admission could not be read from belzec.eu (practical page did not load). The memorial design details (slag field, ravine path, names of towns) are from general knowledge and were not confirmed on a source opened this month. Bełżec is about 120 km south-east of Lublin, near the Ukrainian border.

stops.name: Auschwitz I (main camp), Oświęcim
stops.coord_src: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Auschwitz-Birkenau_State_Museum ; corrected after GPS check: OSM: Auschwitz I museum entrance
stops.text: The Germans turned a former Polish army barracks at Oświęcim, renamed Auschwitz, into a concentration camp in 1940. The first mass transport, 728 Polish political prisoners from Tarnów, arrived on 14 June 1940, and Poles were the main prisoners in the early years. In August and September 1941 the SS first tested Zyklon B on Soviet prisoners of war and sick inmates in the cellars of Block 11 and in the old crematorium. Auschwitz I remained the administrative centre of a complex that grew to include Birkenau and Monowitz. The Red Army's 1st Ukrainian Front liberated the camps on 27 January 1945.
stops.look: Brick blocks behind the 'Arbeit macht frei' gate. The national exhibitions in the blocks hold piles of victims' shoes, suitcases and hair. See Block 11, the 'death block', the execution wall in its yard, and the gas chamber and crematorium beside the SS hospital.
stops.plan: Grounds free, but a named entry card is required, booked only online at visit.auschwitz.org; none are sold on site. At most times entry is only with a paid guide (about 3.5 hours, Auschwitz I then Birkenau). Closed 1 Jan, 25 Dec, Easter Sunday. Check the website before you go.
stops.disputed: The gas chamber and crematorium at Auschwitz I were partly reconstructed by the museum after the war, a fact the museum states openly; Holocaust deniers misuse it.

aar.ev: The first mass transport of 728 Polish political prisoners arrives at the new camp.
aar.st: Auschwitz I was set up in a former Polish army barracks in 1940, and the first mass transport of Polish political prisoners arrived from Tarnów on 14 June. In 1941 the SS first tested Zyklon B here on Soviet prisoners of war. Today you pass through the 'Arbeit macht frei' gate into brick blocks holding victims' belongings, Block 11 and its execution wall, and the gas chamber.
aar.rem: Auschwitz began as a camp for Polish prisoners before it became the centre of the largest German killing complex.

stops.notes: BOOKING RULES (auschwitz.org, checked Oct 2026): (1) Admission to the grounds is free, but every visitor needs a personalised entry card; the number is limited. (2) Since 1 March 2026 entry cards are available ONLY online at visit.auschwitz.org, the only official system; none are sold at the main entrance, and the museum does not work with outside resellers. (3) Book up to about three months ahead; free guide-less passes have been bookable 90 to 7 days before the visit since May 2025. (4) For most of the day a guide-educator is compulsory: guide-free entry is allowed only late in the day (e.g. from 17:00 April–September, from 14:00 in January and November). Guided tours (paid; prices on visit.auschwitz.org) last about 3.5 hours, start at Auschwitz I and continue to Birkenau; offered in Polish, English, French, German, Italian, Spanish and Russian, more in summer; online sales close 15 minutes before a tour. (5) Arrive at least 30 minutes early for security. Bags no larger than 35 x 25 x 15 cm. Dress appropriately. (6) Last entry varies by month (14:00 in December to 19:00 in June–August); visitors may stay 90 minutes after last entry. (7) Closed 1 January, 25 December and Easter Sunday. Some areas (parts of Birkenau, part of Block 5, the Russian exhibition in Block 14) are temporarily closed. A free shuttle bus runs between Auschwitz I and Birkenau (per Wikivoyage). Coordinates are Wikipedia's Google Earth point for the museum entrance (labelled as such in the Auschwitz-Birkenau State Museum article). Oświęcim is about 60 km west of Kraków.

stops.name: Auschwitz II-Birkenau
stops.text: Construction of Birkenau began in October 1941 at Brzezinka, about 3 km from the main camp. It became the main killing centre of the Holocaust: by June 1943 crematoria II–V were working, with gas chambers in II and III. Most of the roughly 1.1 million people murdered at Auschwitz, about 90 per cent of them Jews, died here. In May 1944 a rail spur and ramp were completed inside the camp for the deportation of Hungary's Jews, who arrived from May to early July. On 7 October 1944 the Sonderkommando rose in revolt and destroyed Crematorium IV. The SS blew up the remaining crematoria before evacuating the camp in January 1945.
stops.look: Enter through the brick gatehouse, the 'Gate of Death', and see how vast the camp is. Follow the rails to the unloading ramp, then to the ruins of crematoria II and III and the International Monument. Wooden and brick barracks survive; elsewhere only chimneys remain.
stops.plan: Same entry card as Auschwitz I, booked online only at visit.auschwitz.org; guided tours continue here from Auschwitz I. A free shuttle bus links the two sites. Mostly outdoors and exposed: dress for the weather. Check the website before you go.
stops.disputed: During the communist period plaques at Birkenau gave four million victims; research led by the museum's historian Franciszek Piper established about 1.1 million, and the plaques were replaced in the 1990s.

aar.ev: Trains from Hungary unload at the new ramp inside the camp, beside the gas chambers.
aar.st: Birkenau was begun in October 1941 and became the main killing centre of the Holocaust, with four crematoria working by June 1943. In May 1944 a ramp was completed inside the camp for the transports of Hungarian Jews, and on 7 October 1944 the Sonderkommando revolted. Today you enter through the brick gatehouse and follow the rails to the ramp, the ruined crematoria and the International Monument.
aar.rem: Most of the victims of Auschwitz died at Birkenau; the ruins of the crematoria were left by the SS as they tried to hide the crime.

stops.notes: Coordinates are the 'Gate of Death' gatehouse from Komoot (not one of the brief's preferred sources; Wikipedia's World Heritage point 50.03889, 19.17500 lies inside the camp). Editor may wish to check against Wikidata. Same booking rules as Auschwitz I (see that stop's notes): entry card online only via visit.auschwitz.org since 1 March 2026. The 'sort' date (15 May 1944) marks the start of the Hungarian transports; Wikipedia gives only 'May 1944'. The Piper/four-million point is from general knowledge; the Wikipedia page opened gives 1.1 million but does not discuss the old figure.

stops.name: Oskar Schindler's Enamel Factory, Kraków
stops.text: In November 1939 the German businessman Oskar Schindler took over the bankrupt Rekord enamelware works at Lipowa 4 in Kraków's Zabłocie district and renamed it Deutsche Emailwarenfabrik (DEF). He first hired Jews from the ghetto because they were cheap, but came to protect them. When the ghetto was destroyed he persuaded Amon Göth, commandant of Płaszów, to let him run a sub-camp at the factory; by 1944 about 1,100 Jews worked here. In autumn 1944 he moved his workers to Brünnlitz in Moravia. About 1,200 people on his lists survived. The factory is now a branch of the Museum of Kraków.
stops.look: The original gate and administration building, with Schindler's office and a wall of photographs of the people he saved. The main exhibition, 'Kraków under Nazi Occupation 1939–1945', covers the whole city's war: the invasion, the ghetto, Płaszów and resistance, using reconstructed streets and rooms.
stops.plan: Tue–Sun 9:00–20:00, Mon 10:00–15:00 (free but limited and not bookable); closed the first Tuesday of each month. 60 PLN. Timed tickets online up to 90 days ahead; they often sell out, so book early and bring ID. Check the website before you go.
stops.disputed: Schindler's motives remain debated: he was a profiteer and Abwehr agent who first hired Jews as cheap labour. Several versions of 'Schindler's list' exist because it was retyped as conditions changed.

aar.ev: Oskar Schindler takes over a bankrupt enamel works and soon begins hiring Jews from Kraków.
aar.st: In November 1939 Oskar Schindler took over the Rekord enamel works and renamed it DEF. He first hired Jews because they were cheap, then protected them, running a sub-camp here and moving about 1,200 people to Brünnlitz in 1944. Today the original gate and offices house the Museum of Kraków's exhibition on the whole city under occupation, with Schindler's office at its heart.

q.t: Why did Schindler first employ Jewish workers at his factory?
o: They were cheaper than Polish workers
q.x: At first Schindler hired Jews from the ghetto because they cost less. Over time he came to protect them, and about 1,200 people on his lists survived.

aar.rem: The museum here is about all of Kraków under occupation, not only Schindler; book a timed ticket early.

stops.notes: Wikipedia gives the decimal 50.04740, 19.96175 and a slightly different DMS (50°02′51″N 19°57′42″E); the decimal is used. Wikipedia dates the exhibition to 2007; it is generally reported as opening in June 2010, which the editor may wish to check. Tickets for free Mondays cannot be booked online. Combine with the Eagle Pharmacy in the former ghetto (same ticket within 7 days). The Płaszów camp site, about 2 km south, is a possible extra stop not researched here.

stops.name: Brest: the U-boat base and the Naval Museum
stops.text: German troops entered Brest on 19 June 1940. From 1941 the Organisation Todt built a U-boat base of 15 basins, its roof thickened to 6.1 m, for the 1st and 9th U-boat Flotillas. It survived 82 raids; Tallboys from 617 Squadron pierced the roof but did little damage inside. After D-Day the city became Festung Brest under General Hermann-Bernhard Ramcke. US VIII Corps besieged it from 7 August to 19 September 1944, taking about 38,000 prisoners; the old city was razed and the port wrecked. On 9 September an explosion in the Sadi-Carnot shelter killed 371 French civilians.
stops.look: The medieval château, still the seat of the Maritime Prefecture, houses the National Naval Museum, with ship models, paintings and the harbour's naval history. Its ramparts look over the military port; the U-boat base lies inside the naval zone and cannot be visited. The Sadi-Carnot shelter, with its memorial, is in the city centre.
stops.plan: Naval Museum: 1 Apr–30 Sep daily 10:00–18:30; 1 Oct–31 Mar 13:30–18:30, closed Tuesdays. Adult €12, reduced €10; online booking available. The U-boat base is not open to the public.
stops.disputed: Sources give different dates for the end of the siege, from 18 to 23 September 1944, depending on whether they count the city, Ramcke's own surrender or the last outposts. The cause of the Sadi-Carnot explosion is also uncertain.

aar.ev: After six weeks of siege, the German garrison of Festung Brest surrenders a ruined city.
aar.st: Brest's U-boat pens shrugged off 82 air raids, so after D-Day the Americans had to take the port by siege. US VIII Corps fought from 7 August to 19 September 1944 and captured about 38,000 Germans, but the city and port were destroyed. Today the château houses the National Naval Museum, overlooking a military port where the U-boat base is still off limits.

q.t: What happened to the U-boat pens when Tallboy bombs pierced the roof?
o: Damage inside was slight and the U-boats survived
q.x: Five Tallboys went through the roof, leaving 5-metre craters, but the damage inside was superficial and the U-boats survived.

aar.rem: The Allies won Brest but not its port: the Germans had wrecked it before surrendering.

stops.notes: Name shortened from the stop list. Coordinates are for the Naval Museum in the château. The U-boat base is in the active military port; French Wikipedia notes it is still used for repairs to navy training ships.

stops.name: Keroman submarine base, Lorient
stops.text: On 7 July 1940 Fritz-Julius Lemp's U-30 became the first U-boat to refuel at a French base, at Lorient. From November 1940 to March 1942 Admiral Dönitz directed the Atlantic campaign from a villa at Kernevel, facing the harbour. The Kriegsmarine built three huge pen blocks at Keroman from 1941; the largest, K3, could shelter 13 submarines under a roof over seven metres thick. The 2nd and 10th U-boat Flotillas were based here. Raids from January to February 1943 flattened nearly 90% of Lorient but left the base intact. The garrison held out until May 1945.
stops.look: The grey bulk of K1, K2 and K3 dominates the peninsula. Guided tours go inside K3. Nearby you can board the French submarine Flore (S645) and visit a 1942 bunker used to train submariners in escape, now the Musée sous-marin, as well as the Cité de la Voile.
stops.plan: K3 guided tours from €7 adult (tours also in English). Flore submarine: daily 10:00–18:00 in the autumn school holidays; other dates vary. Musée sous-marin: Sundays 14:00–18:00 all year, daily in summer. Book online at lorientlabase.fr; check the website before you go.
stops.disputed: The surrender of the Lorient pocket is given as 8 May 1945 by uboat.net; other accounts place the formal handover on 10 May.

aar.ev: U-30 puts into Lorient, the first U-boat to use a base on France's Atlantic coast.
aar.st: From July 1940 Lorient put U-boats days closer to the Atlantic convoy routes, and Dönitz ran the wolf packs from a villa at Kernevel. The Keroman pens, built from 1941, survived raids that flattened the town in 1943. Today guided tours enter the vast K3 block, and the submarine Flore and a submariners' rescue bunker are open nearby.

q.t: Where did Dönitz command the Atlantic U-boat campaign from 1940 to 1942?
o: A villa at Kernevel, facing Keroman
q.x: Dönitz's staff worked from a requisitioned house at Kernevel, across the water from the Keroman bunkers, from November 1940 to March 1942.

aar.rem: Bombing destroyed Lorient but not the U-boat pens it was aimed at.

stops.notes: Coordinates are for the K3 entrance (guided-tour meeting point). Wikipedia gives 47.72750, -3.36750 for the base. The French Navy used the base until 1997. 2026 opening hours were not fully published on the pages opened.

stops.name: Saint-Nazaire: U-boat base and Normandie dock
stops.text: Saint-Nazaire's 14-pen U-boat base, built from February 1941 to mid-1942, served the 6th and 7th Flotillas. Beside it lay the Normandie dry dock, the only Atlantic dock that could take the battleship Tirpitz. In Operation Chariot on 28 March 1942, the explosive-packed destroyer HMS Campbeltown, under Lieutenant Commander Stephen Beattie, rammed the dock gate at 01:34 while commandos of No. 2 Commando under Lieutenant Colonel Charles Newman wrecked installations. Campbeltown blew up around noon, and the dock was out of use until 1948. Of 612 men, 169 were killed and 215 captured; five Victoria Crosses were awarded.
stops.look: The vast concrete base, with a fortified lock of 1943–44 and a roof-top viewing terrace, now holds the Escal'Atlantic liner exhibition and the submarine Espadon. The Normandie dock (Forme Joubert) is close by, and a stele to the Chariot raiders stands in Petit-Maroc facing the Loire.
stops.plan: The base and the Chariot stele are freely accessible. Escal'Atlantic adult €15; submarine Espadon €6; timed slots recommended. A guided tour of the Chariot raid sites costs €6. Hours vary by month; check the website before you go.
stops.disputed: Figures for the raid differ: Wikipedia gives 612 men and 169 killed, while the Falmouth memorial gives 611 and 168 in its text and 622 on its plaque.

aar.ev: An explosive-packed British destroyer rams the gate of the only Atlantic dock big enough for Tirpitz.
aar.st: HMS Campbeltown rammed the Normandie dock gate at 01:34 while No. 2 Commando wrecked the port installations. She exploded around noon and the dock stayed out of use until 1948, but 169 of the 612 raiders were killed and 215 captured. Today the U-boat base holds Escal'Atlantic and the submarine Espadon, and the Normandie dock and Chariot stele are a short walk away.

q.t: Why was the Normandie dock the raid's target?
o: It was the main fuel store on the coast
It was the only Atlantic dock that could repair Tirpitz
q.x: Without it, Tirpitz had no dock on the Atlantic coast big enough for repairs, so the battleship was less likely to raid the convoy routes.

aar.rem: The raid aimed at a battleship by destroying the one dock that could repair it.

stops.notes: Name shortened. Coordinates from Wikipedia (base, 5 decimals: 47.27500, -2.20250). Chariot stele: 47.271922, -2.198703 (ryo.co). Whether the roof terrace is free was not stated in the brochure; I believe it is, but check. The raid led Dönitz to move his HQ from Lorient back to Paris (uboat.net).

stops.name: Oradour-sur-Glane: ruined village and Centre de la mémoire
stops.text: Four days after D-Day, the 1st Battalion of the SS Panzergrenadier Regiment 'Der Führer', part of the 2nd SS Panzer Division Das Reich, surrounded Oradour-sur-Glane. Its commander, Adolf Diekmann, acted after a fellow officer, Helmut Kämpfe, had been seized by the Resistance. The men were shot in barns and sheds, which were set alight; the women and children were locked in the church, which was set on fire. 642 people were killed. Marguerite Rouffanche escaped through a church window. In 1953 a Bordeaux military tribunal convicted 19 of 20 defendants, but an amnesty freed the Alsatian conscripts among them, causing lasting bitterness in the Limousin.
stops.look: The ruined village has been left as it was: burnt-out houses, the church, rusting cars, sewing machines and bicycles, tramlines along the main street, and plaques naming families. The Centre de la mémoire, at the entrance between the old and new villages, displays objects recovered from the ruins.
stops.plan: The ruins are reached through the Centre de la mémoire. Guided visits of the village start from the car-park reception point. Hours and prices for 2026 could not be confirmed; check the website before you go.
stops.disputed: The death toll is usually given as 642; a 2020 study identified a 643rd victim. The trigger for the massacre, the capture of Kämpfe, is debated as a motive.

aar.ev: An SS battalion surrounds Oradour-sur-Glane and destroys the village and nearly all its people.
aar.st: Four days after D-Day, troops of the Das Reich division shot the men of Oradour in barns and burned the women and children in the church; 642 people died. After the war de Gaulle decided the ruins should stay as they were and a new village was built alongside. Today you walk the silent main street past burnt-out houses, rusting cars and the church.
aar.rem: Oradour was left exactly as the SS left it, so that no one could forget.

stops.notes: Coordinates from a map link in a German Wikipedia footnote centred on the ruins (en Wikipedia gives 45.9280, 1.0410 for the commune). The official site oradour.org redirects to visitlimousin.com and gave no visitor details; 2026 hours/prices unverified. The last survivor, Robert Hébras, died in 2023. Visitors are asked to keep silence in the ruins.

tours.name: The whole war, west to east
tours.desc: Britain, Dunkirk, Normandy, France, the Ardennes, the Netherlands, Germany, Poland, Prague and Austria: one long drive in war order where the roads allow.

tours.name: Britain's war
tours.desc: The Blitz, the Battle of Britain, the codebreakers and Dover.

tours.name: Dunkirk and Normandy
tours.desc: 1940 and 1944 on the Channel coast: the evacuation, the rocket sites, the D-Day beaches and the Falaise Pocket.

tours.name: France: occupation, resistance, surrender
tours.desc: The U-boat pens, Oradour, Paris, Compiègne, Reims, the Maginot Line and Struthof.

tours.name: The Bulge, the Rhine and Arnhem
tours.desc: Luxembourg, Bastogne, the Ardennes, Remagen, Nijmegen, Arnhem and Amsterdam.

tours.name: Germany: Hamburg to Berlin
tours.desc: Bergen-Belsen, Hamburg, Peenemünde, the camps north of Berlin, Berlin itself and the Seelow Heights.

tours.name: Poland: the invasion, the Rising and the Holocaust
tours.desc: Gdańsk, the Wolf's Lair, Warsaw, the Operation Reinhard camps, Kraków and Auschwitz.

tours.name: Prague to the Alps
tours.desc: Prague, Lidice, Terezín, Dresden, Colditz, Buchenwald, Nuremberg, Dachau, Obersalzberg and Mauthausen.

tours.name: Norway
